shabbos.heading: Shabbos in the Gemara: Candles, Cholent and Modern Questions
shabbos.description: Shabbos in the Gemara: two candles (Shabbos 23), oneg Shabbos (Yevamos 93a), crockpots (Bava Basra 19a), photochromic glasses (Sanhedrin 77a).
shabbos.intro:
The Gemara treats Shabbos as precious, and it shows in small details. In Shabbos 23, Rebbe Shimon bar Yochai meets an old man carrying two bundles of myrtles, one for "zachor" and one for "shamor." [Light Up The Night](/daf/shabbos/23/light-up-the-night) explains that we light more than one candle for the same reason. One light would be enough to see by, but two show that we are honoring Shabbos. Rav Huna taught that one who is careful with Shabbos lights will have children who are talmidei chachamim.

Oneg Shabbos, enjoying Shabbos, can even justify a leniency. In [Oneg Shabbos](/daf/yevamos/93/oneg-shabbos), Rebbe Yannai separates ma'aser for a gift of fruit that has not yet arrived. A dream of "a splintered reed" worries him, but Rebbe Chiya tells him he ruled according to the truth (Yevamos 93a). Rabbi Sebrow adds the Rashba's view that oneg Shabbos is a Torah mitzvah.

Many articles apply old rules to new appliances. Chazal forbade hatmana, insulating food before Shabbos in something that adds heat. Is a crockpot hatmana? [Crockpot Controversies](/daf/bava-basra/19/crockpot-controversies) traces the debate, from Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach's reported last ruling to the Tosfos in Bava Basra 19a about flintstones. Lenses that darken in the sun raise a question too. [A Pair of Glasses, a Spoon, and a Bottle of Beer Walk Into a Halachic Debate](/daf/sanhedrin/77/a-pair-of-glasses-a-spoon-and-a-bottle-of-beer-walk-into-a-halachic-debate) weighs it with Sanhedrin 77a. And [Split Decision](/daf/pesachim/52/split-decision) asks whether someone who made an early Shabbos may ask another Jew to turn on a light.

muktzeh.heading: Muktzeh in the Gemara: What May Be Moved on Shabbos
muktzeh.description: Muktzeh in the Gemara: dirt set aside before yom tov (Beitzah 8b), pets and singing birds (Bava Metzia 46b), a live chick (Shabbos 45a), a get on Shabbos.
muktzeh.intro:
Muktzeh means items that may not be moved on Shabbos or yom tov. In general, something with no use when Shabbos begins is muktzeh. A rock in the garden is muktzeh, but a rock set aside before Shabbos as a doorstop is not. The Gemara in Beitzah 8b says Rava allowed a pile of dirt to be designated before Shabbos for covering a child's accident. [Why Your Pet Rock is Not Muktzeh](/daf/beitzah/8/why-your-pet-rock-is-not-muktzeh) explains a chiddush of Tosfos. On yom tov, muktzeh may be moved for the sake of food. The Magen Avraham adds that the item may be moved but not used.

Are animals muktzeh? Tosfos in Bava Metzia 46b says a cow may be used for kinyan chalipin, because animals have designated uses. Rav Yaakov Hagiz drew from this that a singing bird is not muktzeh. [Are Pets Muktzeh?](/daf/bava-metzia/46/are-pets-muktzeh) weighs this against the debate in Shabbos 45a over a live chick, and explains Rav Moshe Feinstein's view that a pet is not muktzeh.

[Muktzeh Marvels](/daf/gittin/77/muktzeh-marvels) asks why a get should be muktzeh at all, since it has a use. The Rosh links it to the oral law, which once could not be written down. [Calling Doctor Dolittle](/daf/shabbos/109/calling-doctor-dolittle) asks whether a trapped animal may be lifted to ease its pain. It also asks about moving baby fish to save them.

eruv.heading: Eruv in the Gemara: Shared Bread and Carrying on Shabbos
eruv.description: Eruv in the Gemara: a whole loaf from each neighbor, a toothpick fix, on a split esrog (Zevachim 105b), carrying on chol hamoed (Moed Katan 13a).
eruv.intro:
An eruv chatzeiros lets neighbors carry on Shabbos between their homes and a shared courtyard. Each family contributes bread, placed in one home, and this unites all the dwellings. Rebbe Yehoshua required every resident to give a whole loaf. In [Something To Pick At](/daf/eruvin/81/something-to-pick-at), Rabbi Sebrow explains why: for shalom, so no neighbor resents another's half portion. If a child tore the loaf in half, Rav Chisda allowed joining the pieces with toothpicks, as long as it looks whole.

[The Greatest Article Since Sliced Bread?](/daf/zevachim/105/the-greatest-article-since-sliced-bread) follows that toothpick from the eruv to lechem mishneh on Shabbos. The Rokeach extends Rav Chisda's ruling. The Panim Meiros objects, citing Tosfos in Zevachim 105b: a split esrog held together with toothpicks is still two halves. What about a full bag of sliced challah? The Netziv allows it, but Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach ruled that one should not rely on that.

Not every eruv article is about bread. The Mishnah in Eruvin asks how to square off a city before measuring its 2,000 amos of techum. [What’s In A Name?](/daf/eruvin/53/whats-in-a-name) uses Rav and Shmuel's dispute over the spelling of that word to talk about naming children after reshaim. [A Drive-Thru Eiruv](/daf/moed-katan/13/a-drive-thru-eiruv) asks whether carrying is forbidden on chol hamoed. The Chazon Ish checked his pockets, while the Shevet HaLevi disagrees, citing the Mishnah in Moed Katan 13a.

yom-tov.heading: Yom Tov in the Gemara: Cooking, Learning and Chol HaMoed
yom-tov.description: Yom Tov in the Gemara: eruv tavshilin (Pesachim 46), learning 30 days ahead (Pesachim 6a), and a knife Rava would not explain (Beitzah 28a).
yom-tov.intro:
On yom tov some melachos, like cooking, are permitted for the sake of food. But the cooking must be for yom tov itself. In [What’s Cooking?](/daf/pesachim/46/whats-cooking), Rabbi Sebrow explains the debate between Rav Chisda and Rabbah. Rav Chisda says yom tov and Shabbos are one unit of sanctity, so the rabbis only required an eruv tavshilin. Rabbah reasons that any food might be needed for uninvited guests who arrive on yom tov. The Mishnah Berurah therefore advises finishing Shabbos cooking while there is still time in the day.

Some yom tov leniencies may be kept but not taught. Shmuel ruled that flour may not be measured on yom tov, though a Tanna permitted it. In [Can You Keep A Secret?](/daf/beitzah/28/can-you-keep-a-secret), Rava is seen sharpening a knife on yom tov, yet he says he is only cleaning it (Beitzah 28a). This is "halachah v'ein morin kein," a ruling that is true but not taught to the public.

Preparing for yom tov starts early. The Gemara in Pesachim 6a says to learn the laws of Pesach 30 days before. [A Time To Learn](/daf/pesachim/6/a-time-to-learn) shows that this means starting on Purim. Why is a haircut forbidden on chol hamoed, even though it serves yom tov? [Haircuts on Chol Hamoed](/daf/nazir/38/haircuts-on-chol-hamoed) explains, and lists the exceptions, from a freed prisoner to a nazir. [Business Or Pleasure?](/daf/beitzah/36/business-or-pleasure) asks when gifts may be given on Shabbos and yom tov.

pesach.heading: Pesach in the Gemara: Chametz, Matzah and the Seder
pesach.description: Pesach in the Gemara: egg matzah and lechem oni (Pesachim 36a), lettuce for marror (Pesachim 39a), charoses (Pesachim 116a), selling chametz.
pesach.intro:
The Gemara in Pesachim 36a calls matzah lechem oni, poor man's bread. So matzah kneaded with wine, oil or honey is not chametz, but it cannot be used for the mitzvah at the Seder. [Yolk Tales](/daf/pesachim/36/yolk-tales) shows how this makes egg matzah "matzah ashirah," rich man's bread. The Shulchan Aruch allows it on erev Pesach. The Rema writes that the custom is not to eat it on Pesach, since a drop of water could make it chametz quickly.

Every item at the Seder has a reason. Lettuce is not bitter, so why use it for marror? In [Lettuce Discuss Marror](/daf/pesachim/39/lettuce-discuss-marror), Rabbi Sebrow brings the Gemara's answers. Its name "chasa" recalls Hashem's compassion, and it starts soft and turns hard, just as the Egyptians did. [Charoses: Bricks, Straws, and Blood](/daf/pesachim/116/charoses-bricks-straws-and-blood) explains why charoses recalls the mortar, and why the Rema wants spices that look like straw.

Before Pesach comes the chametz. [Searching Ourselves](/daf/pesachim/10/searching-ourselves) explains what to do if one forgot bedikas chametz, and why the chachamim do not fear the searcher will eat what he finds. [Chametz for Sale](/daf/avodah-zarah/63/chametz-for-sale) uses Avodah Zarah 63b to ask whether one may sell chametz he wants to keep. It also tells how Rav Dovid Feinstein bought challos right after Pesach, so as not to be machmir on someone else's parnassah.

sefiras-haomer.heading: Sefiras HaOmer in the Gemara: Counting Seven Complete Weeks
sefiras-haomer.description: Sefiras HaOmer in the Gemara: seven complete weeks and counting at night (Menachos 66a), and a boy who turns bar mitzvah mid-Omer (Sanhedrin 68).
sefiras-haomer.intro:
The Torah commands "seven complete weeks." The Gemara in Menachos 66a says this is why we begin counting at night, so that no night is missing from the first week. [Making Our Days Count](/daf/menachos/66/making-our-days-count) shows how the same idea keeps us from starting Shavuos early. It also brings Tosfos's question: the Torah says to count 50 days, so why do we count only 49?

Is counting the Omer still a Torah mitzvah? On the same daf, Ameimar counted days but not weeks, since today the count only commemorates the Beis HaMikdash. [Make Your Days Count](/daf/menachos/66/make-your-days-count) turns this into a lively shul conversation. If you said "tonight is the first night" without meaning to count, may you still count with a beracha? [Only In Omerica](/daf/sanhedrin/68/only-in-omerica) asks about a boy who becomes bar mitzvah in the middle of the Omer. The Eretz Tzvi proves from the ben sorer u'moreh in Sanhedrin that he may keep counting with a beracha. And [Hair-Raising Thoughts](/daf/bava-basra/113/hair-raising-thoughts) recalls Rebbe Akiva's 24,000 students, who perished for not showing each other respect.

shavuos.heading: Shavuos in the Gemara: Preparing to Receive the Torah
shavuos.description: Shavuos in the Gemara: learning its laws on the day (Megillah 32a), why Shavuos starts late (Menachos 66a), wheat from the sky (Menachos 69b).
shavuos.intro:
The Gemara in Megillah 32a says Moshe enacted that we study the laws of each yom tov on that yom tov, including Shavuos. But which masechta fits Shavuos? [Preparing for Shavuos: More Than Just Cheesecake](/daf/shevuos/7/preparing-for-shavuos-more-than-just-cheesecake) tells of young Pinchas Horowitz, later the Haflaah. He explained that Masechta Shavuos, about oaths, is perfect. At Har Sinai we took an oath to keep the Torah.

Why does Shavuos start so late at night? The Torah demands seven complete weeks of counting. [Making Our Days Count](/daf/menachos/66/making-our-days-count) explains that accepting Shavuos early would cut those weeks short. [Rise and Shine](/daf/yoma/21/rise-and-shine) brings the Shevet HaLevi's concern about davening properly after staying up all night. The Mishnah Berurah allows one who learned all night to daven before netz.

The Shavuos offering in the Beis HaMikdash was the Shtei HaLechem, two loaves from the new wheat of Eretz Yisrael. The Gemara in Menachos 69b tells of wheat that rained down on a merchant named Adi. Could it be used for the offering? [It’s Raining Wheat](/daf/menachos/69/its-raining-wheat) explains the views of Rashi and Tosfos, and links it to the oil of the Chanukah miracle.

rosh-hashanah.heading: Rosh Hashanah in the Gemara: Judgment, Kingship and Simanim
rosh-hashanah.description: Rosh Hashanah in the Gemara: judgment on Rosh Chodesh (Rosh Hashanah 8a), when crops are judged (Rosh Hashanah 16a), the simanim (Horayos 12b).
rosh-hashanah.intro:
The Mishnah teaches that the world is judged four times a year, and on Rosh Hashanah all people are judged. [Rosh Hashana in a Cemetery](/daf/rosh-hashanah/16/rosh-hashana-in-a-cemetery) asks how this fits a story in Berachos 18b. A pious man slept in a cemetery on Rosh Hashanah night and heard spirits speak of hail that would strike the crops. Tosfos on Rosh Hashanah 16a explains that crops are decreed on Pesach and only mentioned on Rosh Hashanah. Tosfos also teaches that public prayer helps even after a bad decree.

Rosh Hashanah is the only Torah holiday that falls on Rosh Chodesh. The Gemara in Rosh Hashanah 8a learns from this that it is the Day of Judgment. [Obviously, Rosh Hashana Falls Out on Rosh Chodesh](/daf/rosh-hashanah/8/obviously-rosh-hashana-falls-out-on-rosh-chodesh) explains why Mussaf skips the verses of the Rosh Chodesh offering. It also asks what happens if one says HaKeil HaKadosh on Rosh Hashanah night.

Abaye taught that on Rosh Hashanah one should gaze at gourd, rubia, leek, beets and dates (Horayos 12b). Yet Sanhedrin 65b forbids relying on omens. In [The Question of Omens](/daf/horayos/12/the-question-of-omens), Rabbi Sebrow brings the Meiri's answer. The simanim are reminders to do teshuvah, and the Yehi Ratzon turns our hearts to Hashem. Kingship is the theme of the day, even in bentching. [Find The Missing Word](/daf/berachos/49/find-the-missing-word) cites the Mateh Ephraim, who says to add "melech" in Ya'aleh V'yavo on Rosh Hashanah.

yom-kippur.heading: Yom Kippur in the Gemara: Atonement, Vows and the Fast
yom-kippur.description: Yom Kippur in the Gemara: Kol Nidrei and vows (Nedarim 77), a Kohen Gadol who bought his post (Yoma 18a), the teshuvah of Purim (Megillah 14a).
yom-kippur.intro:
Before Yom Kippur, the elders would urge the Kohen Gadol to read the passages about the day's service: "perhaps you never learned them" (Yoma 18a). Would anyone appoint such a Kohen Gadol? The Gemara admits that in the Second Beis HaMikdash, Yehoshua ben Gamla's appointment was bought. [An Ignorant Kohen Gadol?](/daf/yoma/18/an-ignorant-kohen-gadol) brings the Ritva's view. He grew into the role, and later made sure every town had teachers for its children.

Kol Nidrei raises a question. The Gemara says a beis din is not convened to annul vows on Shabbos, and Yom Kippur follows the same rules. [Void Where Prohibited](/daf/nedarim/77/void-where-prohibited) explains the Rivash's answer, and Rabbeinu Tam's view that Kol Nidrei is a declaration about future vows. That is why we come to shul early and say it before Yom Kippur begins.

[Required Eating on Yom Kippur?](/daf/shevuos/28/required-eating-on-yom-kippur) tells of the cholera year of 1848, when Rav Yisrael Salanter had the people of Vilna eat on Yom Kippur. Rabbi Sebrow examines the story and the idea of taking an oath before the fast. [Days of Teshuva](/daf/nazir/31/days-of-teshuva) links Yom Kippur to Purim. It also explains, from the Rema, why we say Yizkor: even the departed can gain atonement on this day.

sukkos.heading: Sukkos in the Gemara: The Sukkah and the Four Species
sukkos.description: Sukkos in the Gemara: a sukkah over 20 amos (Sukkah 2b), an elephant as a wall, Shammai's sukkah for a newborn (Yevamos 15a), and the lulav (Sukkah 42a).
sukkos.intro:
Maseches Sukkah opens with a rule: a sukkah taller than 20 amos is invalid. Rabbah explains that a person should be aware he is sitting in a sukkah, and the eye does not naturally look above 20 amos. [Standing Tall](/daf/sukkah/2/standing-tall) asks why the same reasoning applies to a Chanukah menorah, and even to Haman's gallows. It ends with a shul in England whose "sukkah" was a hole in the roof, saved by walls of stacked chairs.

Some cases are unusual. The Gemara discusses using a live elephant as a sukkah wall. [A Sukkah Made Out of Elephants](/daf/sukkah/23/a-sukkah-made-out-of-elephants) asks whether a non-kosher animal may be used for a mitzvah. The Rema forbids a shofar from one. In Yevamos 15a, Shammai's daughter-in-law gave birth over Sukkos, and he put schach over a hole in the roof above her bed. [A Sukkah for a Baby](/daf/yevamos/15/a-sukkah-for-a-baby) asks whom that sukkah was for. The P'nei Yehoshua answers: the newborn.

The lulav and esrog bring their own puzzles. In [Shaking Shailos](/daf/sukkah/42/shaking-shailos), two friends debate why some hold the esrog upside down before the beracha. They also ask how to lend a lulav on the first day. [What Bracha Do You Make on the Sukkah?](/daf/sukkah/56/what-bracha-do-you-make-on-the-sukkah) asks whether Shehechiyanu may be said when building the sukkah. It also explains why we say Leishev BaSukkah first (Sukkah 56a).

chanukah.heading: Chanukah in the Gemara: The Oil, the Menorah and the Miracle
chanukah.description: Chanukah in the Gemara: how the oil became tamei (Pesachim 16a), why eight days (Menachos 88a), and swapping wax candles for olive oil (Shevuos 11b).
chanukah.intro:
The Gemara in Shabbos says the Yevanim defiled the oil, and only one jug with the Kohen Gadol's seal was found. But Rav holds that liquids in the Beis HaMikdash could not become tamei (Pesachim 16a). How, then, was the oil defiled? [Pesachim 16a: Fueling the Flames of Chanukah](/daf/pesachim/16/pesachim-16a-fueling-the-flames-of-chanukah) brings several answers. One is that the oil had congealed and counted as a food. That leads to a modern question: does congealed olive oil fulfill the hiddur of olive oil?

The Beis Yosef famously asks why Chanukah is eight days, when there was enough oil for one. [A Burning Question](/daf/menachos/88/a-burning-question) tests answers against the Mishnah in Menachos 88a, from summer wicks to the Ner Ma'aravi. [Mitzvah Mission](/daf/chullin/7/mitzvah-mission) gives the mussar answer: the first night celebrates that oil burns at all, since nature is also Hashem's will. It begins with Rebbe Pinchas ben Yair and the river that split for him (Chullin 7a).

What if you set up wax candles and then the olive oil arrives? [Waxing About Oil](/daf/shevuos/11/waxing-about-oil) brings the Shevus Yaakov, who says to leave the candles. The Chacham Tzvi learns from the Parah Adumah in Shevuos 11b that one switches to the nicer item. [The Gist Of The Jugs](/daf/shevuos/9/the-gist-of-the-jugs) explains why Yaakov went back for small jugs. One view says the Chashmonaim found one of them over 1,000 years later.

purim.heading: Purim in the Gemara: The Megillah, Mishloach Manos and the Miracle
purim.description: Purim in the Gemara: why there is no Hallel (Megillah 14a), two portions of mishloach manos (Megillah 7b), Haman's descendants (Sanhedrin 96b).
purim.intro:
Why is Hallel not said on Purim? The Gemara in Megillah 14a gives two answers. Rav Nachman says reading the Megillah is our Hallel. Rava says Hallel does not fit, since the Jews were still Achashverosh's subjects. [Hallel On Purim: The Whole Megillah](/daf/megillah/14/hallel-on-purim-the-whole-megillah) asks what someone without a kosher Megillah should do. It explains that the Megillah thanks Hashem for hidden miracles.

Rav Yosef taught that mishloach manos means two portions of food to one person (Megillah 7b). Rebbe Yehuda Nesiah sent Rebbe Oshaya a calf's thigh and a bottle of wine. [Mishloach Manos From Rebbi to Talmid](/daf/megillah/7/mishloach-manos-from-rebbi-to-talmid) explains why Rebbe Oshaya replied that the mitzvah was fulfilled, even from a rebbi to his student. In [Drunk on Mitzvos](/daf/bava-metzia/23/drunk-on-mitzvos), Rabbi Sebrow reads Bava Metzia 23b with the Maharsha. A scholar may say he is drunk on Purim when he is not. Why would he? The article offers many answers.

The story itself raises questions. [When Purim Was on Pesach](/daf/megillah/16/when-purim-was-on-pesach) works out how Esther's three-day fast fell on Pesach (Megillah 16a). [Should Mordechai Have Bowed to Haman?](/daf/sanhedrin/61/should-mordechai-have-bowed-to-haman) weighs Sanhedrin 61b, which allows bowing out of respect. And [Haman’s Sons in Bnei Brak](/daf/sanhedrin/96/hamans-sons-in-bnei-brak) asks how Haman's descendants could convert and teach Torah, as Sanhedrin 96b says.

fast-days.heading: Fast Days in the Gemara: Fasting, Teshuvah and the Churban
fast-days.description: Fast Days in the Gemara: the 17th of Tammuz (Rosh Hashanah 18), fasting for rain (Taanis 15), and why Tu B'Av was a joyous day (Taanis 30b).
fast-days.intro:
The Mishnah says Beis Din sent messengers to announce Tishah B'Av, but not the 17th of Tammuz or Asarah B'Teves. Rav Papa explains that those fasts were once required only in times of harsh decrees. [Think Fast](/daf/rosh-hashanah/18/think-fast) uses this to answer a common question: may one shower on a minor fast? The Ritva says Klal Yisrael accepted these fasts without the stringencies of Tishah B'Av. The Mishnah Berurah still advises a ba'al nefesh to follow the Ramban.

In a drought, Beis Din decreed a series of communal fasts, up to 13 in all. [Not So Fast](/daf/taanis/16/not-so-fast) brings the Rambam's ruling that if rain falls in the middle, the community may end the fast. The Rosh explains why: they should thank Hashem right away, while the joy is fresh. The Gemara in Taanis 15 adds that these fasts do not begin on a Thursday, so food prices will not jump before Shabbos. [Something Fishy](/daf/taanis/15/something-fishy) carries that concern for prices to a boycott of costly fish.

Some fast on the 8th and 9th of Teves as well. [Ta’anis In Teves](/daf/megillah/9/taanis-in-teves) explores why, from the Greek translation of the Torah to the passing of Ezra HaSofer. Rabbi Sebrow ends with the Mishnah Berurah: the fast is only a preparation for teshuvah. And [Who Knows Fifteen?](/daf/taanis/30/who-knows-fifteen) explains why Tu B'Av, at the very end of Maseches Taanis, was one of the happiest days of the year.

rosh-chodesh.heading: Rosh Chodesh in the Gemara: The New Moon and Its Customs
rosh-chodesh.description: Rosh Chodesh in the Gemara: Rabban Gamliel's moon pictures (Avodah Zarah 43), four aliyos (Megillah 21b), and Chizkiyahu's leap month (Sanhedrin 12b).
rosh-chodesh.intro:
In the days of the Sanhedrin, Beis Din declared the new month based on witnesses who saw the moon. Rabban Gamliel kept pictures of the moon to help question them. But the Torah forbids making images of the moon. [Over the Moon](/daf/avodah-zarah/43/over-the-moon) explains the Gemara's answers. A non-Jew drew them for the sake of the mitzvah, and the Nasi was never alone, so no one would suspect him. Rav Dovid Feinstein said there is no need to cover moon pictures in children's textbooks today.

The Gemara in Megillah 21b says four people are called to the Torah on Rosh Chodesh, since it is not a workday. [A Rosh Chodesh Holiday](/daf/megillah/21/a-rosh-chodesh-holiday) brings Rashi's explanation: it is a holiday for women. It was their reward for refusing to give their jewelry for the Golden Calf. The Turei Even suggests it was once a holiday for everyone, because of the Korban Mussaf.

Some customs have deep roots. Why do many add "V'kapparas pesha" to Mussaf in a leap year? [A Rosh Chodesh Addition – Sometimes](/daf/sanhedrin/12/a-rosh-chodesh-addition-sometimes) traces it to Chizkiyahu. He added a leap month so the people could become tahor before Pesach, then asked Hashem's forgiveness (Sanhedrin 12b). [Our Better Halves](/daf/megillah/17/our-better-halves) explains why half Hallel on Rosh Chodesh is only a custom, and what happens if one says a verse out of order.

tefillah.heading: Tefillah in the Gemara: Davening From the Heart
tefillah.description: Tefillah in the Gemara: praying at length (Berachos 32b), standing like the Avodah (Zevachim 23b), the four like the dead (Nedarim 64b), eating in shul.
tefillah.intro:
The Gemara in Berachos 32b says that whoever davens at length will not be turned away empty-handed. Yet it also says that one whose prayer was not answered should daven again. [Prayer And Unity](/daf/berachos/32/prayer-and-unity) brings Rabbi Akiva Grunblatt's answer: every tefillah has an effect, though perhaps not the one we hoped for. Rabbi Sebrow ends with Rav Aryeh Levin's words to a widow about her tears.

Tefillah stands in place of the korbanos. Avodah done while sitting is invalid (Zevachim 23b), so Shemoneh Esrei is said standing. [Davening on a Plane](/daf/zevachim/23/davening-on-a-plane) explains when one may sit, from a rider on a donkey to a passenger on a plane. [The Avodah of Shemoneh Esrei](/daf/zevachim/46/the-avodah-of-shemoneh-esrei) tackles kavanah. The Chofetz Chaim compared it to dogs grabbing a vendor's rolls: if they grab, you grab too.

The Mishnah in Sotah says one may pray in any language, because Hashem wants a prayer from the heart. [Can One Daven in Klingon?](/daf/sotah/33/can-one-daven-in-klingon) asks, with a smile, what counts as a language. [A Powerful Tefillah](/daf/nedarim/64/a-powerful-tefillah) explains why the Gemara counts four kinds of people as if dead (Nedarim 64b). Tosfos says it is so we daven for them with more feeling. And [Don’t Talk, Just Daven](/daf/megillah/28/dont-talk-just-daven) asks how shuls serve tikkun or seudah shlishis, when Megillah 28a forbids eating in shul.

krias-shema.heading: Krias Shema in the Gemara: Kavanah, Timing and Integrity
krias-shema.description: Krias Shema in the Gemara: a chassan on his wedding night (Berachos 16b), davening on the road (Berachos 30a), and Rav Safra (Bava Basra 89a).
krias-shema.intro:
The Gemara in Berachos 16b exempts a chassan from Shema on his wedding night, since he cannot concentrate. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says a groom who says it anyway is showing off. [Beyond The Letter Of The Law](/daf/chullin/105/beyond-the-letter-of-the-law) notes that today the halachah is reversed: even a groom says Shema, because our usual concentration is so weak. In [Fasten Your Seatbelts](/daf/berachos/30/fasten-your-seatbelts), a traveler must choose. Should he daven Shemoneh Esrei early while standing, or wait and keep Shema right before it, while sitting? The Gemara in Berachos 30a records a dispute, and the halachah follows Levi and Shmuel's father.

The kohanim in the Beis HaMikdash had little time to daven, so the Sages set a minimum, including one beracha before Shema. [Wandering Jews](/daf/berachos/11/wandering-jews) learns from this, with the Rashba, that the berachos of Shema may be said out of order. [Oneg Shabbos](/daf/yevamos/93/oneg-shabbos) asks whether one may shop for Shabbos before saying the morning Shema. And [In All Honesty](/daf/bava-basra/89/in-all-honesty) tells how Rav Safra would not interrupt his Shema to answer a customer. Afterward he kept the price he had accepted in his heart (Bava Basra 89a).

berachos.heading: Berachos in the Gemara: Blessings on Food, Miracles and More
berachos.description: Berachos in the Gemara: hearts of palm (Berachos 36), birkas hagomel (Zevachim 7a), Hashem's name (Nedarim 7b), and Yosef's beracha (Yevamos 65a).
berachos.intro:
The Gemara says the beracha on hearts of palm is Shehakol, because no farmer would cut them and harm the tree. But today some farms grow palms for the hearts alone. [Fruits Of Our Labor](/daf/berachos/36/fruits-of-our-labor) asks whether the beracha has changed, comparing sugar cane and caper leaves. When in doubt between Ha'eitz and Ha'adamah, one says Ha'adamah. [A Cornucopia of Blessings](/daf/gittin/83/a-cornucopia-of-blessings) tackles the order of berachos. What if you like an apple more than a pickle, and the pickle more than a grape? The Steipler and Rav Wosner both rule to start with Ha'eitz on the grape.

Some berachos thank Hashem for being saved. Rashi in Zevachim 7a lists four reasons to bring a korban todah, and birkas hagomel took its place. [Many Thanks Or Just One?](/daf/zevachim/7/many-thanks-or-just-one) asks about a man who survived all four dangers in one week. Does he say it four times? In [She’asah Nissim](/daf/yevamos/65/sheasah-nissim), Yosef says the beracha at the pit where he was saved, and his brothers grow afraid. The Gemara in Yevamos 65a says their message from Yaakov was invented.

The Gemara in Nedarim 7b warns sharply against saying Hashem's name in vain. Still, [Not Saying Hashem’s Name in Vain](/daf/nedarim/7/not-saying-hashems-name-in-vain) explains that parents and teachers may say it to teach children berachos. Should one answer amen to a young child's beracha? Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach would say it while leaving off the final letter.

hamotzi-and-bread.heading: Hamotzi and Bread in the Gemara: Challah, Salt and Lechem Mishneh
hamotzi-and-bread.description: Hamotzi in the Gemara: where to cut the bread (Sanhedrin 102b), two loaves (Shabbos 117b), covering the challah (Pesachim 100a), salt (Menachos 20a).
hamotzi-and-bread.intro:
Where should one begin cutting the bread at Hamotzi? The Gemara in Sanhedrin 102b says this halachah came from a surprising teacher. King Menashe appeared to Rav Ashi in a dream and taught that one cuts from where the bread first bakes. [Breaking Bread](/daf/sanhedrin/102/breaking-bread) brings the Maharsha's reason: bread is a sign that Hashem accepts teshuvah. Rabbi Sebrow also explains why, on Shabbos, one only marks the spot with a small cut, to keep the loaves whole.

Rebbe Abba teaches that on Shabbos one says Hamotzi on two loaves, for the double portion of manna (Shabbos 117b). [A Challah Covering Quiz](/daf/pesachim/100/a-challah-covering-quiz-pesachim-100) tests the three reasons for covering the challah from Pesachim 100a. It applies them to cases like a clear plastic cover and seudah shlishis. What if a roll split in two? [Something To Pick At](/daf/eruvin/81/something-to-pick-at) brings Rav Chisda's toothpicks and asks whether they work for lechem mishneh.

Our table is compared to the mizbe'ach, and every korban was salted (Menachos 20a). [Worth Its Salt](/daf/menachos/20/worth-its-salt-menachos-20) explains why salt belongs on the table before Hamotzi, and why one should not wait for it after the beracha. [The Friday Night Food Fight](/daf/zevachim/62/the-friday-night-food-fight) asks whether a father may toss the challah to his family. [Fresh, Hot Challah](/daf/menachos/96/fresh-hot-challah) weighs fresh bakery challah against baking at home, and links warm challah to the Lechem HaPanim (Menachos 96b).

birkas-hamazon.heading: Birkas HaMazon in the Gemara: Bentching and Its Questions
birkas-hamazon.description: Birkas HaMazon in the Gemara: kingship in the fourth beracha (Berachos 49), when a meal ends (Chullin 86b), overeating (Gittin 70a), Sheva Brachos.
birkas-hamazon.intro:
The Gemara in Berachos says Hashem's kingship is mentioned extra times in the fourth beracha of bentching. This makes up for the third beracha, which speaks of the kingdom of Dovid instead. [Find The Missing Word](/daf/berachos/49/find-the-missing-word) explains why the Shulchan Aruch says not to mix the two kingships. That is why some bentchers put "melech" in Ya'aleh V'yavo in parentheses.

When does a meal end? The Gemara in Chullin 86b says that one who calls for the wine to bentch has finished his meal. If he eats more, he needs a new beracha. [A Minimalist Diet](/daf/chullin/86/a-minimalist-diet) applies this to a sick person eating small amounts on Yom Kippur. [Biblical or Rabbinic: That is the Question](/daf/nedarim/80/biblical-or-rabbinic-that-is-the-question) asks what a woman should do if she is unsure whether she bentched. The Gemara in Berachos leaves open whether her obligation is from the Torah. Rebbe Akiva Eiger says she need not bentch again, but Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach disagrees.

At a wedding feast, bentching is followed by Sheva Brachos. [Sheva Brachos Shailos](/daf/kesubos/8/sheva-brachos-shailos) gathers rulings of Rav Moshe Feinstein: who counts as panim chadashos, and what to do if you must leave early. [Eat but Don’t Overeat](/daf/gittin/70/eat-but-dont-overeat) brings Gittin 70a on stopping before you are full. It also explains the Shulchan Aruch's option to bentch and begin a new meal for seudah shlishis.

kiddush-and-havdalah.heading: Kiddush and Havdalah in the Gemara: Wine, Timing and Guests
kiddush-and-havdalah.description: Kiddush and Havdalah in the Gemara: kiddush on schnapps (Zevachim 31b), mevushal wine (Avodah Zarah 30a), and children and late havdalah (Bava Metzia 5a).
kiddush-and-havdalah.intro:
Kiddush is ideally made on wine or grape juice. On Friday night without wine, the Rosh says to use challah, and by day one may use a significant drink. [The Kiddush Cup Runneth Over](/daf/zevachim/31/the-kiddush-cup-runneth-over) explains when schnapps may be used, and why the Mishnah Berurah requires a cup that holds a revi'is. Zevachim 31b supports a fine point: if several people share the cup, they must all drink within the same short time.

Which wine is best for kiddush? In Avodah Zarah 30a, Shmuel drank wine in front of a gentile scholar. Since it was cooked, his touch did not matter. [Don’t Make a “Pour” Decision](/daf/avodah-zarah/30/dont-make-a-pour-decision) explains why American and Israeli poskim disagree about pasteurized wine. That is how one bottle can say "mevushal" in English and "lo mevushal" in Hebrew.

Some questions are about timing. When havdalah comes late in summer, should young children say it on Sunday? [Children and Havdalah](/daf/bava-metzia/5/children-and-havdalah) cites a view, based on Bava Metzia 5a, that children have no make-up mitzvos. [Be Our Guest](/daf/rosh-hashanah/6/be-our-guest) tells how the Chofetz Chaim made kiddush right away for hungry guests and sang Shalom Aleichem later. Why might a bochur in Eretz Yisrael suddenly make havdalah on yom tov sheni? [A Tale of Two Riddles: The Vacuuming Wife and the Havdala Surprise](/daf/chullin/18/a-tale-of-two-riddles-the-vacuuming-wife-and-the-havdala-surprise) explains.

hallel.heading: Hallel in the Gemara: Full Hallel, Half Hallel and No Hallel
hallel.description: Hallel in the Gemara: half Hallel on Pesach (Arachin 10a), the angels at the Yam Suf (Sanhedrin 39b), and no Hallel on Purim (Megillah 14a).
hallel.intro:
Why do we say only half Hallel on the last days of Pesach? The Gemara in Arachin 10a explains that each day of Sukkos has its own Mussaf offering. The later days of Pesach all share one. [Half And Half](/daf/sanhedrin/39/half-and-half) adds the Mishnah Berurah's reason, from Sanhedrin 39b. The angels wanted to sing as the Egyptians drowned, and Hashem stopped them: "My creations are drowning." Rabbi Sebrow concludes that half Hallel should still be said with full joy.

Half Hallel on Rosh Chodesh is only a custom. [Our Better Halves](/daf/megillah/17/our-better-halves) explains what that means for one who says a verse out of order. Purim has no Hallel at all. In Megillah 14a, Rav Nachman says the Megillah is its Hallel. Rava says Hallel does not fit, since the Jews remained Achashverosh's subjects. [Hallel On Purim: The Whole Megillah](/daf/megillah/14/hallel-on-purim-the-whole-megillah) asks what someone without a Megillah should do.

On Seder night, Hallel is tied to the Korban Pesach, which had to be eaten by chatzos (Zevachim 56b). [Racing Towards Chatzos](/daf/zevachim/56/racing-towards-chatzos) explains why the Rema says it is best to finish Hallel before midnight. Some do not say Hallel in shul on Pesach night. [Make Your Days Count](/daf/menachos/66/make-your-days-count) brings Rav Moshe's warning not to walk out while others say it. [Do We Need to Suffer for Torah?](/daf/bava-kamma/61/do-we-need-to-suffer-for-torah) tells of the Baal HaTanya, who said it after the congregation left.

krias-hatorah.heading: Krias HaTorah in the Gemara: Aliyos, Haftarah and Who Gets Called Up
krias-hatorah.description: Krias HaTorah in the Gemara: four aliyos on Rosh Chodesh (Megillah 21b), the 21-verse haftarah (Megillah 23a) and a kohen with no Levi (Gittin 59).
krias-hatorah.intro:
The Gemara shapes the weekly Torah reading around people's lives. On Mondays and Thursdays only three are called up, so no one comes late to work. Megillah 21b adds a fourth aliyah on Rosh Chodesh and Chol HaMoed, since they are not workdays. Why is Rosh Chodesh not a workday? Rashi says it is a holiday for women, a reward for refusing to give their jewelry for the Golden Calf. The Turei Even says the Korban Mussaf once made it a holiday for everyone. Rabbi Sebrow explains both in [A Rosh Chodesh Holiday](/daf/megillah/21/a-rosh-chodesh-holiday).

The order of aliyos is Kohen, Levi, Yisrael. What happens when there is no Levi? The Gemara in Gittin says a second kohen is not called, so no one suspects the first was unfit. The same kohen takes both aliyos. Yet in the Munkacser beis midrash a Yisrael was sometimes called first. [Kohen Conundrums](/daf/kesubos/25/kohen-conundrums) explains why: the Minchas Elazar praised a kohen who gave up his aliyos to avoid extra berachos.

The haftarah must have 21 pesukim, but Megillah 23a shows Rebbe Yochanan stopping after ten when a translator was present. A bachur pledged 1,000 blatt for a Simchas Torah honor. In [Another Repeat](/daf/megillah/23/another-repeat), Rav Yitzchok Zilberstein uses this Gemara to ask if he may review the same pages. [Marrying Meirav and Michal](/daf/sanhedrin/19/marrying-meirav-and-michal) asks how an adopted boy is called to the Torah. Sanhedrin 19b teaches that raising an orphan is like giving birth to him, and Rav Moshe Feinstein allows the adoptive father's name.

When several readings meet, the rule of tadir kodem decides the order. On Shabbos Rosh Chodesh Chanukah, Rosh Chodesh is read before Chanukah because it is more frequent. The haftarah, though, is Chanukah's, because publicizing the miracle comes first. Boruch and Shimon work it out in [Tumult Over Tadir](/daf/zevachim/89/tumult-over-tadir).

shul.heading: Shul in the Gemara: Honoring the Beis Knesses
shul.description: Shul in the Gemara: a shul taller than every house (Shabbos 11a), eating in shul (Megillah 28a), and extra steps to a farther shul (Sotah 22a).
shul.intro:
The Gemara gives the shul special honor. Rav taught that a city whose houses are taller than its shul will become desolate. Rav Ashi saw a crack in the shul of Masa Machsya and had it taken down. He slept in the ruins until a taller one was built. In [Reaching New Heights](/daf/shabbos/11/reaching-new-heights), Rabbi Sebrow asks whether a pole on the roof counts toward the shul's height. The Magen Avraham said a plain steel rod does not, and the Mishnah Berurah follows him.

Which shul should you choose? A widow walked past her local shul to daven in Rebbe Yochanan's beis midrash, saying there is reward for every step (Sotah 22a). The Magen Avraham rules that one should go to the farther shul. [A Mitzvah for Each Footstep](/daf/zevachim/51/a-mitzvah-for-each-footstep) asks whether this skips over a mitzvah, and answers from Tosfos in Zevachim 51a.

Megillah 28a forbids eating and drinking in shul. So how do shuls serve tikkun or shalosh seudos? [Don’t Talk, Just Daven](/daf/megillah/28/dont-talk-just-daven) traces the answer to a condition made when Babylonian shuls were built. Rav Moshe Feinstein says the common custom follows Rashi and the Ohr Zarua. Rav Shlomo Zalman applied the same idea to talking about mundane matters after davening. Still, talking during davening must be taken very seriously.

Even a door handle can raise a question. One may not destroy any part of a shul. Does drilling two screw holes count? [Getting A Handle On Shul Rules](/daf/zevachim/98/getting-a-handle-on-shul-rules) weighs the Taz against the Elya Rabba, whom the Mishnah Berurah seems to follow. [Fair and Square](/daf/bava-basra/14/fair-and-square) tells how Rav Moshe Sternbuch ruled on a shul's round-topped Luchos. He found no real problem, but had them squared off for the sake of peace.

zmanim.heading: Zmanim in the Gemara: When the Day Begins and Ends
zmanim.description: Zmanim in the Gemara: the lazy shift of the Korban Pesach (Pesachim 65a), moonlight mistaken for dawn (Yoma 28a), Rabbeinu Tam's night (Pesachim 94a).
zmanim.intro:
Many mitzvos depend on the clock, and the Gemara cares about both the time and our attitude to it. The Korban Pesach was brought in three shifts, and the last was called the lazy shift. Someone has to be last, the Gemara says, but it does not have to be you (Pesachim 65a). In [Minutes Till Minchah](/daf/pesachim/65/minutes-till-minchah-pesachim-65), Rabbi Sebrow applies this to Minchah. The preferred start is nine and a half hours into the day, when the afternoon Tamid was brought. Still, the Mishnah Berurah allows davening from half an hour after midday.

The Mishnah in Yoma 28a tells how kohanim once mistook moonlight for dawn and slaughtered the Tamid too early. Why not simply wait for sunrise? [Mincha Motivation](/daf/yoma/28/mincha-motivation) quotes the Siach Yitzchok: they wanted to do the mitzvah at the earliest possible moment. The same daf then discusses the earliest time for Minchah.

When does the day end? The Vilna Gaon says definite daytime ends at sunset. Rabbeinu Tam, in Tosfos on Pesachim 94a, extends it well past sunset. [Rabbeinu Tam & the Lawsuit](/daf/pesachim/94/rabbeinu-tam-the-lawsuit) tells of a frum couple served court papers 59 minutes after sunset on Shabbos. They said they keep Rabbeinu Tam, and the judge dismissed the suit.

Travelers face their own questions. [Fasten Your Seatbelts](/daf/berachos/30/fasten-your-seatbelts) starts from Berachos 30a, which lets a rider daven on his donkey. Rav Chaim Kanievsky ruled that davening Minchah sitting before sunset beats davening standing after it. [Making Our Days Count](/daf/menachos/66/making-our-days-count) explains why Shavuos starts late: the seven weeks of the Omer must be complete.

tefillin.heading: Tefillin in the Gemara: The Sign Between Hashem and Klal Yisrael
tefillin.description: Tefillin in the Gemara: the shin on the shel rosh (Menachos 35), Rashi and Rabbeinu Tam together (Menachos 34), tefillin on Chol HaMoed (Chagigah 18a).
tefillin.intro:
The Gemara calls tefillin an os, a sign of the bond between Hashem and Klal Yisrael. On Shabbos and yom tov, resting from melachah is the sign, so tefillin are not worn. What about Chol HaMoed? [The Great Tefillin Divide](/daf/chagigah/18/the-great-tefillin-divide) ties the dispute to Chagigah 18a, which asks whether melachah on Chol HaMoed is forbidden by the Torah. The Shulchan Aruch rules that tefillin are not worn, while the Rema reports the Ashkenazic custom to wear them.

Menachos 35 teaches that a shin on the tefillin shel rosh is a halachah given to Moshe at Sinai. In [Mordechai’s Tefillin](/daf/menachos/35/mordechais-tefillin), Rabbi Sebrow cites the Orchos Chaim: the shin equals 300, about the number of days tefillin are worn each year. The Ateres Zekeinim notes the math works only if one wears them on Chol HaMoed. The article then asks how the Vilna Gaon, who opposed the practice, pictured Mordechai in tefillin on Chol HaMoed Pesach.

Many wear both Rashi and Rabbeinu Tam tefillin. Is that adding to the mitzvah? [The Tiff Over Two Tefillin](/daf/zevachim/81/the-tiff-over-two-tefillin-menachos-34) brings the Chofetz Chaim's answer. One pair is surely invalid, and one intends the mitzvah only with the kosher pair. [Left Foot, Right Foot](/daf/yevamos/104/left-foot-right-foot) explains that tefillin go on the weaker arm, so a lefty wears them on his right.

May a man check his tefillin in a mirror? The Divrei Chaim called it the mark of an am ha'aretz. The Brisker Rav answered that he would rather be one and know his tefillin were in place. Rabbi Sebrow tells the story in [A Moment of Reflection](/daf/avodah-zarah/29/a-moment-of-reflection). [Attitude Of Gratitude](/daf/menachos/75/attitude-of-gratitude) asks whether a bar mitzvah boy says Shehecheyanu on his first tefillin. Rav Shlomo Zalman suggested the father give the tefillin as a gift on that day.

mezuzah.heading: Mezuzah in the Gemara: Which Doors, Which Side, Which Angle
mezuzah.description: Mezuzah in the Gemara: a renter's thirty days (Menachos 44a), leaving mezuzos when moving out (Bava Metzia 102a), and two mezuzos on one door (Yoma 57).
mezuzah.intro:
The Gemara places the mezuzah on the right doorpost, because most people step into a room with the right foot first. What about a left-footed person? [Left Foot, Right Foot](/daf/yevamos/104/left-foot-right-foot) brings the Mordechai, who follows the majority of the household. The Shach insists on the right side always, and notes that this is the custom.

When does the obligation begin? A buyer must put up mezuzos right away. Menachos 44a teaches that a renter becomes obligated after thirty days. Tosafos offers two reasons: after thirty days he looks like the owner, or the home is no longer temporary. In [On Borrowed Time](/daf/menachos/44/on-borrowed-time), Rabbi Sebrow asks what happens with a one-year lease. Rav Moshe Feinstein says to put them up at once, though it is better to wait thirty days for the bracha. [Muktzeh Marvels](/daf/gittin/77/muktzeh-marvels) tells how Rebbe Zalman of Vilna found invalid mezuzos at an inn on Shabbos. The innkeeper declared the inn ownerless to keep his guest.

Bava Metzia 102a says a renter may not take his mezuzos with him when he moves out. Yet tzitzis strings may be moved to another garment. [Removing a House’s Mezuzos](/daf/bava-metzia/102/removing-a-houses-mezuzos) gives four answers. Tosfos says the mezuzah protects the next residents, and the Ritva says it brings sanctity to the home.

Why is the mezuzah slanted? Rashi says it stands upright and Rabbeinu Tam says it lies flat, and the angle is a compromise. [The Right Angle](/daf/bava-basra/14/the-right-angle) adds that a mezuzah at an angle teaches that compromise belongs in a Jewish home. Could one simply put up two mezuzos? [Multiple Mezuzos?](/daf/yoma/57/multiple-mezuzos) compares a Catskills bungalow with an old and new mezuzah to the Kohen Gadol's blood sprinklings in Yoma 57. The Pischei Teshuva and Rav Moshe warn that a second mezuzah adds to the mitzvah.

tzitzis.heading: Tzitzis in the Gemara: Strings, Garments and Intent
tzitzis.description: Tzitzis in the Gemara: wool strings on linen (Yevamos 4a), tzitzis in a cemetery (Berachos 18), a child's start (Sukkah 42a), beautiful tzitzis (Nazir 2b).
tzitzis.intro:
The Torah forbids wearing wool and linen together, and the very next verse commands tzitzis. Yevamos 4a learns from this that wool tzitzis with techeiles could be put on a linen garment. Today, without definite techeiles, the Shulchan Aruch no longer allows it. In [Match But Don’t Mix](/daf/yevamos/4/match-but-dont-mix), Rabbi Sebrow brings Rabbi Akiva Eiger's point. Even then, a garment made of wool and linen was never allowed, since putting it on comes before the mitzvah.

Rebbe Chiya and Rebbe Yonasan were walking in a cemetery, and Rebbe Yonasan's tzitzis dragged over the graves. Rebbe Chiya told him to lift them, lest the dead feel mocked. [Do Knot Disturb](/daf/berachos/18/do-knot-disturb) asks why dragging tzitzis on the ground was not itself a problem. The Aruch HaShulchan says the concern is strings being stepped on, and asks how anyone could learn without them touching the floor.

When does a child begin? Sukkah 42a says a minor who knows how to wrap himself is obligated in tzitzis. [A Knotty Situation](/daf/sukkah/42/a-knotty-situation) brings opinions from age three to age nine. It also explains how to discard old tzitzis with dignity.

Nazir 2b lists beautiful tzitzis as a way of beautifying a mitzvah. Must one beautify the garment too? In [Hiddur Miss](/daf/nazir/2/hiddur-miss), Rav Moshe Feinstein answers yes, but only for a garment worn for the sake of the mitzvah. Intent matters in other ways too. [Nod If You’re Awake](/daf/yevamos/55/nod-if-youre-awake) warns about grabbing a tallis for a Shabbos Minchah aliyah without thinking of the mitzvah. [On Borrowed Time](/daf/menachos/44/on-borrowed-time) explains why a borrowed garment needs tzitzis after thirty days.

sefer-torah.heading: Sefer Torah in the Gemara: Writing, Storing and Honoring the Torah
sefer-torah.description: Sefer Torah in the Gemara: the last eight pesukim (Menachos 30a), writing single pesukim (Gittin 60a), the Aron (Yoma 52b), the Luchos (Bava Basra 14a).
sefer-torah.intro:
The Gemara treats every part of a Sefer Torah with care. Menachos 30a teaches that the last eight pesukim, describing Moshe's death, are different from the rest of the Torah. One view says Yehoshua wrote them; Rebbe Shimon says Moshe wrote them with tears. In an article on the presidential autopen, Rabbi Sebrow asks how Moshe could have written on Shabbos if he died that day.

May one write a few pesukim outside a Sefer Torah? Rabba in Gittin 60a forbade a scroll of one parashah, even for teaching children. [Chapter And Verse](/daf/yoma/37/chapter-and-verse) starts from Queen Hilney's golden tablet in Yoma 37a. It explains how the Rif and the Shach allow writing pesukim for the sake of learning. The Mishnah Berurah still forbids writing them just to decorate a sukkah.

How should a Sefer Torah stand in the Aron? Bava Basra 14a describes the Luchos lying in the Aron. Rabbeinu Tam concluded that our sifrei Torah should also lie flat. In [The Right Angle](/daf/bava-basra/14/the-right-angle), the Radvaz defends our custom of keeping them upright. Yoma 52b says the Kohen Gadol walked out backward so as not to turn his back on the Aron. [Back to Respect](/daf/yoma/52/back-to-respect) explains why a rav may still speak with his back to the Aron Kodesh. The sifrei Torah rest more than ten tefachim high.

Some questions are practical. If a Sefer Torah was wrongly declared pasul and replaced, which one is read? [What Came First?](/daf/yoma/64/what-came-first) brings the Torah Lishmah: the first one, since it was kosher all along. [A More Mehudar Mitzvah](/daf/shevuos/27/a-more-mehudar-mitzvah) asks whether to write a plain Sefer Torah yourself or hire an expert scribe. In [Of Minhagim And Manhigim](/daf/gittin/33/of-minhagim-and-manhigim), the Chasam Sofer judges a Torah by its last column. Many people writing the final letters shows a Jewish scribe.

tashmishei-kedushah.heading: Tashmishei Kedushah in the Gemara: Treating Holy Objects With Respect
tashmishei-kedushah.description: Tashmishei Kedushah in the Gemara: used wood for the Mizbeach (Menachos 22b), a nicer Parah Adumah (Shevuos 11b) and a renter's mezuzos (Bava Metzia 102a).
tashmishei-kedushah.intro:
Objects used for a mitzvah carry a special dignity. Menachos 22b debates whether wood from a demolished house may be burned on the Mizbeach. The Agudah applies this to a Sefer Torah: its mantle should not be made from used clothing. [The Emperor’s Used Clothes – For the Aron Kodesh?](/daf/menachos/22/the-emperor-s-used-clothes-for-the-aron-kodesh--menachos-22) tells how Napoleon's cloak reportedly became a paroches in Yerushalayim. The Magen Avraham allows it once the garment's form is changed, and the Mishnah Berurah says the practice is to be lenient.

Once an item is set aside for a mitzvah, may it be swapped for a nicer one? [Waxing About Oil](/daf/shevuos/11/waxing-about-oil) asks about wax candles already in the menorah when olive oil arrives. The Shevus Yaakov says removing them degrades a mitzvah object. The Chacham Tzvi cites Shevuos 11b, where a nicer Parah Adumah replaces the first. [Removing a House’s Mezuzos](/daf/bava-metzia/102/removing-a-houses-mezuzos) brings Rav Achai Gaon: a kosher mezuzah should not be put away in a drawer.

Even a small trace of holiness can matter. [When Less Is Too Much](/daf/bechoros/15/when-less-is-too-much) asks whether one may keep a stone fragment that may be from the Kosel. Rav Moshe Feinstein rules that displaying it is forbidden personal benefit. [A Knotty Situation](/daf/sukkah/42/a-knotty-situation) explains how to discard worn-out tzitzis with dignity. The Rema says not to throw them straight into the trash, and many wrap them in a bag first.

mitzvah-principles.heading: Mitzvah Principles in the Gemara: How We Do Mitzvos
mitzvah-principles.description: Mitzvah Principles in the Gemara: not passing over a mitzvah (Yoma 58b), tadir kodem (Zevachim 89), and choosing a nicer mitzvah (Shevuos 11b).
mitzvah-principles.intro:
Beyond the mitzvos themselves, the Gemara teaches rules for how to do them. Ein ma'avirin al hamitzvos means we do not pass over a mitzvah. That is why one view in the Gemara wants Purim in the first Adar of a leap year. In [Double Trouble](/daf/yoma/58/double-trouble), Rabbi Sebrow shows from Yoma 58b that the Kohen Gadol even returned to a corner of the Altar he had passed. The Radvaz told a prisoner allowed one furlough a year to take the earliest day with a mitzvah.

When two mitzvos meet, the more frequent one usually comes first. [Tumult Over Tadir](/daf/zevachim/89/tumult-over-tadir) works through Borchi Nafshi and L'Dovid, Havdalah and Chanukah candles, and a bris on Purim. Sometimes publicizing the miracle wins instead, as with the Chanukah haftarah.

Intent matters too. Yevamos 55 discusses doing a mitzvah while dozing. [Nod If You’re Awake](/daf/yevamos/55/nod-if-youre-awake) explains that intent at the start can carry through the whole Megillah reading. A man who grabs a tallis for a Shabbos Minchah aliyah without thinking may not fulfill the mitzvah at all. Adding to a mitzvah is also forbidden. [Multiple Mezuzos?](/daf/yoma/57/multiple-mezuzos) asks whether a second mezuzah on one doorpost is allowed when the first may be invalid.

What about doing a mitzvah more beautifully? Shevuos 11b replaces a Parah Adumah when a nicer one is found. [Waxing About Oil](/daf/shevuos/11/waxing-about-oil) uses this to ask about switching wax candles for olive oil. [A More Mehudar Mitzvah](/daf/shevuos/27/a-more-mehudar-mitzvah) weighs personal effort against a nicer result. Several poskim rule that the more beautiful mitzvah comes first.

bris-milah.heading: Bris Milah in the Gemara: Customs and Questions Around the Bris
bris-milah.description: Bris Milah in the Gemara: no bris in the midbar (Yevamos 71b), candles as a secret sign of a bris (Sanhedrin 32b), and the shalom zachar (Bava Kamma 80a).
bris-milah.intro:
The Gemara says bris milah was not done during the forty years in the desert, because it would have endangered the babies (Yevamos 71b). Uncircumcised men, and parents of uncircumcised sons, may not eat the Korban Pesach. So the mitzvah of Korban Pesach suffered too. In [Clouds in the Forecast](/daf/yevamos/71/clouds-in-the-forecast), Rabbi Sebrow brings Tosafos: the harsh weather was a punishment for the sin of the spies. That is why Klal Yisrael was still held responsible.

When bris milah was outlawed, Jews used secret signals to announce a simcha (Sanhedrin 32b). Rashi says a millstone sounded for a bris and candles were lit for a wedding; others say the reverse. Tosfos notes a custom to light candles at a bris. [Illuminating The Shabbos Blessing](/daf/sanhedrin/32/illuminating-the-shabbos-blessing) uses this to ask how we bless Shabbos candles in a home lit by electricity.

Bava Kamma 80a tells that Rav, Shmuel and Rav Assi went to a bris or a Yeshua HaBen. Tosfos explains it as a meal of thanks for a safe birth. In [Shalom, Zachor!](/daf/bava-kamma/80/shalom-zachor), the Terumas HaDeshen calls this the source of the shalom zachar. The Noda BeYehuda ties it to the night before the bris. [What Came First?](/daf/yoma/64/what-came-first) asks which of two babies has his bris first. Based on Yoma 64a, the one born first has no priority, since both become obligated at the same time.

pidyon-haben.heading: Pidyon HaBen in the Gemara: Redeeming the Firstborn
pidyon-haben.description: Pidyon HaBen in the Gemara: Rav Kahane and the redemption (Kiddushin 8a), pidyon haben and Shabbos (Yoma 13b), and the firstborns' avodah (Zevachim 112).
pidyon-haben.intro:
A father redeems his firstborn son by giving a kohen five silver coins. Kiddushin 8a tells that Rav Kahane accepted an item of value for a pidyon haben. At one pidyon haben meal, a guest asked why the man leading bentching did not mention the kohanim present. The Chasam Sofer quipped that perhaps no male kohen was there. Rav Kahane, he said, may have accepted the redemption for his wife, a kohen's daughter. In [Do You Need a Kohein to Perform a Pidyon HaBen?](/daf/kiddushin/8/do-you-need-a-kohein-to-perform-a-pidyon-haben), Rabbi Sebrow shows how horrified the Chasam Sofer was to be quoted as halachah. The Rav Kahane in Kiddushin was a kohen. Only if no kohen can be found may a kohen's son-in-law fill in, and the baby must be redeemed again later. [A Kohen By Any Other Name](/daf/kiddushin/8/a-kohen-by-any-other-name) tells the same story.

Pidyon haben is not done on Shabbos, since transactions are not completed then. Could a father give the coins on Friday, to take effect on Shabbos? [Is eBay For-Bid-Den?](/daf/yoma/13/is-ebay-for-bid-den) brings the Terumas HaDeshen: it works, but the father loses the bracha. [Firstborn Offerings](/daf/zevachim/112/firstborn-offerings) goes back to the beginning, when firstborns performed the avodah before the Mishkan was built.

kibbud-av-vaem.heading: Kibbud Av VaEm in the Gemara: Honoring Parents
kibbud-av-vaem.description: Kibbud Av VaEm in the Gemara: Rebbe Tarfon and his mother (Kiddushin 31), Esav's royal garments (Chullin 105a), and Shmuel calling Rav Abba (Yevamos 57b).
kibbud-av-vaem.intro:
The Gemara holds up remarkable models of honoring parents. Rebbe Tarfon would bend down so his mother could climb on his back into bed. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel admitted that Esav served Yitzchak far better than he served his own father. Esav wore royal garments to serve his father, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel wore ordinary clothes. In [Word To The Wise](/daf/kiddushin/31/word-to-the-wise), Rabbi Sebrow explains why only someone like Rebbe Tarfon could ask his mother to avoid mundane talk on Shabbos. [Beyond The Letter Of The Law](/daf/chullin/105/beyond-the-letter-of-the-law) asks why Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel did not simply improve. Rav Yisrael Salanter answers that growth must come step by step.

What may a child call his father? In Yevamos 57b, Shmuel called Rav "Abba." Rashi says it was a title of honor, and Tosefos says it was Rav's real name. [Abba, My Dear](/daf/yevamos/57/abba-my-dear) asks whether a son may call his father Abba if that is his actual name. The Shulchan Aruch adds that one should not call a friend by a parent's rare name.

The mitzvah continues after a parent's passing. A son promised his dying mother that a relative would settle any inheritance dispute. Later he refused. [Sworn Statements](/daf/bava-basra/147/sworn-statements) weighs the Rema, who frees a person from a promise made only to calm the dying. The Shvus Yaakov says a child must still honor a parent's last wishes. [Hitting Rock Bottom](/daf/sanhedrin/44/hitting-rock-bottom) shows the reward for honoring a parent. Shem covered his father Noach, and generations later Sancheriv's soldiers died with their bodies left intact.

tzedakah.heading: Tzedakah in the Gemara: How Much to Give and Why It Matters
tzedakah.description: Tzedakah in the Gemara: losses decreed on Rosh Hashanah (Bava Basra 10a), the 20% limit (Kesubos 50a), Mar Ukva (Kesubos 67b), Nakdimon (Kesubos 66b).
tzedakah.intro:
The Gemara teaches that tzedakah never really costs us. Bava Basra 10a says that just as a person's income is decided on Rosh Hashanah, so are his losses. If he merits it, the loss goes to charity; if not, the money is lost anyway. Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai saw in a dream that his nephews would lose 700 dinarim. He pushed them to give 683 to tzedakah, and the Kaiser's officers took exactly the remaining 17. Rabbi Sebrow tells the story in [Your Loss Is Your Gain](/daf/bava-basra/10/your-loss-is-your-gain). [Rosh Hashana in a Cemetery](/daf/rosh-hashanah/16/rosh-hashana-in-a-cemetery) tells of a pious man who gave a poor man a dinar in a famine year (Berachos 18b). That year his crops were spared from the hail.

How much should a person give? The Sages at Usha ruled that one should not give away more than a fifth of one's money (Kesubos 50a). Yet Kalba Savua gave Rabbi Akiva half his wealth (Kesubos 63a). And the dying Mar Ukva gave away half of what he had left (Kesubos 67b). [More Than Twenty Percent](/daf/kesubos/63/more-than-twenty-percent) works through the answers. Supporting Torah is a partnership, and a dying person need not save for himself.

Why we give matters too. Nakdimon ben Gurion's daughter was found gathering barley from dung (Kesubos 66b). The Gemara explains that her father's great giving had been partly for his own honor. [Charity with Uncharitable Intentions](/daf/kesubos/66/charity-with-uncharitable-intentions) explores giving for ulterior motives. It starts from the teaching in the Gemara in Rosh Hashanah that one who gives "so that my son may live" is completely righteous. [Bidding on Buildings and Baby Boys](/daf/moed-katan/9/bidding-on-buildings-and-baby-boys) tells of a poor man who secretly gave nearly everything he had for the Maharsha's yeshiva. The next year, he was blessed with a son.

chesed.heading: Chesed in the Gemara: Guests, the Sick and Acts of Kindness
chesed.description: Chesed in the Gemara: delaying a charity pledge (Rosh Hashanah 6a), visiting the sick (Bava Metzia 30b), and Abaye's years of kindness (Yevamos 105a).
chesed.intro:
Avraham Avinu was speaking with Hashem when three travelers appeared, and he left to greet them. The Gemara learns that hosting guests is greater than greeting the Divine Presence. In [Be Our Guest](/daf/rosh-hashanah/6/be-our-guest), Rabbi Sebrow tells how the Chofetz Chaim made Kiddush right away for hungry Friday night guests. He sang Shalom Aleichem later in the meal. The Dvar Avraham links this to Rosh Hashanah 6a: one who delays a pledge to the poor transgresses the Torah's ban on delaying vows.

Bava Metzia 30b finds visiting the sick in the verse about "the path they shall walk." The Ramban counts it as a Torah mitzvah, while the Rambam calls it rabbinic. The Rema says a visitor who did not pray for the patient has not fulfilled the mitzvah. [Visiting the Sick](/daf/bava-metzia/30/visiting-the-sick) asks whether a phone call counts. Rav Elyashiv reportedly said no, while Rav Moshe Feinstein said it fulfills the mitzvah to some degree. [The Power of Bikur Cholim](/daf/nedarim/39/the-power-of-bikur-cholim) brings the Kli Yakar: the visitor himself learns how fragile life is.

Kindness also brings long life. Abaye and Rabbah descended from Eli, whose family was cursed to die young. Rabbah, who learned Torah, lived to 40. Abaye, who added acts of kindness, lived to 60 (Yevamos 105a). [Keep Calm And Chesed On](/daf/yevamos/105/keep-calm-and-chesed-on) brings the Chofetz Chaim, who says the halachah follows Abaye. [Putting You First](/daf/bava-kamma/92/putting-you-first) cites the Gemara in Bava Kamma: one who prays for a friend with the same need is answered first. A rosh yeshiva saw it happen when he helped JEP secure the bequest that built Camp Nageela.

talmud-torah.heading: Talmud Torah in the Gemara: Learning and Teaching Torah
talmud-torah.description: Talmud Torah in the Gemara: Rebbe Chiya the teacher (Bava Metzia 85b), learning Pesach laws early (Pesachim 6a) and stopping for the Megillah (Megillah 3).
talmud-torah.intro:
The Gemara promises that one who toils in Torah will find success. Avimi forgot Maseches Menachos and traveled to his own student, Rav Chisda, to relearn it. Rashi explains that he wanted the extra toil. In [Toil For Torah](/daf/menachos/7/toil-for-torah), Rabbi Sebrow brings the Vilna Gaon's point: the verse says "I toiled and found," because success in Torah is a gift. Even the effort of getting to a shiur counts.

Rebbe Chiya planted flax, made nets, and hunted deer to make parchment. He then taught five children the five books of the Torah and had them teach each other (Bava Metzia 85b). [Rebbe Chiya: The Ultimate Teacher](/daf/bava-metzia/85/rebbe-chiya-the-ultimate-teacher) explains, with the Maharsha, that Torah built on a pure foundation succeeds. [Lifelong Goal](/daf/makkos/10/lifelong-goal) tells how the Angel of Death could not take Rav Chisda while he learned without stopping.

When may one stop learning? Rebbe Yehuda HaNasi closed his yeshiva on Purim so his students could hear the Megillah with a large crowd. [Yearn To Learn](/daf/megillah/3/yearn-to-learn) asks why the Gemara calls this bitul Torah. One answer is that leaving deep study for a simple reading is itself a loss. The Gemara in Pesachim 6a says to learn the laws of Pesach thirty days ahead. [A Time To Learn](/daf/pesachim/6/a-time-to-learn) notes this means starting at the Purim seudah.

Must one suffer for Torah? Bava Kamma 61b tells of three warriors who crossed enemy lines to bring Dovid HaMelech's questions to the Sanhedrin. Dovid was displeased that they risked their lives. [Do We Need to Suffer for Torah?](/daf/bava-kamma/61/do-we-need-to-suffer-for-torah) ends with Rav Meir Shapiro defending a yeshiva with a dining room and dormitory. Students should toil over Torah, not over meals and lodging.

eretz-yisrael-mitzvos.heading: Eretz Yisrael Mitzvos in the Gemara: Ma'aser, Orlah, Shemittah and Bikkurim
eretz-yisrael-mitzvos.description: Eretz Yisrael Mitzvos in the Gemara: orlah outside Israel (Kiddushin 39), who gets ma'aser (Yevamos 86b) and Shemittah fruit as wages (Sukkah 44a).
eretz-yisrael-mitzvos.intro:
Many mitzvos are tied to the produce of Eretz Yisrael, yet some apply everywhere. Kiddushin 39 teaches that orlah and kilayim of trees apply in the Diaspora too. [Barking Up the Wrong Tree](/daf/kiddushin/39/barking-up-the-wrong-tree) shows why this matters today. A blueberry bush counts as a tree, so fruit in its second year is orlah. Creating a pluot by cross-pollination is permitted, but grafting one species onto another is forbidden.

Yevamos 86b tells of a dispute over ma'aser rishon. Rebbe Elazar ben Azariah, a kohen, held that kohanim may receive it and collected it from a certain garden. Rebbe Akiva, who used it to feed the poor, had the owner move the entrance so it could only be reached through a cemetery. Only then did he send a student to convince Rebbe Elazar ben Azariah. In [Ma’aser Motivations](/daf/yevamos/86/maaser-motivations), Rabbi Sebrow explains that personal interest can cloud judgment. [Oneg Shabbos](/daf/yevamos/93/oneg-shabbos) tells how Rebbe Yannai separated ma'aser for fruit that had not yet arrived, so he could enjoy it on Shabbos.

A wealthy man asked Rebbe Elazar bar Tzadok whether villagers could take Shemittah olives as pay. Told it was improper, he left at once to stop it (Sukkah 44a). [Without Delay](/daf/sukkah/44/without-delay) brings Rav Yisrael Salanter: his speed was what impressed Rebbe Elazar. [Lying Waze](/daf/bava-basra/82/lying-waze) starts from Bava Basra 82a. A man unsure whether he owns the land under his trees brings bikkurim without the declaration, since it may be false.

shatnez.heading: Shatnez in the Gemara: Wool, Linen and Hidden Threads
shatnez.description: Shatnez in the Gemara: tzitzis beside the wool-and-linen ban (Yevamos 4a), and wearing shatnez to hide one's identity in danger (Avodah Zarah 18b).
shatnez.intro:
The Torah forbids wearing wool and linen together, and the very next verse commands tzitzis. Yevamos 4a learns that wool tzitzis with techeiles could once be put on a linen garment. Rabbi Akiva Eiger adds that a garment made of wool and linen was never allowed. In [Match But Don’t Mix](/daf/yevamos/4/match-but-dont-mix), Rabbi Sebrow visits shatnez labs. Linen hides in collar stiffeners, shoulder pads, pockets and tie linings. A lawyer's ten custom suits from Hong Kong were all shatnez, and so were the two replacements. [Yibum and Tzitzis](/daf/yevamos/4/yibum-and-tzitzis) retells the lawyer's story alongside the Gemara.

May a Jew wear shatnez to save his life? [Keeping the Faith](/daf/avodah-zarah/26/keeping-the-faith) starts from Rebbe Meir, who escaped by letting people think he was not Jewish (Avodah Zarah 18b). The Rema allows wearing a non-Jew's shatnez garment to hide one's identity in mortal danger. The Bach says one should not travel a dangerous road planning to do so. The Shach explains that he only forbids walking into that danger.

shiluach-haken.heading: Shiluach HaKen in the Gemara: Sending Away the Mother Bird
shiluach-haken.description: Shiluach HaKen in the Gemara: no mitzvah with your own birds (Chullin 138), whether to say a bracha (Chullin 140), and women and weapons (Nazir 59a).
shiluach-haken.intro:
The Mishnah at the end of Chullin teaches that one cannot do shiluach haken with one's own birds. A nest in your own tree may already belong to you, since your property acquires things for you. In [The Test Of A Nest](/daf/chullin/138/the-test-of-a-nest), Rabbi Sebrow describes a mourning dove nesting outside his window. Rav Chaim Kanievsky says most people do not want such eggs, so they stay ownerless. Only the mother bird counts, and she usually sits on the eggs in the evening. Rav Chaim advises intending that anything that scares her away fulfills the mitzvah.

[Talking Turkey About Shiluach Hakein](/daf/chullin/140/talking-turkey-about-shiluach-hakein) adds more questions. Some Rishonim say the mitzvah only repairs the sin of taking the eggs, so no bracha is said. Rashi and the Rambam seem to require actively sending the bird away. The Chasam Sofer warns that a doubtful attempt may cause needless pain to animals. [What’s at Stake?](/daf/nazir/59/whats-at-stake) notes the Yalkut Yehudah's point. The Torah places this mitzvah next to the ban on women carrying weapons, showing how dear caring for children is to Hashem.

kilayim.heading: Kilayim in the Gemara: Mixing Species
kilayim.description: Kilayim in the Gemara: grafting trees outside Israel (Kiddushin 39), hybrid fruits, and the Rashbam's horse-and-mule wagon (Bava Basra 133b).
kilayim.intro:
Kiddushin 39 teaches that kilayim of trees applies outside Eretz Yisrael. In [Barking Up the Wrong Tree](/daf/kiddushin/39/barking-up-the-wrong-tree), Rabbi Sebrow explains what this means in a modern orchard. Grafting a branch of one species onto another is forbidden, and nearly all fruit trees sold today are grafted. Some Rishonim forbid even watering a fruit cocktail tree bought already grafted, though its fruit may be eaten. Pluots and plumcots begin with cross-pollination, which is permitted, and only the later grafting is a problem.

Kilayim also forbids working different species together. The Mordechai tells that the Rashbam, who always kept his eyes lowered, nearly boarded a wagon pulled by a horse and a mule. His younger brother Rabbeinu Tam stopped him. [Of Mules and Mussar](/daf/bava-basra/133/of-mules-and-mussar) brings Rav Nosson Gestetner's explanation from the Rashbam on Bava Basra 133b. The Rashbam trusted Hashem to guard tzaddikim from mistakes. Rabbeinu Tam held that this protection covers only forbidden foods.

bal-tashchis.heading: Bal Tashchis in the Gemara: Fruit Trees and Wasting Food
bal-tashchis.description: Bal Tashchis in the Gemara: when a fruit tree may be cut down (Bava Kamma 91b), the pomegranate spit (Pesachim 74) and spilled wine (Eruvin 65a).
bal-tashchis.intro:
The Torah forbids cutting down fruit trees during a siege, and this is the source of bal tashchis. Bava Kamma 91b says a palm still yielding a kav of dates may not be cut. Ravina permits it when the wood is worth more than the fruit. Shmuel and Rav Chisda had palms cut down to protect their more valuable vines. Yet Rabbi Chanina said his son died for cutting a fig tree before its time. In [A Fruity Matter](/daf/bava-kamma/91/a-fruity-matter), Rabbi Sebrow explains why poskim treat such cases with extra care even when the halachah permits.

What about cutting for a mitzvah? The Korban Pesach was roasted on a spit of pomegranate wood. [Sowing The Seeds For Mitzvos](/daf/pesachim/74/sowing-the-seeds-for-mitzvos) brings the Panim Yafos: for a great mitzvah, one may even cut down a fruit tree. [A Halachic Argument](/daf/bava-metzia/59/a-halachic-argument) tells how the Belzer Rebbe advised the Pupa yeshiva to build its beis midrash around a fruit tree. Rav Gestetner suggests Rebbe Eliezer's carob tree in Bava Metzia 59b stood inside the beis midrash for the same reason.

Bal tashchis applies to food too. [The Noble Pas Price](/daf/bava-kamma/91/the-noble-pas-price) brings the Minchas Yitzchak: discarding bread to keep a custom of pas Yisrael is not wasteful, since it serves a mitzvah. [Don’t Cry Over Spilled Wine](/daf/eruvin/65/dont-cry-over-spilled-wine) starts from Eruvin 65a, which calls a house where wine is spilled like water blessed. The Rema records a custom to spill Havdalah wine. Many Acharonim call it wasteful, and the Taz simply let the cup overflow.

haircuts-and-peyos.heading: Haircuts and Peyos in the Gemara: Barbers, Peyos and Yom Tov
haircuts-and-peyos.description: Haircuts and Peyos in the Gemara: peyos near the ear (Makkos 20), haircuts on Chol HaMoed (Nazir 38) and a mirror at the barber (Avodah Zarah 29a).
haircuts-and-peyos.intro:
The Torah forbids cutting the peyos. The Rambam explains that idol worshippers cut theirs, though this reason is not in the Gemara. In [Peyos Prohibitions](/daf/makkos/20/peyos-prohibitions), Rabbi Sebrow brings the Rosh, who forbids cutting the peyos of the head close to the skin, even without a razor. The Shulchan Aruch urges following the Rosh. Since the peyos cover the area above and around the ear, a barber should not shave a clean circle there.

A haircut before yom tov is a mitzvah, but the Sages forbade haircuts on Chol HaMoed. [Haircuts on Chol Hamoed](/daf/nazir/38/haircuts-on-chol-hamoed) lists the exceptions, such as a prisoner just released. A nazir who completed his term may also cut his hair then, as the Gemara in Moed Katan says. Based on the custom of a returning ba'al teshuvah, poskim allow a haircut on Chol HaMoed for a mitzvah purpose.

The Mishnah in Avodah Zarah forbids using a non-Jewish barber, who could easily harm his customer. The Gemara advises watching in a mirror, so the barber assumes the customer has government ties (Avodah Zarah 29a). [Mirror Image](/daf/avodah-zarah/29/mirror-image) explains why Tosfos otherwise forbids men to look in a mirror, and why the Rema permits it where it is customary. [Nezirus and Annulling Vows](/daf/nazir/14/nezirus-and-annulling-vows) turns to the Nazir Shimshon, who may never cut his hair. Nazir 14a teaches that his vow cannot be annulled.

tattoos.heading: Tattoos in the Gemara: Permanent Ink and Writing on Skin
tattoos.description: Tattoos in the Gemara: the Mishnah's definition of a forbidden tattoo (Makkos 21a), and whether writing on one's hand is a rabbinic problem (Gittin 20b).
tattoos.intro:
The Torah forbids getting a tattoo. The Mishnah in Makkos 21a defines it. One is liable only for puncturing the skin and inserting ink, or anything that leaves a permanent mark. Is temporary writing on the skin also forbidden, the way temporary writing is rabbinically forbidden on Shabbos? In [The Rights and Wrongs of Writing](/daf/gittin/20/the-rights-and-wrongs-of-writing), Rabbi Sebrow brings the Minchas Chinuch's reading of Tosfos in Gittin 20b. In his view, writing on the skin may be forbidden rabbinically. The Mishnas Chachamim notes that Jews commonly wrote notes on their skin.

Rav Vozner and Rav Chaim Kanievsky both hold that temporary writing on the skin is permitted. Rav Shlomo Zalman allowed doctors to mark the skin before surgery. Rabbi Sebrow also cites Rabbi Dr. Ari Zivotofsky on a common myth. Contrary to popular belief, a Jew with a tattoo may be buried in a Jewish cemetery.

lo-yilbash.heading: Lo Yilbash in the Gemara: Mirrors, Weapons and Men's Clothing
lo-yilbash.description: Lo Yilbash in the Gemara: why men avoid mirrors (Avodah Zarah 29a) and why a woman does not carry weapons (Nazir 59a), with Yael and the tent peg.
lo-yilbash.intro:
The Torah says, "A man's utensils should not be on a woman" (Devarim 22:5). Its simple meaning is that a woman may not wear a man's clothing, and a man may not wear a woman's. Rebbe Eliezer ben Yaakov reads the verse as also forbidding a woman to go out to war with weapons (Nazir 59a).

In [What’s at Stake?](/daf/nazir/59/whats-at-stake), Rabbi Sebrow applies this to Yael. Why did she kill Sisera with a tent peg and not a sword? One commentary says she would not wield a man's weapon. The Avnei Tzedek says she simply had no sword at hand. The Maharsham connects it to a dispute about a woman wearing a man's raincoat in the rain.

The prohibition also covers acts done mainly by women. The Gemara in Avodah Zarah 29a tells a man with a non-Jewish barber to watch in a mirror. The barber will then think he has government ties. Tosfos infers that otherwise a man may not look in a mirror to beautify himself. He permits it for shaving or an eye problem. The Shulchan Aruch agrees, while the Ran and the Rema permit it where men customarily use mirrors.

[Mirror Image](/daf/avodah-zarah/29/mirror-image) explains why many chassidishe wedding halls have no mirrors in the men's rooms. [A Moment of Reflection](/daf/avodah-zarah/29/a-moment-of-reflection) adds a debate about checking tefillin in a mirror. The Divrei Chaim of Sanz opposed it, while the Brisker Rav and Rav Henoch Leibowitz checked their tefillin every day.

hafrashas-challah.heading: Hafrashas Challah in the Gemara: Baking, Matzah and Shabbos
hafrashas-challah.description: Hafrashas Challah in the Gemara: fruit-juice dough that cannot become chametz (Menachos 57a) and the Lechem HaPanim that stayed warm (Menachos 96b).
hafrashas-challah.intro:
The Rema writes of a custom to knead enough dough for hafrashas challah when baking for Shabbos. One should not deviate from it, he adds. Rabbi Sebrow's articles look at what happens when that mitzvah meets other values. In [Fresh, Hot Challah](/daf/menachos/96/fresh-hot-challah), a reader asks a question. Is it better to bake a large batch every three weeks and freeze it, or bake fresh each week and skip the mitzvah? Based on Rav Elyashiv, oneg Shabbos comes first, so fresh challah may win. The article also traces warm Friday challah to the Lechem HaPanim, which stayed warm all week (Menachos 96b).

[The Mysterious Matzah](/daf/menachos/57/the-mysterious-matzah) starts from Menachos 57a: dough made with fruit juice cannot become chametz. Egg matzah made without water cannot become tamei, so the challah taken from it cannot be burned. The Mishnah Berurah advises giving it to a kohen's young child. The article ends by solving a family mystery: a grandfather's half-matzah in the bedikas chametz bag was challah, burned with the chametz.

pidyon-shevuyim.heading: Pidyon Shevuyim in the Gemara: Redeeming Captives
pidyon-shevuyim.description: Pidyon Shevuyim in the Gemara: how Rebbe Meir freed Bruriah's sister (Avodah Zarah 18), and does a ransom pay off an old loan? (Kesubos 91b).
pidyon-shevuyim.intro:
Redeeming a captive is a tremendous mitzvah. In [Rebbe Meir and the Power of “Eloka d’Meir Aneini”](/daf/avodah-zarah/18/rebbe-meir-and-the-power-of-eloka-dmeir-aneini), Rabbi Sebrow retells the Gemara's story in Avodah Zarah 18. Bruriah's sister was held captive, and Rebbe Meir bribed the guard to free her. He taught the guard to say, "G-d of Meir, answer me," which stopped vicious dogs and later saved the guard from execution. The story became the source of a well-known segulah for finding lost items.

What if the person who paid the ransom owed the captive money? In [A Ring of Truth](/daf/kesubos/91/a-ring-of-truth), Shimon gives his ring to free Reuven, who then asks Shimon to repay an old loan. The Ben Ish Chai cites Kesubos 91b, where orphans paid a creditor without saying what the money was for. Abaye ruled it counted as paying their father's debt.
