So too, Shimon's ring was simply the mitzvah of pidyon shevuyim, and he still owes the loan. The same case appears in [Paying It Forward (And Back)](/daf/kesubos/91/paying-it-forward-and-back).

kashrus.heading: Kashrus in the Gemara: Kosher Food Then and Now
kashrus.description: Kashrus in the Gemara: checking lungs and glatt meat (Chullin 46), bee honey and civet coffee (Bechoros 7a), Yalta's kosher substitutes (Chullin 109b).
kashrus.intro:
The Gemara in Chullin lists many defects that make an animal treif even after proper shechitah. We rely on the rule that most animals are not treif, so we do not check every organ. But lesions on cows' lungs are common, so the lungs must be checked. In [Glatt Or Not?](/daf/chullin/46/glatt-or-not), Rabbi Sebrow explains that "glatt" means a smooth lung. He also explains how Beis Yosef glatt sets a stricter standard than ordinary glatt kosher.

Modern foods raise new questions. Bechoros 7a teaches that bee honey is kosher, though the bee is not. One view says the bee only carries the nectar. [Is Civet Coffee Kosher?](/daf/bechoros/7/is-civet-coffee-kosher) applies this to coffee beans that pass through a civet. Rav Dovid Feinstein permitted the coffee, since the beans come out whole and unchanged.

Some questions turn on small creatures. In [Bugging Out](/daf/chullin/100/bugging-out), a flea jumps into the stew at the Chavos Yair's Tu B'Av meal. A whole bug is never nullified, so he would not eat. The Panim Meiros first permitted the stew, then agreed he was right.

Other articles look at the person eating. [The Accidental Aveirah](/daf/kesubos/85/the-accidental-aveirah) asks whether people who bought treif meat from a butcher who only looked frum must do teshuvah. Rav Moshe Feinstein's answer draws on Rava's trust in his wife in Kesubos 85a. Another article, on kosher pork, recalls Yalta's teaching that for every forbidden food Hashem made a permitted twin (Chullin 109b).

basar-bechalav.heading: Basar BeChalav in the Gemara: Meat, Milk and Waiting
basar-bechalav.description: Basar BeChalav in the Gemara: Mar Ukva's waiting between meat and milk (Chullin 105a), fish on a meat plate (Chullin 111b), meat bread (Pesachim 30a).
basar-bechalav.intro:
How long should one wait after meat before eating dairy? Mar Ukva said, "I am like vinegar from wine compared to my father" (Chullin 105a). His father waited 24 hours, while he waited only from one meal to the next. In [Skipping Steps or Grabbing Dessert?](/daf/chullin/105/skipping-steps-or-grabbing-dessert), Rabbi Sebrow asks why Mar Ukva did not simply wait longer. Rav Yisrael Salanter answers that spiritual growth comes step by step, like the courses of a fine meal.

The Gemara also deals with flavor that passes through a utensil. Pesachim 30a forbids baking bread in an oven smeared with fat, so all bread stays pareve. Chullin 111b says hot fish placed on a meat plate may be eaten with milk. This is "nat bar nat," two steps of flavor transfer. [The Hot Dog That Got Nathan in Hot Water](/daf/chullin/111/the-hot-dog-that-got-nathan-in-hot-water) applies it to a son who cooks hot dogs in his mother's coffee urn. Based on the Vilna Gaon and the Chochmas Adam, after cleaning it and waiting 24 hours, she may add milk to its water. The same story, with the Pesachim side, appears in [In Hot Water](/daf/pesachim/30/in-hot-water).

Modern products bring new questions. In [What’s the Right ‘Whey’?](/daf/zevachim/74/whats-the-right-whey), two friends argue over "non-dairy" creamer that contains a milk derivative. The answer, from Rav Yisrael Belsky, depends on whether the drinker keeps cholov Yisrael.

shechitah.heading: Shechitah in the Gemara: Kosher Slaughter and Treifos
shechitah.description: Shechitah in the Gemara: a treif knife on kosher meat (Chullin 8b), a cut windpipe (Chullin 44b), and the whole neck fit for shechitah (Chullin 45a).
shechitah.intro:
Masechta Chullin deals mainly with preparing kosher meat. The Gemara in Chullin 8b discusses an animal slaughtered with a treif knife. Rav says the area the knife touched must be peeled, while Rabbah bar bar Chanah says washing is enough. In [Trimming The Fat](/daf/chullin/8/trimming-the-fat), Rabbi Sebrow asks if butchers must peel meat cut with the knife used to remove cheilev. Tosfos and other Rishonim say no, since the fat is cold. He confirmed with a supervisor at Gourmet Glatt that this is still the practice.

Where on the neck may one shecht? Chullin 45a teaches that the entire neck is fit, from the top ring of the windpipe down to the lung. So, as [From Savanna to Supper?](/daf/chullin/45/from-savanna-to-supper) notes, the old answer about the giraffe's long neck is wrong. The real question is mesorah, a tradition of eating a species, which also affects zebu and bison.

In Chullin 44b, an animal with a partly cut windpipe came before Rav, who left it undecided. Rabba bar bar Chana then ruled it kosher and bought its meat. [The Watermelon Mystery: From Chullin to the Dessert Table](/daf/chullin/44/the-watermelon-mystery-from-chullin-to-the-dessert-table) uses this to ask when one rabbi may rule on what another forbade.

Other articles look at the animal's organs. [Glatt Or Not?](/daf/chullin/46/glatt-or-not) explains why cows' lungs must be checked for lesions. [Kosher Questions](/daf/chullin/17/kosher-questions) asks about meat killed without shechitah in the desert and then brought into Eretz Yisrael (Chullin 17a).

bishul-akum-and-pas-akum.heading: Bishul Akum and Pas Akum in the Gemara: Food Made by a Non-Jew
bishul-akum-and-pas-akum.description: Bishul Akum and Pas Akum in the Gemara: Shmuel's cooked wine and Avleit (Avodah Zarah 30a), and cooked food, bread and oil (Avodah Zarah 35b).
bishul-akum-and-pas-akum.intro:
Chazal forbade some foods made by a non-Jew even when every ingredient is kosher. The Gemara in Avodah Zarah 35b lists cooked food, bread and oil. A special beis din later permitted the oil, but bishul akum still stands. Pas palter, bread from a non-Jewish bakery, is the subject of a dispute. In [Top-seeded Treat](/daf/avodah-zarah/35/top-seeded-treat), Rabbi Sebrow explains that the Rema permits it even where pas Yisrael is available. He also offers a playful reason why hamantaschen need their dough.

Wine has its own rules. In Avodah Zarah 30a, the gentile scholar Avleit avoided touching Shmuel's wine, but Shmuel said it made no difference, since the wine was cooked. [Mevushal or Lo Mevushal: That Is The Question](/daf/avodah-zarah/30/mevushal-or-lo-mevushal-that-is-the-question) asks whether pasteurized wine counts as cooked. Rav Moshe Feinstein said yes, while Rav Elyashiv, Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach and others disagreed.

Factory foods raise a modern question. [Pasta Imposter](/daf/avodah-zarah/74/pasta-imposter) explains why one brand's oven-ready lasagna lacks an OU. Rav Moshe held that bishul akum may not apply to food made with specialized factory equipment. The OU relies on this only together with another leniency. [The Noble Pas Price](/daf/bava-kamma/91/the-noble-pas-price) discusses the custom to eat only pas Yisrael during the Aseres Yemei Teshuvah. May one throw out bakery bread, or is that bal tashchis?

tevilas-keilim.heading: Tevilas Keilim in the Gemara: Immersing New Utensils
tevilas-keilim.description: Tevilas Keilim in the Gemara: the mitzvah in Avodah Zarah 75, a borrowed utensil after 30 days (Menachos 44a), and toveling on Shabbos (Beitzah 36a).
tevilas-keilim.intro:
The end of Masechta Avodah Zarah discusses the biblical mitzvah of tevilas keilim. A metal or glass food utensil acquired from a gentile must be immersed in a mikveh. In [Tevilas Keilim: Clearing The Confusion](/daf/avodah-zarah/75/tevilas-keilim-clearing-the-confusion), Rabbi Sebrow corrects common myths. A utensil may not be used even once before tevilah. Yet food cooked in it by mistake is not treif. Not every lake is a kosher mikveh, and much silver Judaica is made outside Israel and needs tevilah.

A utensil borrowed from a gentile needs no tevilah. [On Borrowed Time](/daf/menachos/44/on-borrowed-time) links this to Menachos 44a: a garment borrowed for thirty days needs tzitzis, since it starts to look owned. So too, the Mishnah Berurah says, a borrowed utensil needs tevilah after thirty days, at least rabbinically. The article applies this to a Keurig machine that would break if immersed.

The same trick helps on Shabbos. The Shulchan Aruch notes a dispute about toveling on Shabbos, and suggests giving the utensil to a gentile and borrowing it back. [Business Or Pleasure?](/daf/beitzah/36/business-or-pleasure) asks how this fits with the Mishnah Berurah's ruling against giving gifts on Shabbos.

Other articles bring the mitzvah home. In [Mishloach Manos From Rebbi to Talmid](/daf/megillah/7/mishloach-manos-from-rebbi-to-talmid), Rabbi Sebrow toveled 100 glass saltshakers given as Purim gifts. [On Amtrak, Alabama, and Assumptions](/daf/rosh-hashanah/22/on-amtrak-alabama-and-assumptions) asks when a child can be trusted to say a utensil was toveled.

chadash-and-yashan.heading: Chadash and Yashan in the Gemara: New Grain and the Omer
chadash-and-yashan.description: Chadash and Yashan in the Gemara: new grain before the Omer (Menachos 68), and why Rebbe Yochanan ben Zakkai waited all of 16 Nissan (Rosh Hashanah 30a).
chadash-and-yashan.intro:
The Torah forbids eating from the new crop of grain until the Omer is offered on the 16th of Nissan (Vayikra 23:14). Without a Beis HaMikdash, the day itself permits the grain. In [Everything Old Is New Again](/daf/menachos/68/everything-old-is-new-again), Rabbi Sebrow explains the dispute in Menachos. Rav and Shmuel permit the new grain from the morning of the 16th, while Rebbe Yehudah says the whole day must pass. He uses a New York sidewalk ticket written at exactly 9:00 a.m. to explain "ad v'lo ad bichlal." The article also explains why many in the Diaspora are lenient about yashan.

The Mishnah in Rosh Hashanah 30a records that Rebbe Yochanan ben Zakkai forbade new grain for the entire 16th. When the Beis HaMikdash is rebuilt, people might eat it in the morning out of habit. He made this decree together with the one to take the lulav all seven days. Why together? In [Takana Considerations](/daf/rosh-hashanah/30/takana-considerations), Rebbe Moshe Betzalel explains that the lulav decree made people fear the Beis HaMikdash was far off. The grain decree showed it could be rebuilt next year. [Don’t Despair](/daf/rosh-hashanah/30/dont-despair) draws from this a lesson about overcoming despair in teshuvah.

cholov-yisrael.heading: Cholov Yisrael in the Gemara: Milk Supervised by a Jew
cholov-yisrael.description: Cholov Yisrael in the Gemara: may one who keeps cholov Yisrael use non-dairy creamer with a milk derivative? A debate set while learning Zevachim 74.
cholov-yisrael.intro:
Some people see cholov Yisrael as a chumrah, while others treat it as required. In [What’s the Right ‘Whey’?](/daf/zevachim/74/whats-the-right-whey), Rabbi Sebrow tells of two friends learning the perek on mixtures in Zevachim. Shimon pours "non-dairy" creamer into his coffee, and Boruch points out that it contains a milk derivative. Is the small amount nullified? Boruch argues that buying it means relying on bittul on purpose, which is forbidden.

The answer, from Rav Yisrael Belsky, depends on the person. For someone strict about cholov Yisrael, the milk is a forbidden ingredient, so he may not use the creamer. For someone who does not keep cholov Yisrael, the creamer is fully kosher, just not pareve. He may drink it in coffee even after a meat meal.

marriage.heading: Marriage in the Gemara: Kiddushin, Weddings and Shidduchim
marriage.description: Marriage in the Gemara: why weddings were held on Wednesday (Kesubos 2a), an unnamed kallah (Kiddushin 52a), and marrying for money (Kiddushin 70a).
marriage.intro:
The first Mishnah in Kesubos says a first-time bride generally marries on Wednesday. The courts met on Thursday, so any question could be settled the next day. Bar Kapara adds a blessing: the marriage begins on the fifth day, when Hashem blessed the fish to be fruitful. [Wednesday is the Day to Wed](/daf/kesubos/2/wednesday-is-the-day-to-wed) asks why so few dates are left once customs are added. It ends with the Steipler's advice: the best date is the earliest one.

Kiddushin must be clear. Tosfos in Kiddushin 52a tells of Rav Oshaya HaLevi's son, who gave a ring for "your daughter" without saying which one. A sage ruled he could marry none of them. In [Kiddushin Conundrum](/daf/kiddushin/52/kiddushin-conundrum), Rabbi Sebrow explains Rav Moshe Feinstein's view that marrying the oldest daughter first is a custom, not a halacha. And [Egg-sploring the Halacha](/daf/kiddushin/60/egg-sploring-the-halacha) asks whether an egg is worth the perutah needed for kiddushin.

What about choosing a spouse? Kiddushin 70a warns that one who marries only for money will have children who act wrongly. [Marrying for Money](/daf/kiddushin/70/marrying-for-money) shows the Rivash limiting this to a woman of tainted lineage. The Vilna Gaon says a man may not end a shidduch just over money. In [Leave the Rest to Hashem](/daf/yevamos/49/leave-the-rest-to-hashem), Chizkiya foresaw wicked children and refused to marry. Yeshaya HaNavi told him to keep the halacha and leave the future to Hashem.

kesubah.heading: Kesubah in the Gemara: The Marriage Contract
kesubah.description: Kesubah in the Gemara: R' Meir's rule that a couple needs a valid kesubah (Kesubos 54b), and Abaye's plan for the poor Rav Huna (Bava Basra 174b).
kesubah.intro:
Chazal wanted a wife to feel secure that her husband would not divorce her on a whim. So R' Meir taught that a couple may not live together if the kesubah is cut below the minimum (Kesubos 54b). The Gemara adds that the same is true if it is lost. In [Kesubah Conundrums](/daf/kesubos/54/kesubah-conundrums-kesubos-54), Rabbi Sebrow explains what to do when a kesubah is lost. He works out that the basic 200 zuz comes to about $519. He also warns that blank spaces and unnoted cross-outs can make a kesubah invalid.

A kesubah can be guaranteed by someone else. In [A Matter of Opinion](/daf/bava-basra/174/a-matter-of-opinion), Rav Huna's wealthy father guaranteed his daughter-in-law's kesubah but did not support his poor son. Abaye thought Rav Huna could divorce his wife so she could collect from the father, and then remarry her. Then he learned Rav Huna was a kohen, who could not remarry her (Bava Basra 174b).

divorce.heading: Divorce in the Gemara: The Laws of the Get
divorce.description: Divorce in the Gemara: a get found in the trash (Gittin 3b), who may write a get (Gittin 22b), and a get forced by beis din (Bava Basra 48).
divorce.intro:
Must a get be written for the couple who will use it? R' Meir says no, as long as the witnesses sign at the husband's request. So the Gemara in Gittin 3b says a man who found a get with matching names in the trash may use it. In [Down In The Dumps](/daf/gittin/3/down-in-the-dumps), Rabbi Sebrow asks why the Gemara uses the past tense. The Yad Paltiel answers that the man should not see the found get as a sign from Heaven to divorce his wife. The lesson is that we cannot always read Divine signals.

The Mishnah in Gittin 22b says anyone may write a get, even a child. Tosfos explains that the writer need not be the husband's agent. [No Monkeying Around](/daf/gittin/22/no-monkeying-around) cites the Chasam Sofer that, in theory, even a monkey could write it. In practice, though, one may not rely on this.

The Gemara in Bava Basra 48 rules that a get is valid when beis din compels a stubborn husband to give it. [Harping on Divided Real Estate](/daf/bava-basra/48/harping-on-divided-real-estate) brings Tosfos' explanation: the mitzvah of divorcing her counts as his payment. In [Muktzeh Marvels](/daf/gittin/77/muktzeh-marvels), a dying man wants to give a get on Shabbos to spare his wife yibbum. The Rishonim debate whether the get is muktzeh.

yibbum-and-chalitzah.heading: Yibbum and Chalitzah in the Gemara: Levirate Marriage
yibbum-and-chalitzah.description: Yibbum and Chalitzah in the Gemara: removing the shoe from the right foot (Yevamos 104), a nicer parah adumah (Shevuos 11b), and the hardest masechta.
yibbum-and-chalitzah.intro:
When a married man dies without children, his widow falls to yibbum with his brother. Nowadays chalitzah is almost always done instead. The widow removes her brother-in-law's shoe and is then free to remarry. The Gemara in Yevamos 104 requires the shoe to come off his right foot. In [Left Foot, Right Foot](/daf/yevamos/104/left-foot-right-foot), Rabbi Sebrow asks what to do if the yavam is left-footed. There are four opinions, and the Rema says the custom is to remove a shoe from both feet.

[Waxing About Oil](/daf/shevuos/11/waxing-about-oil) brings the Beis Yaakov's ruling: once chalitzah has begun with a younger brother, we do not switch to the older one. The Shevus Yaakov applies this to wax candles already in the menorah. The Chacham Tzvi disagrees, based on Shevuos 11b, where a nicer parah adumah replaces the first one. [Yibum and Tzitzis](/daf/yevamos/4/yibum-and-tzitzis) explains why Yevamos is known as one of the hardest masechtos in Shas.

chinuch.heading: Chinuch in the Gemara: Raising and Teaching Children
chinuch.description: Chinuch in the Gemara: training children to keep mitzvos (Yevamos 114a), Rebbe Chiya's pupils teaching each other (Bava Metzia 85b), Eruvin 13a.
chinuch.intro:
A father has a mitzvah to train his children to keep mitzvos and avoid sins. Yevamos 114a tells how Rav Yitzchak bar Bisna lost the beis midrash keys on Shabbos. Rebbe Pedas told him to let children play near them and lead them back. In [The Key to Success in Chinuch](/daf/yevamos/114/the-key-to-success-in-chinuch), Rabbi Sebrow explains when this mitzvah of chinuch begins. Rav Moshe Feinstein adds that parents must show children how much they enjoy a mitzvah.

The Gemara also teaches how to teach. Rebbe Chiya planted flax, made nets, hunted deer and wrote Chumashim on their hides (Bava Metzia 85b). Then each child he taught had to teach the others. [Rebbe Chiya: The Ultimate Teacher](/daf/bava-metzia/85/rebbe-chiya-the-ultimate-teacher) explains why he did it all himself. In [Teaching Lessons From The Tanna’im](/daf/eruvin/13/teaching-lessons-from-the-tannaim), Rebbe Akiva praises a student's wrong idea to sharpen his students' minds (Eruvin 13a).

Children must also learn to think. [Yearn To Learn](/daf/megillah/3/yearn-to-learn) tells how Rav Moshe Feinstein opposed funding a Torah picture book. Children must use their minds, not be spoon-fed. [Schooled On The Competition](/daf/bava-basra/21/schooled-on-the-competition) cites Ezra's decree in Bava Basra that teachers may open next to each other. Competition among teachers increases wisdom, but a school may not recruit another school's students.

jewish-names.heading: Jewish Names in the Gemara: Naming and the Power of a Name
jewish-names.description: Jewish Names in the Gemara: Amrafel and Nimrod (Eruvin 53), the names of Avraham's and Dovid's mothers (Bava Basra 91a), and Rav called Abba (Yevamos 57b).
jewish-names.intro:
The Gemara in Yoma says one may not name a child after a rasha. In [What’s In A Name?](/daf/eruvin/53/whats-in-a-name), Rabbi Sebrow brings the dispute in Eruvin 53 over whether Amrafel's real name was Nimrod. The Toras Chaim suggests the ban covers only real names, not nicknames. So it matters which name was the real one.

Some names carry hidden meaning. Bava Basra 91a records the names of Avraham Avinu's mother, Dovid HaMelech's mother, and even Shimshon's sister. [What’s in a Name?](/daf/bava-basra/91/whats-in-a-name-2024) brings Rav Yaakov Kamenetsky's view of why the sister's name was recorded. It shows Shimshon had a father and mother, an answer to heretics. In [What’s In A Name?](/daf/sanhedrin/10/whats-in-a-name-2017), the odd names of Achashveirosh's seven advisers recall the Beis HaMikdash service.

Names also touch on respect and marriage. Shmuel called Rav "Abba" (Yevamos 57b). Rashi says it was a title of honor, while Tosfos says it was Rav's real name. [Abba, My Dear](/daf/yevamos/57/abba-my-dear) asks whether a child may call his father "Abba" if that is his name. [Cautionary Customs](/daf/menachos/29/cautionary-customs) discusses Rebbi Yehuda HaChassid's warning against marrying someone with a parent's name. The Noda BeYehuda said it was meant only for his own descendants. Yet the Steipler had one sick man's wife change her name, and he recovered.

tznius.heading: Tznius in the Gemara: Modesty in Dress and Conduct
tznius.description: Tznius in the Gemara: Rabbi Chanina ben Teradyon's daughter and her gait (Avodah Zarah 18), and Yael, Sisera and a woman's weapons (Nazir 59a).
tznius.intro:
The Gemara in Avodah Zarah 18 asks why Rabbi Chanina ben Teradyon's family suffered under Rome. His daughter once heard Roman nobles praise her gait, and she tried to walk even more gracefully. That was a lapse in the modesty expected of a bas Yisrael, and as a tzadeikes she was judged strictly. In [Accounting For All](/daf/avodah-zarah/18/accounting-for-all), Rabbi Sebrow adds the Chasam Sofer's view: her mother should have made sure the daughter kept tznius.

[What’s at Stake?](/daf/nazir/59/whats-at-stake) looks at Yael. Rebbe Eliezer ben Yaakov teaches that a woman should not go to war with a man's weapons (Nazir 59a). One commentary says that is why Yael killed Sisera with a tent peg. An article on Torah.org, which he quotes, sees in this how Yael kept her modesty even in a moment of crisis.

taharas-hamishpacha.heading: Taharas HaMishpacha in the Gemara: The Mikvah
taharas-hamishpacha.description: Taharas HaMishpacha in the Gemara: water in the ground as a mikvah and the size of a mikvah (Pesachim 17b), and an Omaha mikvah drained by mistake.
taharas-hamishpacha.intro:
A mikvah used by people must hold 40 seah of water, about 575 liters according to the Chazon Ish. Rav Papa explains in Pesachim that water gathered in the ground is a mikvah and cannot become tamei. Tosfos in Pesachim 17b says the ban on filling a mikvah with drawn water is rabbinic. Most mikvaos are filled with rainwater carried from the roof.

In [The Iceman Cometh](/daf/pesachim/17/the-iceman-cometh), Rabbi Sebrow tells of the only mikvah in Omaha, which a custodian drained by mistake during a drought. The Shulchan Aruch rules that melted ice is like rain, so the community brought in more than a ton of ice. Then a heavy storm filled the rainwater pool anyway. Rabbi Yaakov Weiss saw the rain as Hashem answering the community's effort.

adoption.heading: Adoption in the Gemara: Raising Another's Child
adoption.description: Adoption in the Gemara: why Meirav's sons are called Michal's (Sanhedrin 19b), and calling an adopted son to the Torah by his adoptive father's name.
adoption.intro:
The Navi says that Michal, Shaul's daughter, had five sons, though Michal died childless. The Gemara in Sanhedrin 19b explains that they were her sister Meirav's sons. Rebbe Yehoshua ben Korcha says Michal raised them after Meirav died. The Navi calls them hers to teach that one who raises an orphan is considered as if he gave birth to him.

In [Marrying Meirav and Michal](/daf/sanhedrin/19/marrying-meirav-and-michal), Rabbi Sebrow shows how this lesson reaches practical halacha. The Rema permits a document to call a stepson a son, and the Vilna Gaon traces this to the Gemara. Based on this, Rav Moshe Feinstein ruled that an adopted son may be called to the Torah by his adoptive father's name. Rav Shlomo Zalman reportedly disagreed.

ribbis.heading: Ribbis in the Gemara: The Prohibition of Interest
ribbis.description: Ribbis in the Gemara: lending a loaf of bread (Bava Metzia 75a), a borrower's blessing (Shevuos 44a), and a moneylender's grave (Bava Metzia 70b).
ribbis.intro:
Lending money is a mitzvah, but charging interest is forbidden. Lending food is tricky. Tosfos in Bava Metzia 75a explains that if the price rises before it is repaid, the lender profits. So Chazal forbade lending food items. In [Neither a Lender Nor a Borrower Be?](/daf/bava-metzia/75/neither-a-lender-nor-a-borrower-be), Rabbi Sebrow explains when neighbors may still borrow bread, eggs or ketchup. A borrower of eleven eggs may not return a full dozen.

Even words can be ribbis. A borrower may not bless his lender. Tosafos uses this to explain Rebbi Yitzchak's teaching in Shevuos 44a that a lender acquires the collateral. One article on the word "shkoyach" asks whether a borrower may say it to his lender. The Nesivos Shalom permits it when said without thinking of its literal meaning.

In [A Matter Of Great Interest](/daf/bava-metzia/70/a-matter-of-great-interest), Rabbi Akiva Eiger explains why a moneylender's grave cost 2,000 rubles. The article traces his source to a Targum quoted by Tosfos in Bava Metzia 70b.

loans.heading: Loans in the Gemara: Lending, Repaying and Collecting
loans.description: Loans in the Gemara: repaying loans that saved lives (Kesubos 19a), what a creditor leaves a debtor (Bava Metzia 113b), unclear payments (Kesubos 91b).
loans.intro:
Must a loan that saved lives be repaid? In [Stealing to Save a Life?](/daf/kesubos/19/stealing-to-save-a-life), the Bobover Rebbe borrowed to buy visas during the Holocaust. A lender later demanded full repayment at once. Kesubos 19a teaches that saving a life overrides almost every prohibition. Still, Rav Moshe Feinstein ruled that the loans must be repaid, just as one who steals to save a life must pay it back.

The Gemara also protects debtors. A beraisa in Bava Metzia 113b says a creditor must leave a debtor two beds, one for eating and one for sleeping. [Walks of Life](/daf/bava-metzia/113/walks-of-life) explains why: Shmuel warns against sleeping right after eating without a short walk. In [Can You Save Me a Seat?](/daf/gittin/11/can-you-save-me-a-seat), two friends debate saving a bus seat. They draw on Gittin 11b, about seizing a debtor's assets for one creditor at the others' expense.

Repayment must be clear. In [A Ring of Truth](/daf/kesubos/91/a-ring-of-truth), orphans paid a creditor without saying what for, and Abaye counted it toward their father's debt (Kesubos 91b). In [Purim Torah Rings True](/daf/bava-basra/45/purim-torah-rings-true), Rabbi Sebrow applies a rule of Bava Basra 45a to Haman's ring. A borrower who took an item without witnesses may claim he returned it.

damages.heading: Damages in the Gemara: Fire, Goring Oxen and Saving Lives
damages.description: Damages in the Gemara: fire as an arrow (Bava Kamma 60), escaped lions and goring oxen (Bava Kamma 15), and cargo thrown overboard (Bava Kamma 116).
damages.intro:
Seder Nezikin deals with an ox, a pit, fire and a person who causes damage. The Gemara in Bava Kamma 60 records a basic dispute about fire. Rebbe Yochanan holds that fire is like an arrow a person shoots: the one who lit it is responsible wherever it spreads. In [We Need To Start The Fire](/daf/bava-kamma/60/we-need-to-start-the-fire), Rabbi Sebrow brings a question of the Nemukei Yosef. If every flame counts as the lighter's act, how can anyone light Shabbos candles? The answer is that all of it is considered lit at the moment of ignition, on erev Shabbos.

Animals fill much of Bava Kamma. Bava Kamma 15b asks whether a lion can ever be tame. [Roaring Lions and Goring Oxen](/daf/bava-kamma/15/roaring-lions-and-goring-oxen) uses an escaped circus lion in Italy to explain the dispute. It also covers Rebbe Meir's view on an ox that gores three times in one day. That view became a real halacha about saying Vesein Tal Umatar. A shepherd who leaves his flock is the subject of [It’s a Miracle](/daf/bava-metzia/106/its-a-miracle). Can the owner claim that a miracle would have saved the sheep?

Sometimes damage is done to save lives. Bava Kamma 61b tells how Dovid HaMelech asked whether his army could burn a private field where the Philistines were hiding. Three warriors risked their lives to bring the answer from the Sanhedrin, as told in [Do We Need to Suffer for Torah?](/daf/bava-kamma/61/do-we-need-to-suffer-for-torah). In [Gold Overboard](/daf/bava-kamma/116/gold-overboard), two travelers argue over who pays when cargo is thrown into a stormy sea to keep a ship afloat.

theft-and-robbery.heading: Theft and Robbery in the Gemara: Returning What Was Taken
theft-and-robbery.description: Theft in the Gemara: a stolen item after the owner despairs (Bava Kamma 67), stealing to save a life (Kesubos 19), paying the butcher on time (Yoma 86).
theft-and-robbery.intro:
The Gemara teaches that a thief who does teshuvah must return what he took. If he still has the item itself, he must give it back and cannot pay money instead. But what if the owner has already given up hope of ever seeing it again? That question, called yiush, was debated in the beis medrash for decades (Bava Kamma 67b). Rabbi Sebrow tells the story in [Do Not Despair](/daf/bava-kamma/67/do-not-despair). Rav Yosef held the item must still be returned, and after 22 years he finally answered Abaye's strong question. The halacha follows him.

What about someone who eats stolen food without knowing it? In [Stolen Wedding Food](/daf/bava-kamma/111/stolen-wedding-food), a father of the bride accidentally takes the wrong food from the caterer. Can the caterer collect from the guests who ate it? The two friends work through Rav Chisda, the Baal HaMaor, Tosfos and the Machne Efraim, and end with the rule of paying for benefit received.

May a person steal to save a life? The Gemara in Kesubos 19a says that nothing stands in the way of saving lives except murder, idolatry and arayos. After the Holocaust, the Bobover Rebbe was asked to repay loans he had used to save Jews. [Stealing to Save a Life?](/daf/kesubos/19/stealing-to-save-a-life) explains why Rav Moshe Feinstein ruled that such loans must be repaid. Honesty also means avoiding suspicion. Rav said it would be a chillul Hashem if he did not pay the butcher promptly (Yoma 86a). Rabbi Sebrow applies this to a case of seltzer in [Shopping Cart Considerations](/daf/yoma/86/shopping-cart-considerations).

lost-objects.heading: Lost Objects in the Gemara: Finding and Returning
lost-objects.description: Lost objects in the Gemara: items switched at a wedding (Bava Basra 46), healing as returning what was lost (Yoma 49), and Rebbe Meir (Avodah Zarah 18).
lost-objects.intro:
The mitzvah of returning a lost object reaches further than we might think. Suppose utensils were accidentally switched at a house of mourning or a wedding. The Gemara in Bava Basra 46a says you may not use the one left with you without permission. In [Lost in the Shuffle](/daf/bava-basra/46/lost-in-the-shuffle), Rabbi Sebrow applies this to a wrong coat taken from a shul on a rainy night. Rav Moshe Feinstein advised every shul to post a sign granting permission in advance. Rav Asher Weiss adds that an unclaimed item can often be kept if its value is written down.

The Rambam writes that healing a person is part of the mitzvah of returning a lost object, since one returns his health. [Good Help Is Hard To Find](/daf/yoma/49/good-help-is-hard-to-find) uses this to ask whether a doctor may charge. A finder may charge for time taken off paid work, and so may a doctor. And for those still searching, [Rebbe Meir and the Power of “Eloka d’Meir Aneini”](/daf/avodah-zarah/18/rebbe-meir-and-the-power-of-eloka-dmeir-aneini) tells how Rebbe Meir rescued Bruriah's sister. That story is the source of the well-known segulah of giving tzedakah in memory of Rebbe Meir Baal Hanes.

business-ethics.heading: Business Ethics in the Gemara: Honesty, Prices and Fair Competition
business-ethics.description: Business ethics in the Gemara: Rav Safra's honesty (Bava Basra 89), lowering prices (Bava Basra 166), and competing teachers (Bava Basra 21).
business-ethics.intro:
The Torah asks for honesty beyond what the law requires. Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakai spent forty years in business and knew every trick of dishonest dealers. He hesitated to teach about them, fearing cheats would learn new methods. In the end he gave the shiur (Bava Basra 89a). [In All Honesty](/daf/bava-basra/89/in-all-honesty) also tells of Rav Safra, who was saying Shema when a customer kept raising his offer. Rav Safra sold at the first price, which he had already accepted in his heart.

The Gemara also teaches that leaders may step in when prices are unfair. Bava Basra 166a tells how birds for korbanos rose to a gold dinar a pair. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel made a ruling that dropped the price to a hundredth. In [A Sea-rious Story](/daf/bava-basra/166/a-sea-rious-story), the Tzemach Tzedek follows his lead and bans buying fish, even for Shabbos, when fishmongers raise prices too high.

What about competition? Ezra decreed that teachers could open next to other teachers, because rivalry among scholars increases wisdom (Bava Basra 21). [Schooled On The Competition](/daf/bava-basra/21/schooled-on-the-competition) explains that a new school may open, but may not actively recruit students from another. Even saving a seat on a crowded bus raises questions of fairness. [Can You Save Me a Seat?](/daf/gittin/11/can-you-save-me-a-seat) works through the Gemara in Gittin 11b about grabbing a debtor's money for one creditor at the expense of others.

workers-and-employers.heading: Workers and Employers in the Gemara: Rights on Both Sides
workers-and-employers.description: Workers in the Gemara: a worker may quit (Bava Metzia 10), sick pay for a servant (Kiddushin 17), and forgiving porters who broke barrels (Bava Metzia 83).
workers-and-employers.intro:
The Gemara teaches that a worker is never truly owned. Bava Metzia 10a says a day laborer may quit in the middle of the day. Jews are servants of Hashem, not servants of servants. [One, Two, Three Years You're Out At The Old Ball Game](/daf/bava-metzia/10/one-two-three-years-youre-out-at-the-old-ball-game) starts with a baseball contract. Rabbi Sebrow asks whether a work contract may run longer than three years.

What if a worker gets sick? The Gemara in Kiddushin 17a says an eved Ivri who was ill for two years owes his master nothing. [The Price to Pay](/daf/kiddushin/17/the-price-to-pay) compares a day laborer and a rebbe who falls ill. Tosfos and the Maharam Mi'Rottenberg offer two different explanations, one of them revealed in a dream. An employer must also keep to what was agreed. [Rise and Shine](/daf/yoma/21/rise-and-shine) learns from the kohanim in Yoma 21a that rising early is harder than staying up late. So a worker hired for night shifts need not accept a predawn shift.

The Gemara also asks employers to go beyond the letter of the law. Porters broke Rabbah bar bar Chana's barrels of wine, and he took their cloaks (Bava Metzia 83a). Rav told him to return them and even pay their wages, since the workers were poor. Rabbi Sebrow tells the story, along with a nick at the barbershop, in [A Cut Above](/daf/bava-metzia/83/a-cut-above).

buying-and-selling.heading: Buying and Selling in the Gemara: Kinyanim, Raffles and Sales
buying-and-selling.description: Buying and selling in the Gemara: trapped animals (Gittin 59), a sale made under duress (Bava Basra 48), and redoing a raffle (Bava Basra 106).
buying-and-selling.intro:
The Gemara teaches that ownership begins with a proper kinyan, an act of acquisition. Looking at an object or chasing it is not enough. The Mishna in Gittin 59b says that animals caught in a trap are not fully acquired until the trapper takes hold of them. In [Catch 22](/daf/gittin/59/catch-22), Rabbi Sebrow asks how a beis din would rule in the famous fox case of Pierson v. Post.

Can a sale made under pressure be valid? In Bava Basra 48, Tavi hung Pafi in a tree until he agreed to sell his harp. Rav Huna rules that the sale stands, since Pafi was paid. [Harping on Divided Real Estate](/daf/bava-basra/48/harping-on-divided-real-estate) shows how a family pressured into a bad deal used a shtar modaa to protest in advance. A house sale raises its own questions. [Small Talk](/daf/bava-basra/61/small-talk) uses the Mishna in Bava Basra 61a, on what a house sale includes, to ask about a mezuzah on a tiny room.

Raffles also have rules. Two brothers divided an inheritance by lottery, and then a third brother appeared (Bava Basra 106b). The Chavas Yair learned from this that a raffle missing one ticket must be redone, as explained in [A Winning Ticket](/daf/bava-basra/106/a-winning-ticket). Some things cannot be sold at all. In [Is Olam Habah for Sale?](/daf/shekalim/14/is-olam-habah-for-sale), the Netziv rules that a man who sold his share in the World to Come made no sale.

neighbors.heading: Neighbors in the Gemara: Paths, Water and Shared Space
neighbors.description: Neighbors in the Gemara: a public path on private land (Bava Basra 100), a lost path to a field (Yevamos 37), and a neighbor's well (Avodah Zarah 59).
neighbors.intro:
Living next to others means sharing space fairly. Rav Yehuda says in Bava Basra 100a that a strip of private land the public has used as a path may not be taken back. In [Bench-Pressed](/daf/bava-basra/100/bench-pressed), Rabbi Sebrow applies this to a low wall that bus riders use as a bench. Rav Zilberstein rules that since deeds are recorded today, the owner may build it higher.

The Gemara in Yevamos 37b describes a farmer who returns from a long trip to find the path to his field overgrown. He does not even know which neighbor's field it crossed. [Flyover Country](/daf/yevamos/37/flyover-country) explains the Nesivos HaMishpat's ruling. If the farmer owned the strip of land, one buyer of all the fields must give him a path. What about water? [Water Works](/daf/avodah-zarah/59/water-works) brings Yehoshua's rule that a spring on one's land may be used by all (Avodah Zarah 59a). Tosfos limits it to a spring, not a well a person dug himself.

Neighbors must also avoid harming one another's property. In [A Fruity Matter](/daf/bava-kamma/91/a-fruity-matter), birds from Rava bar Rav Chanan's palm trees damaged Rav Yosef's vineyard. And in [A Snag in the Plans](/daf/chullin/125/a-snag-in-the-plans), two neighbors argue over clotheslines strung above the spot for a sukkah.

inheritance.heading: Inheritance in the Gemara: Wills, Gifts and a Parent's Debts
inheritance.description: Inheritance in the Gemara: a deathbed gift (Bava Basra 145), a gift for a specific need (Nazir 24), and paying off a father's debt (Kesubos 91).
inheritance.intro:
The Gemara teaches that a gift before death can shape a family's feelings as well as its finances. In Bava Basra 145, the dying sister of Rav Tovi signed all her property over to him. His brother Rav Achadvoi feared people would think he was no scholar, so she gave it to him instead. In [A Grab Bag Of Halachos](/daf/bava-basra/145/a-grab-bag-of-halachos), Rabbi Sebrow brings Rav Elchanan Wasserman's questions on how this was allowed.

A gift may be limited to its purpose. A father left a valuable Russian army exemption card to his youngest son. The son then failed his army physical and tried to sell the card. In [Where Is Rashi?](/daf/nazir/24/where-is-rashi), the Rogatchover Gaon settles the brothers' dispute from Nazir 24a. An animal a husband gave his wife for her korban returns to him once she no longer needs it.

Heirs also have duties. The Gemara in Kesubos 91b tells of orphans who paid a creditor 50 zuz to buy back their father's land. Abaye ruled that since they did not say what the money was for, it paid off their father's debt. [Paying It Forward (And Back)](/daf/kesubos/91/paying-it-forward-and-back) shows how the Ben Ish Chai used this ruling. And [A Winning Ticket](/daf/bava-basra/106/a-winning-ticket) explains why brothers who divided an estate by lottery must redo it when a third brother appears (Bava Basra 106b).

avadim.heading: Avadim in the Gemara: Servants, Their Rights and Their Release
avadim.description: Avadim in the Gemara: the eved Ivri gets the only pillow (Kiddushin 20), a servant who falls ill (Kiddushin 17), and freeing a half-slave (Gittin 41).
avadim.intro:
The Torah's laws of servants protect the servant more than the master. Kiddushin 20a teaches that an eved Ivri must eat and drink as well as his master. Chazal said that buying one is like buying a master for oneself. Tosfos adds that if there is only one pillow, the servant gets it. [Water in the Desert and Pillows for Servants](/daf/kiddushin/20/water-in-the-desert-and-pillows-for-servants) brings the Maharam Schiff's question from the two travelers with one canteen (Bava Metzia 62a).

An eved Ivri who was ill for two of his six years owes his master nothing (Kiddushin 17a). [The Price to Pay](/daf/kiddushin/17/the-price-to-pay) explains why he is treated better than a sick day laborer. The same idea limits all work. Jews are servants of Hashem, not servants of servants. [One, Two, Three Years You're Out At The Old Ball Game](/daf/bava-metzia/10/one-two-three-years-youre-out-at-the-old-ball-game) asks whether a long work contract can make a worker like an eved.

The Mishna in Gittin 41a discusses a servant who is half free, after one of his two owners freed him. We force the other owner to free him so he can marry. In [Of Baptisms and Half-Slaves](/daf/gittin/41/of-baptisms-and-half-slaves), Rabbi Sebrow uses Tosfos on this Mishna to judge a Shabbos phone call that saved an airman from baptism. [Converting Bad Into Good](/daf/gittin/57/converting-bad-into-good) brings a Midrash that Haman once sold himself as Mordechai's slave.

vows-and-oaths.heading: Vows and Oaths in the Gemara: Making, Keeping and Annulling Them
vows-and-oaths.description: Vows in the Gemara: why we say bli neder (Nedarim 8), annulling a vow with a pesach (Nedarim 65), Kol Nidrei (Nedarim 77), and a vain oath (Nedarim 15).
vows-and-oaths.intro:
The Gemara takes every promise seriously. A neder forbids an object, while a shevuah, an oath, binds a person to do or not do an action. Rav Gidal said in Rav's name that one who says he will rise early to learn a chapter has made a great vow (Nedarim 8a). [Loath To Make An Oath](/daf/nedarim/8/loath-to-make-an-oath) follows this to a man who vowed to move to Eretz Yisrael in wartime. It also explains why we are quick to say bli neder.

A vow can be undone. A sage looks for a pesach, an opening, by asking whether the person knew some fact when he vowed. [What Makes a Valid Pesach?](/daf/nedarim/65/what-makes-a-valid-pesach) explains the Mishnah in Nedarim 65b. It also shows why Moshe's oath to stay in Midyan could be released once Dasan and Aviram became poor. [Void Where Prohibited](/daf/nedarim/77/void-where-prohibited) asks how Kol Nidrei can be said on Yom Kippur, when vows are not annulled on Shabbos. The Rivash and Rabbeinu Tam give two different answers.

Some oaths never take hold at all. Nedarim 15a calls an oath not to sleep for three days a vain oath, since no one can stay awake that long. Rabbi Sebrow tells a Dubno Maggid story and a TV-watching record in [Sleeping Duty](/daf/nedarim/15/sleeping-duty-2022). [Required Eating on Yom Kippur?](/daf/shevuos/28/required-eating-on-yom-kippur) brings a version of the 1848 cholera story in Vilna. Rav Yisrael Salanter reportedly had people take an oath before Yom Kippur so they could eat less on the fast.

parnassah.heading: Parnassah in the Gemara: Earning a Living and Trusting Hashem
parnassah.description: Parnassah in the Gemara: your father's trade (Arachin 16), Elisha and the water sellers (Sotah 46), and no one takes what is destined for you (Yoma 38).
parnassah.intro:
The Gemara teaches that a person works for a living, but his livelihood comes from Hashem. Rebbe Yochanan says a person should not leave his own trade or the trade of his fathers (Arachin 16b). In [Like Father, Like Son](/daf/arachin/16/like-father-like-son), Rabbi Sebrow brings the Ben Yehoyada's three reasons. One is that a son in his father's trade inherits all the specific prayers his father said for success. When Elisha healed the water of Yericho, the youths who sold bottled water lost their business. [A Miracle Within a Miracle](/daf/sotah/46/a-miracle-within-a-miracle) explains that they were called little because they had little faith (Sotah 46b).

The Gemara in Yoma 38b says no one can take even a hair's breadth of what is destined for another. [Tzaraas Rulings](/daf/yoma/42/tzaraas-rulings) tells of a poor kohen whose wife convinced him not to travel abroad for work. If Hashem feeds every hair, He will surely feed your family. And [Taster’s Choice](/daf/menachos/103/tasters-choice) asks why the Gemara in Menachos calls buying food day by day a curse. Rav Chaim Shmulevitz answers that an empty cupboard is a blessing for one who trusts in Hashem.

beis-din.heading: Beis Din in the Gemara: Judges, Fairness and Justice
beis-din.description: Beis din in the Gemara: litigants dressed unequally (Shevuos 31), compromise (Sanhedrin 6), and why a unanimous guilty verdict acquits (Sanhedrin 44).
beis-din.intro:
The Gemara holds judges to a very high standard of fairness. Suppose one litigant comes in fine clothing and the other in rags. The judge tells the wealthy one to dress down or dress up his opponent (Shevuos 31a). In [Courtly Appearances](/daf/shevuos/31/courtly-appearances), Rabbi Sebrow brings Rav Yehuda Leib Chasman's lesson. Even a righteous judge can be swayed by what he sees.

Should a beis din push for compromise? Sanhedrin 6a records Rabbi Elazar's view that a judge who compromises is a sinner. Yet in practice we encourage compromise. [Choosing The Lesser Evil](/daf/sanhedrin/6/choosing-the-lesser-evil) also discusses Aharon and the Golden Calf. The Meiri holds we may not call a sin permitted to stop a worse one.

Capital cases came with many protections. Witnesses had to warn the sinner first, and if all the judges found him guilty at once, he was set free. [Hitting Rock Bottom](/daf/sanhedrin/44/hitting-rock-bottom) reviews these laws, with plenty of stone puns. Even then, beis din chose the most humane method. Kesubos 37b learns this from "Love your neighbor as yourself," as explained in [Love Thy Neighbor](/daf/kesubos/37/love-thy-neighbor). The first Mishnah in Horayos adds that one who knows the Sanhedrin erred may not rely on it. [A Standout Moment](/daf/horayos/2/a-standout-moment) links this to the Novardok yeshiva's training against fear of public opinion.

testimony.heading: Testimony in the Gemara: Witnesses and Who Is Believed
testimony.description: Testimony in the Gemara: a third false witness (Makkos 5), converted brothers as witnesses (Yevamos 22), and Rava trusting his wife (Kesubos 85).
testimony.intro:
The Gemara builds its courts on the word of two witnesses. A third adds nothing, yet Rebbe Akiva teaches that a third false witness is punished like the first two (Makkos 5b). He learns from this that one who joins others in a mitzvah shares the full reward. In [App-ortioned Learning](/daf/makkos/5/app-ortioned-learning), Rabbi Sebrow shows how this idea powers the chevrah Shas and a modern siyum app.

Witnesses may not be related, so two brothers can never testify together. But Yevamos 22a teaches that a convert is like a newborn. So twin brothers who convert together may testify as a pair, as explained in [Department Of Redundancy Department](/daf/yevamos/22/department-of-redundancy-department).

Who is believed outside of court? Rav Kahana says anyone is believed about the calendar, because people do not lie about what will soon be known (Rosh Hashanah 22b). [On Amtrak, Alabama, and Assumptions](/daf/rosh-hashanah/22/on-amtrak-alabama-and-assumptions) applies this to a boy who says he is bar mitzvah. The Gemara in Kesubos 85a tells how Rava trusted his wife's word about a litigant but not Rav Papa's lone testimony. [The Accidental Aveirah](/daf/kesubos/85/the-accidental-aveirah) brings Rav Moshe Feinstein's explanation: Rava knew firsthand that his wife never lied. And [Bar Mitzvah Bewilderment](/daf/kiddushin/63/bar-mitzvah-bewilderment) asks who may testify that a boy has turned 13 (Kiddushin 63b).

shlichus.heading: Shlichus in the Gemara: Agents and Doing It Yourself
shlichus.description: Shlichus in the Gemara: why the Nasi bought the cow himself (Makkos 14), who may write a get (Gittin 22), and when a sender is liable (Sanhedrin 95).
shlichus.intro:
The Gemara teaches that a person's agent is like himself. Yet it is a greater mitzvah to do a mitzvah yourself than through an agent. In Makkos 14a, Rabban Gamliel, the Nasi, went to the market himself to buy a cow for his son's wedding. [Raising the Steaks: Why the Nasi Bought the Cow](/daf/makkos/14/raising-the-steaks-why-the-nasi-bought-the-cow) explains why this was no insult to his honor. [Holy Cows](/daf/makkos/14/holy-cows) adds the Shulchan Aruch's list of sages who prepared for Shabbos with their own hands.

Sometimes no real agent is needed at all. The Mishnah in Gittin 22b says anyone may write a get, even a minor. In [No Monkeying Around](/daf/gittin/22/no-monkeying-around), the Chasam Sofer uses this to say mishloach manos could even be delivered by a monkey. And [A More Mehudar Mitzvah](/daf/shevuos/27/a-more-mehudar-mitzvah) asks what to choose when an agent can do the mitzvah more beautifully than you can.

Sending someone can also carry responsibility. Dovid HaMelech was held to account for the city of Nov (Sanhedrin 95a). From this the Be'er Sheva ruled that a merchant whose agent was murdered on a business trip needs atonement. [Agents Of Destruction](/daf/sanhedrin/95/agents-of-destruction) brings the Tzemach Tzedek and Noda B'Yehudah on that ruling.

psak-halacha.heading: Psak Halacha in the Gemara: How Halacha Is Decided
psak-halacha.description: Psak halacha in the Gemara: a ruling not taught in public (Beitzah 28), Eliyahu HaNavi's rulings (Bava Metzia 114), and Moshiach (Bava Metzia 85).
psak-halacha.intro:
The Gemara shows that deciding halacha takes both effort and humility. Some rulings are true but not taught to the public. In Beitzah 28, Rava was asked if he was sharpening his knife on Yom Tov. He said he was only cleaning it, since he held "halacha v'ein morin kein." [Can You Keep A Secret?](/daf/beitzah/28/can-you-keep-a-secret) explains when such a halacha may be shared.

When the Gemara cannot resolve a question, it says teiku, which some read as a hint that Eliyahu will answer it. Yet Tosfos lists rulings of Eliyahu HaNavi that we do not follow, starting with Bava Metzia 114b. [Eliyahu HaNavi Zachur La’Tov](/daf/bava-metzia/114/eliyahu-hanavi-zachur-latov) explains each one. Even brilliance is not enough. In [A Minor Point](/daf/sanhedrin/2/a-minor-point), the Vilna Gaon shows that a passage about a minor's kiddushin really deals with the parah adumah water. The Satmar Rebbe adds that one must daven for help in reaching the right halacha.

Halacha also applies old principles to new questions. In [Da’as Torah](/daf/bava-metzia/33/daas-torah), Rav Henoch Leibowitz explains that Rav Moshe Feinstein ruled on toasters and hearing aids by applying the Gemara's principles. And halacha may not be bent even for the loftiest goal. Rebbe had Rebbe Chiya lead the prayers that might bring Moshiach (Bava Metzia 85b). The Brisker Rav learns from Tosfos's question there that halacha still comes first, as told in [Not Above The Law](/daf/bava-metzia/106/not-above-the-law).

safek.heading: Safek in the Gemara: How Halacha Handles Doubt
safek.description: Safek in the Gemara: following the majority of animals (Chullin 46), a doubt in rabbinic law (Kesubos 6), and a woman unsure if she bentched (Nedarim 80).
safek.intro:
The Gemara gives clear tools for when we are unsure. We follow the majority, and a doubt in Torah law is treated strictly, while a doubt in rabbinic law is treated leniently. [Glatt Or Not?](/daf/chullin/46/glatt-or-not) shows the majority rule at work. Most animals are not treifos, so we need not check every organ. But lung lesions are common, so lungs must be checked, and a smooth lung is glatt.

What if we do not know whether a law is from the Torah or the Rabbis? Nedarim 80b asks whether the Yom Kippur bans on bathing and leather shoes carry kares. Tosfos says they are rabbinic, while the Rambam holds they are from the Torah. [Biblical or Rabbinic: That is the Question](/daf/nedarim/80/biblical-or-rabbinic-that-is-the-question) also brings Rebbe Akiva Eiger's double doubt for a woman unsure if she bentched. In [Machmir Or Make Cool?](/daf/kesubos/6/machmir-or-make-cool), Rabbi Sebrow applies safek d'Rabbanan l'kula to opening a freezer on Shabbos.

Doubt also shapes how a mitzvah is done. Rav Chaim Brisker advised making the berachah on a beautiful but doubtful esrog, then taking the plain kosher one. [Separate And Unequal](/daf/sukkah/46/separate-and-unequal) weighs whether that creates an interruption. And [Grave Concerns](/daf/nazir/59/grave-concerns) follows a kohen on a plane who asks whether the majority rule helps when cemeteries are fixed in place.

rabbinic-decrees.heading: Rabbinic Decrees in the Gemara: Why Chazal Made Them
rabbinic-decrees.description: Rabbinic decrees in the Gemara: Rebbe Yochanan ben Zakai's takanos (Rosh Hashanah 30), leaning on a tree on Shabbos (Eruvin 100), and bishul akum.
rabbinic-decrees.intro:
Chazal made decrees to guard the Torah and to keep its memory alive. After the Churban, Rebbe Yochanan ben Zakai made two takanos together (Rosh Hashanah 30a). Everyone takes the lulav all seven days of Sukkos, as was done in the Beis HaMikdash. And no one eats new grain the whole sixteenth of Nissan. [Takana Considerations](/daf/rosh-hashanah/30/takana-considerations) asks why they came at the same time. Rabbi Moshe Betzalel answers that the second takana gave hope the Beis HaMikdash might be rebuilt next year. [Don’t Despair](/daf/rosh-hashanah/30/dont-despair) brings the same idea in the name of the Imrei Emes.

Some decrees guard against mistakes. Eruvin 100a forbids using a tree on Shabbos, even leaning on it. A dead tree is allowed in summer, but not in winter, when no one can tell which trees are alive. [Seeking A Shady Exemption](/daf/eruvin/100/seeking-a-shady-exemption) explains why the Shulchan Aruch follows Rav's stricter rule.

Other decrees keep healthy distance. Chazal forbade food cooked by a non-Jew, even when every ingredient is kosher. [Pasta Imposter](/daf/avodah-zarah/74/pasta-imposter) explains why one brand of oven-ready lasagna carries a different hechsher. And Chazal declared lands outside Eretz Yisrael tamei, a decree at the heart of [When The Sky Is Not The Limit](/daf/nazir/55/when-the-sky-is-not-the-limit) about a kohen's flight.

minhagim.heading: Minhagim in the Gemara: Customs and How Binding They Are
minhagim.description: Minhagim in the Gemara: customs of a new home (Chullin 18), Rosh Hashanah simanim (Horayos 12), birthdays (Avodah Zarah 5), a Torah scroll (Gittin 33).
minhagim.intro:
Jewish custom carries real weight. The Chasam Sofer was once asked how to know whether a Sefer Torah was written by a Jew. He answered, "Minhag Yisrael Torah hee." He meant, check whether the last column has the uneven letters many people write by custom. In [Of Minhagim And Manhigim](/daf/gittin/33/of-minhagim-and-manhigim), Rabbi Sebrow also tells of a fight over a custom of the Maharil, and why Ashkenaz guarded its customs fiercely.

Whose custom do you follow when you move? Rebbe Zeira moved to Eretz Yisrael and ate meat that Bavel's custom forbade. Rav Ashi explained that one who settles in a new place takes on its customs (Chullin 18b). [A Tale of Two Riddles: The Vacuuming Wife and the Havdala Surprise](/daf/chullin/18/a-tale-of-two-riddles-the-vacuuming-wife-and-the-havdala-surprise) applies this to Yom Tov Sheni.

Some customs seem to clash with halacha. Abaye says one should be accustomed to eat simanim on Rosh Hashanah (Horayos 12b), yet relying on omens is forbidden. [The Question of Omens](/daf/horayos/12/the-question-of-omens) brings the Meiri and the Maharal to reconcile them. Birthdays are debated too. The Gemara in Avodah Zarah lists Roman rulers' birthdays as festivals. [Happy Birthday](/daf/avodah-zarah/5/happy-birthday) gathers the views of gedolim on celebrating one.

mesorah.heading: Mesorah in the Gemara: The Chain of Tradition
mesorah.description: Mesorah in the Gemara: a tradition held for 22 years (Nedarim 12), the copper snake (Chullin 6), and kosher birds and animals (Chullin 45, Chullin 47).
mesorah.intro:
The Gemara teaches deep respect for what earlier generations handed down. A question troubled Rabbah and Rav Yosef for 22 years (Nedarim 12). Tosfos explains that Rabbah received a tradition from his teachers and would not drop it, even against a Mishnah. In [A Matter Of Mesorah](/daf/nedarim/12/a-matter-of-mesorah), Rabbi Sebrow contrasts this with King Uziyahu, who did not learn from the kings before him. Yet tradition is not frozen. Chizkiyahu destroyed the copper snake that his righteous ancestors had left standing (Chullin 6b). [Serpentine Path to Prominence](/daf/chullin/6/serpentine-path-to-prominence) asks what this teaches about new movements in Judaism.

Mesorah also decides what we eat. Since we cannot identify all the non-kosher birds, the Rema rules that we eat only birds with a tradition. [It Clucks Like a Chicken, But Is It Kosher?](/daf/chullin/47/it-clucks-like-a-chicken-but-is-it-kosher) follows the debates over the five-toed Faverolles chicken and the Braekel chicken. [From Savanna to Supper?](/daf/chullin/45/from-savanna-to-supper) shows that the Gemara in Chullin 45a disproves the old answer for why we do not eat giraffe. The real issue is whether new animals need a mesorah, which also affects zebu and bison.

semichah.heading: Semichah in the Gemara: Ordination From Rebbe to Student
semichah.description: Semichah in the Gemara: Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava's last ordination under Roman decree (Sanhedrin 14) and a rebbe who withholds Torah (Sanhedrin 92).
semichah.intro:
Semichah once passed in an unbroken chain from rebbe to student, going back to Moshe Rabbeinu. After the Bar Kochva revolt, Rome decreed death for anyone who gave or received it. In [No Ordinary Ordination](/daf/sanhedrin/92/no-ordinary-ordination), Rabbi Sebrow tells how Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava ordained Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and others between Usha and Shafram. When Roman soldiers came, he stayed behind so the new rabbis could flee. They killed him with 300 spears and "made him like a sieve" (Sanhedrin 14a). The Iyun Yaakov links this to Sanhedrin 92a, where a rebbe who withholds Torah becomes like a sieve.

Today's semichah is often a simple handwritten page. [Kesubah Conundrums](/daf/kesubos/54/kesubah-conundrums-kesubos-54) opens with a new rabbi who feared his plain semichah would not impress a congregation. He showed them his fancy kesubah instead.

machlokes.heading: Machlokes in the Gemara: Disputes for the Sake of Heaven
machlokes.description: Machlokes in the Gemara: the oven of Achnai (Bava Metzia 59), a Mishnah with two views (Bava Metzia 41), and Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel (Yevamos 15).
machlokes.intro:
The Gemara is full of disputes, and it teaches how to argue well. In Bava Metzia 59b, Rebbe Eliezer called on a carob tree, a canal and the walls of the beis midrash to prove his view. The Sages refused to accept such proofs. [A Halachic Argument](/daf/bava-metzia/59/a-halachic-argument) brings the Maharsha's reading of each sign as a real argument about logic and Torah lishmah.

Sometimes even the Mishnah holds two views. In Bava Metzia 41a, Rebbe Yochanan concludes that one Mishnah follows both Rebbe Yishmael and Rebbe Akiva. He promised to carry the clothes of anyone who could explain it by one view. [Two Points of View](/daf/bava-metzia/41/two-points-of-view) tells what happened when Rebbe Heschel tried.

Disagreement does not cancel respect. Rebbe Yochanan HaChorani would not eat olives from Rebbe Tzadok, a student of Beis Shammai, unless they met Beis Hillel's standard (Yevamos 15). Rather than say so, he said, "I don't eat olives." [Olive What He’s Having](/daf/yevamos/15/olive-what-hes-having) explains why. On the same daf, Shammai put schach over his daughter-in-law's bed for his newborn grandson. [A Sukkah for a Baby](/daf/yevamos/15/a-sukkah-for-a-baby) explains where Hillel disagreed.

chumros.heading: Chumros in the Gemara: When to Be Strict and When Not To
chumros.description: Chumros in the Gemara: Mar Ukva's wait between meat and milk (Chullin 105a), a groom's Shema (Berachos 16b), chametz under rubble (Bava Metzia 42a).
chumros.intro:
The Gemara teaches that a chumrah has to fit the person who takes it on. In Taanis, Rabbi Meir says that not everyone who wants to fast as a pious individual may do so. Berachos 16b says a groom who insists on saying Shema on his wedding night is showing off his concentration. Rabbi Sebrow explains both in [Beyond The Letter Of The Law](/daf/chullin/105/beyond-the-letter-of-the-law).

On Chullin 105a, Mar Ukva says he is like vinegar from wine compared to his father, who waited 24 hours after meat. So why not simply wait longer? Rav Yisrael Salanter compared growth to a fine meal served course by course: you climb step by step. Rav Henoch Leibowitz warned that a chumrah without real feeling behind it is a kind of falsehood and breeds arrogance. [Skipping Steps or Grabbing Dessert?](/daf/chullin/105/skipping-steps-or-grabbing-dessert) adds a warning from Rav Mattisyahu Solomon against mocking anyone else's stringencies.

A chumrah should never cost someone else. Rav Dovid Feinstein did not buy chametz from stores that relied on the sale of chametz. Yet the day after Pesach he bought a bakery's challos: "This woman closed her store for nine days and I shouldn't give her parnassah?!" The story is in [Chametz for Sale](/daf/avodah-zarah/63/chametz-for-sale). In [Of Mules and Mussar](/daf/bava-basra/133/of-mules-and-mussar), the Rashbam kept his eyes lowered and nearly boarded a wagon pulled by a horse and a mule. His brother Rabbeinu Tam stopped him: "Don't be a big tzaddik!"

It also matters to know where halacha ends. Bava Metzia 42a says chametz buried under three tefachim of rubble may stay over Pesach. [Chametz and Chumros](/daf/bava-metzia/42/chametz-and-chumros) applies this to a mixer with stuck dough and to heavy furniture, and reminds us to tell halacha apart from minhag.

beis-hamikdash.heading: Beis HaMikdash in the Gemara: Its Holiness, Vessels and Avodah
beis-hamikdash.description: Beis HaMikdash in the Gemara: the site's lasting holiness (Zevachim 107), no seven-branch menorah (Rosh Hashanah 24a), Kosel stones (Bechoros 15b).
beis-hamikdash.intro:
The Gemara teaches that the holiness of the Beis HaMikdash did not end with the churban. On Zevachim 107, Rebbe Yochanan and Reish Lakish argue whether the site keeps its sanctity after the destruction. The Rambam rules like Rebbe Yochanan, and the Mishnah Berurah codifies it. [Still Sacred](/daf/zevachim/107/still-sacred) explains the difference between Har HaBayis and the place of the Mikdash itself. It also explains why the Steipler, Rav Shach and Dayan Weiss ruled that no one should go up.

The vessels of the Beis HaMikdash may not be copied. Rosh Hashanah 24a says one may not make a candelabra like the Menorah, though five, six or eight branches are fine. In [Rules For Temple Tools](/daf/rosh-hashanah/24/rules-for-temple-tools), Rabbi Sebrow tells how his family almost bought his mother-in-law a seven-branch leichter. Rav Dovid Feinstein said there is indeed a problem.

What about a small stone that may have come from the Kosel? Bechoros 15b discusses an animal whose leftover kedushah is too slight to be redeemed. [When Less Is Too Much](/daf/bechoros/15/when-less-is-too-much) uses it to explain why Kosel stones stay holy. Rav Moshe Feinstein rules that even displaying such a fragment as a keepsake is forbidden benefit.

Other articles bring the daily life of the Mikdash to life. In [Calm and Collected](/daf/menachos/107/calm-and-collected), six collection boxes kept the kohen families from feuding over animal hides. [The Mystery of the Kalya Orev: Avian Architecture in the Beis Hamikdash](/daf/menachos/107/the-mystery-of-the-kalya-orev-avian-architecture-in-the-beis-hamikdash) asks how birds were kept off the roof. Was it a frightening image, iron spikes, or a sloped roof with a flat peak?

korbanos.heading: Korbanos in the Gemara: Offerings and Their Lessons for Today
korbanos.description: Korbanos in the Gemara: salt on every offering (Menachos 20a), no honey on the mizbeach (Menachos 58a), the Tamid and the moonlight (Yoma 28a).
korbanos.intro:
The Gemara teaches that a korban must be brought exactly as the Torah commands. Menachos 20a explains that salting every korban is a mitzvah, and the Rambam rules that an offering without salt is invalid. Chazal compare our table to the mizbeach, so the Rema says to have salt on the table before Hamotzi. [Worth Its Salt](/daf/menachos/20/worth-its-salt-menachos-20) tells of Uncle Dov's silent campaign to get the saltshaker, and why he should simply have eaten.

Many laws of korbanos still touch our lives. Menachos 58a forbids mixing honey into offerings. The Rambam therefore says Kiddush wine must be fit for the mizbeach, with no honey added. [Wine and Honey](/daf/menachos/58/wine-and-honey) brings the Rishonim who disagree, and asks about wine with added sugar.

Other articles show the eagerness behind the avodah. Yoma 28a tells how they once slaughtered the Tamid by mistake, taking moonlight for sunrise. Why not simply wait for full daylight? The Siach Yitzchok answers that they wanted to do the mitzvah at the earliest moment. [Mincha Motivation](/daf/yoma/28/mincha-motivation) connects this to davening Minchah early. In [Sowing The Seeds For Mitzvos](/daf/pesachim/74/sowing-the-seeds-for-mitzvos), the Korban Pesach is roasted on a spit of pomegranate wood. Does cutting the branch violate the ban on destroying fruit trees?

The Korban Pesach also explains the Seder. Pesachim 61a teaches that one may eat from a Korban Pesach only if he signed up before it was slaughtered. So how can Ha Lachma Anya invite anyone to join? [Korban Pesach Conundrums](/daf/pesachim/61/korban-pesach-conundrums) gives the Bnei Yissaschar's answer.

kohanim.heading: Kohanim in the Gemara: Honor, Duties and Purity
kohanim.description: Kohanim in the Gemara: a kohen at a tzaddik's funeral (Kesubos 103b), a kohen doctor (Yoma 49a), Birkas Kohanim (Sotah 38), a Kohen Gadol (Yoma 18a).
kohanim.intro:
The Gemara teaches that a kohen is set apart: he carries special duties, deserves special honor and must guard his purity. Sotah 38 says a kohen has a positive mitzvah to bless Klal Yisrael. Does the listener have a mitzvah too? [Saying Amein to Birkas Kohanim](/daf/sotah/38/saying-amein-to-birkas-kohanim) brings Rav Elyashiv, Rav Moshe Feinstein and Rav Shlomo Zalman on what to do in the middle of Shemoneh Esrei.

A kohen's honor raises practical questions. In [Good Help Is Hard To Find](/daf/yoma/49/good-help-is-hard-to-find), Rabbeinu Tam lets a kohen pour water on his hands, and a student challenges him. Then the Zera Chaim asks: may a patient see a kohen doctor? He brings proof from Rebbe Chanina, a medical expert mentioned on Yoma 49a. In [Kohen Conundrums](/daf/kesubos/25/kohen-conundrums), a Yisrael gets the first aliyah in Munkacs though a kohen is present. The reason: no Levi was there, and the kohen chose not to take two aliyos.

Kohanim must avoid tumas meis even today. On Kesubos 103b, Rabbeinu Chaim HaKohen says he would have become tamei to attend Rabbeinu Tam's funeral. [Can a Kohen Go to a Tzaddik’s Funeral?](/daf/kesubos/103/can-a-kohen-go-to-a-tzaddiks-funeral) explains his reasoning and why poskim warn kohanim away from tzaddikim's graves. [Grave Concerns](/daf/nazir/59/grave-concerns) is a lively airplane dialogue about a kohen flying over a cemetery.

Finally, the Kohen Gadol. Yoma 18a admits that in the Second Beis HaMikdash some were appointed who never learned the Torah's verses. Marta bas Baitos paid for Yehoshua ben Gamla's appointment. In [An Ignorant Kohen Gadol?](/daf/yoma/18/an-ignorant-kohen-gadol), Rabbi Sebrow brings the Ritva: he grew into the role and later set up schools for children everywhere.

tumah-and-taharah.heading: Tumah and Taharah in the Gemara: Ritual Purity Then and Now
tumah-and-taharah.description: Tumah and Taharah in the Gemara: the Chanukah oil (Pesachim 16a), Eliyahu in a cemetery (Bava Metzia 114b), a kohen forced into tumah (Zevachim 100a).
tumah-and-taharah.intro:
The Gemara teaches that tumah follows exact rules. Produce becomes able to receive tumah only after touching certain liquids, such as olive oil. During a famine, Rebbe Yochanan HaChorani refused moist olives with the words "I don't eat olives," until told they were tahor. In [Olive What He’s Having](/daf/yevamos/15/olive-what-hes-having), Rav Aharon Kotler learns two lessons: the sages' care in kashrus, and their care not to offend.

Sometimes the rules raise surprising questions. Pesachim 16a quotes Rav that liquids in the Beis HaMikdash could not become tamei. So how did the Chanukah oil become impure? [Pesachim 16a: Fueling the Flames of Chanukah](/daf/pesachim/16/pesachim-16a-fueling-the-flames-of-chanukah) brings three answers. One is that the oil had congealed, and congealed oil counts as a food.

Kohanim must avoid tumas meis. On Bava Metzia 114b, Eliyahu HaNavi tells Rabbah bar Avuhah that non-Jewish graves do not spread tumah upward, yet Tosfos rule against him. [Eliyahu HaNavi Zachur La’Tov](/daf/bava-metzia/114/eliyahu-hanavi-zachur-latov) explores why. In [A Grave Problem](/daf/sukkah/5/a-grave-problem), a kohen in South Fallsburg sees a tree over a non-Jewish grave touching a thick Verizon cable. Could the tumah travel three miles down the cable to his bungalow colony?

Tumah could even be forced on someone. Zevachim 100a tells of Yosef HaKohen, whose wife died on Erev Pesach. He held that an onen may still bring the Korban Pesach. His friends disagreed and pushed him under the tent at her funeral. [A Forced Tumah](/daf/zevachim/100/a-forced-tumah) retells the story, and shows how he still thought first of his orphaned children.

churban.heading: Churban in the Gemara: Why the Beis HaMikdash Fell and How We Rebuild
churban.description: Churban in the Gemara: Kamtza and Bar Kamtza (Gittin 55b), strict justice (Bava Metzia 30b), Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's takanos (Rosh Hashanah 30a).
churban.intro:
The Gemara looks hard at why the Beis HaMikdash was destroyed. Gittin 55b tells the story of Kamtza and Bar Kamtza. Rabbi Yochanan concludes that the Temple fell because of the anavah, the humility, of Rabbi Zecharia ben Avkolos. How could humility be to blame? [Misplaced Modesty](/daf/gittin/55/misplaced-modesty) explains: he failed to protest Bar Kamtza's shame, and then did not dare issue the lenient ruling the moment demanded.

Bava Metzia 30b says Yerushalayim was destroyed because its people insisted on the strict letter of the law. The Chofetz Chaim explains that Hashem dealt with them the way they dealt with others. [A Cut Above](/daf/bava-metzia/83/a-cut-above) pairs this with Bava Metzia 83a. Rav told Rabbah bar bar Chana to return the cloaks of his negligent workers and even pay their wages.

After the churban, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai made new takanos. Rosh Hashanah 30a lists two: taking the lulav all seven days in memory of the Mikdash, and waiting longer to eat new grain. Why were they made together? In [Takana Considerations](/daf/rosh-hashanah/30/takana-considerations), Rav Moshe Betzalel tells the Brisker Rav that the second takana gave the people hope. It was made in case the Mikdash would be rebuilt by next year.

The Gemara also offers comfort. In Menachos, Avraham Avinu pleads for his exiled children, and Hashem compares Klal Yisrael to an olive tree that will yet bear fruit. [It’s Never Too Late](/daf/menachos/53/its-never-too-late) draws the lesson that no Jew is ever beyond teshuvah. [Who Knows Fifteen?](/daf/taanis/30/who-knows-fifteen) adds the miracle of Beitar's dead, whose bodies did not decay before burial was allowed on Tu B'Av.

hekdesh.heading: Hekdesh in the Gemara: The Laws of Consecrated Property
hekdesh.description: Hekdesh in the Gemara: no me'ilah for sound, sight and smell (Pesachim 26a), stones of the Kosel (Bechoros 15b), a vow to donate iron (Menachos 107a).
hekdesh.intro:
The Gemara teaches that one may not benefit from hekdesh, property consecrated to the Beis HaMikdash. But what counts as benefit? Pesachim 26a says there is no me'ilah for sounds, sights and smells, such as enjoying the music of the Leviyim. Rava infers that it is still forbidden on a lesser level. [Something In The Air](/daf/pesachim/26/something-in-the-air) applies this to church bells, a church clock and the smell of a gentile's fresh bread on Pesach.

Hekdesh can also be hard to undo. Bechoros 15b teaches that an animal with only a trace of kedushah cannot be redeemed at all. [When Less Is Too Much](/daf/bechoros/15/when-less-is-too-much) uses this to discuss a stone fragment that may have come from the Kosel. Rav Moshe Feinstein rules that even displaying it is forbidden benefit. And what does a vague vow to donate iron obligate? According to Menachos 107a, enough to make a kalya orev, as [The Mystery of the Kalya Orev: Avian Architecture in the Beis Hamikdash](/daf/menachos/107/the-mystery-of-the-kalya-orev-avian-architecture-in-the-beis-hamikdash) explains.

teshuvah.heading: Teshuvah in the Gemara: Repentance and Return
teshuvah.description: Teshuvah in the Gemara: Avraham at the Churban (Menachos 53b), Reish Lakish (Bava Metzia 84a), King Menashe (Sanhedrin 102b), Korach (Bava Basra 74a).
teshuvah.intro:
The Gemara's message about teshuvah is that it is never too late. When the Beis HaMikdash was destroyed, Avraham Avinu came to plead for his children and asked whether there was no hope for them. Hashem answered that Klal Yisrael is like an olive tree: slow to bear fruit, but it will (Menachos 53b). In [It’s Never Too Late](/daf/menachos/53/its-never-too-late), Rabbi Sebrow draws the lesson: no Jew is ever too far gone. [We are Hashem’s Children](/daf/kiddushin/36/we-are-hashems-children) brings Rebbe Meir's view that Klal Yisrael are called Hashem's children even when they sin (Kiddushin 36a).

The Gemara is full of people who came back from far away. A bandit chief leapt into the river beside Rebbi Yochanan and became the great Reish Lakish (Bava Metzia 84a). King Menashe, who did terrible evil, appeared to Rav Ashi in a dream (Sanhedrin 102b). [Dough Adir](/daf/sanhedrin/102/dough-adir) explains Rebbi Yochanan's view that Menashe's teshuvah was accepted, as a lesson for every baal teshuvah. Even Korach's followers, swallowed alive, called out "Moshe and his Torah are true" (Bava Basra 74a). The Belzer Rebbe says Moshe Rabbeinu asked for that very punishment so they would still have a chance to repent. Rabbi Sebrow writes about this in [The Gift of Teshuvah](/daf/bava-basra/74/the-gift-of-teshuvah).

The greatest obstacle, Rabbi Sebrow writes, is despair. [Don’t Despair](/daf/rosh-hashanah/30/dont-despair) looks at Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's enactments after the Churban. One was hiding the red wool of Yom Kippur, because people who saw it stay red gave up instead of repenting more. It also asks of any gloomy thought: does it help your avodas Hashem, or hold it back? And it brings Rabbeinu Yonah's advice: on the day you resolve to return, see yourself as newborn.

humility.heading: Humility in the Gemara: Seeing Ourselves Truthfully
humility.description: Humility in the Gemara: Hillel restores the Torah (Sukkah 20a), Moshe admits he forgot (Zevachim 101a), Rebbe Yehoshua ben Levi's rainbow (Kesubos 77b).
humility.intro:
The Gemara links humility with Torah greatness. Sukkah 20a says Hillel restored Torah that had been forgotten, and the Imrei Pinchas explains that he merited it through his humility. Yet humility does not mean pretending to be nothing. Rav Yosi openly said, "I have true humility." In [Humblebrags](/daf/sukkah/20/humblebrags), Rabbi Sebrow explains with the Mesillas Yesharim: arrogance is self-deception, and humility is seeing oneself truthfully.

Humility means admitting mistakes. Zevachim 101a praises Moshe Rabbeinu for admitting that he heard a halacha and forgot it. [Excuses, Excuses](/daf/zevachim/101/excuses-excuses) brings the Chochmas HaMitzpun. Moshe had a good reason to cover it up, for the Torah's sake. Yet he saw that his real motive would be his own honor. In [Toil For Torah](/daf/menachos/7/toil-for-torah), Avimi forgets Maseches Menachos and travels to his own student, Rav Chisda, to relearn it.

Sometimes the humble even hide their greatness. Kesubos 77b tells that Rebbe Yehoshua ben Levi claimed rainbows appeared in his lifetime, though none did, so as not to show off. [A G-d-Based Moral Bucket List](/daf/kesubos/77/a-g-d-based-moral-bucket-list) asks why he kept this up even in Gan Eden. In [Focusing on the Positive](/daf/nedarim/50/focusing-on-the-positive), Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya answers the emperor's daughter: Torah spoils in a handsome vessel, as wine spoils in gold.

Humility also protects others. On Bava Kamma 88b, Rav Chisda asks Rabbah not to tell the students that his idea was disproved. Rashi explains that they might rejoice at his error and be punished. [Happy Accidents](/daf/bava-kamma/88/happy-accidents) adds that Rav Henoch Leibowitz did not show the other gedolim the proof that he had been right.

hakaras-hatov.heading: Hakaras HaTov in the Gemara: Gratitude to Hashem and to People
hakaras-hatov.description: Hakaras HaTov in the Gemara: Rebbe Akiva and the straw (Nedarim 50a), the korban todah and Birkas HaGomel (Zevachim 7a), martyrs of Lod (Bava Basra 10b).
hakaras-hatov.intro:
The Gemara teaches that gratitude often begins with seeing what we already have. Nedarim 50a describes Rebbe Akiva and Rachel sleeping on straw in poverty. Eliyahu HaNavi came begging for straw for his wife who had just given birth. Rebbe Akiva said, "Look, there are people who have even less than us." [Cultivating Gratitude](/daf/nedarim/50/cultivating-gratitude) draws the lesson: look at those with less and feel thankful, not at those with more and feel envy.

Thanking Hashem has its own halachos. Rashi on Zevachim 7a lists four people who brought a korban todah. They are one who crossed the sea, crossed a desert, recovered from grave illness, or was freed from captivity. Today they say Birkas HaGomel. [Many Thanks Or Just One?](/daf/zevachim/7/many-thanks-or-just-one) asks what a man who survived all four in one week should say. In [Not So Fast](/daf/taanis/16/not-so-fast), a community fasting for rain ends the fast once rain falls. The Rosh explains: so they can thank Hashem right away.

Gratitude is owed to people too. Bava Basra 10b says no one can stand in the place of those killed by the government in Lod. These brothers gave their lives to save the Jewish community. In [A Holy Place in the World to Come](/daf/bava-basra/10/a-holy-place-in-the-world-to-come), Rav Chaim Shmuelevitz applies this to soldiers protecting Eretz Yisrael. If we thank someone who opens a door for us, how much more must we daven for them. [Happy Birthday](/daf/avodah-zarah/5/happy-birthday) adds a different view of birthdays: a day of thanks for the miracle of birth.

honesty.heading: Honesty in the Gemara: Truth in Word, Business and Torah
