honesty.description: Honesty in the Gemara: Rav Safra's silent promise (Bava Basra 89a), breaking bad news without lying (Moed Katan 20a), Rav pays the butcher (Yoma 86a).
honesty.intro:
The Gemara holds us to a very high standard of truth. On Bava Basra 89, Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai debates whether to teach the tricks of dishonest merchants. In the end he does, so that even tzaddikim avoid small, unintended errors. [In All Honesty](/daf/bava-basra/89/in-all-honesty) also brings the Rashbam's story of Rav Safra. A customer kept raising his offer while Rav Safra said Shema. Afterward, Rav Safra sold at the first price, which he had already accepted in his heart.

Honesty also shapes how we speak. On Moed Katan 20a, Rav arrives from Bavel and his uncle Rabbi Chiya asks after his parents. Rav answers with questions, so the sad news gets across without a lie. [Spreading The News](/daf/moed-katan/20/spreading-the-news) explains the halachos the Mordechai learns from this. In [Lying Waze](/daf/bava-basra/82/lying-waze), Rabbi Sebrow asks whether one may tell a phone app he is a passenger. He brings the bikkurim declaration on Bava Basra 82a, and Rav's warning to his son Chiya, who lied to keep the peace at home.

Some truths may never be bent. Two Roman officers studied in a yeshiva and found one law they objected to. Why didn't the rabbis just claim the law was different? The Yam Shel Shlomo concludes that one may never falsify the Torah, even to avoid danger. Rabbi Sebrow discusses this in [A Case of Pikuach Nefesh](/daf/bava-kamma/60/a-case-of-pikuach-nefesh). And on Yoma 86a, Rav says it would be a chillul Hashem if he did not pay the butcher promptly. [Shopping Cart Considerations](/daf/yoma/86/shopping-cart-considerations) applies this to an unpaid case of seltzer under a shopping cart.

anger.heading: Anger in the Gemara: Patience and Self-Control
anger.description: Anger in the Gemara: spilled wine (Eruvin 65a), raising a hand (Sanhedrin 58b), a quarrel on Rosh Hashanah (Berachos 18b), patience (Bava Basra 145a).
anger.intro:
The Gemara often teaches about anger through small, everyday moments: a spilled cup, a raised fist, a long wait. Eruvin 65a says that a home where wine is "spilled like water" is a blessed home. In [Don’t Cry Over Spilled Wine](/daf/eruvin/65/dont-cry-over-spilled-wine), Rabbi Sebrow explains the custom of spilling wine at Havdalah. He also brings the Taz's reading: the Gemara means a homeowner who stays calm when someone spills his expensive wine. The punishment for anger is poverty, so calm brings blessing.

The Gemara in Sanhedrin 58b calls anyone who raises his hand to strike another Jew a rasha. In [Hitting A Nerve](/daf/sanhedrin/58/hitting-a-nerve), a wedding witness winds up to punch a man who screams "Thief!" under the chuppah. Is the kiddushin still valid? Rav Zilberstein rules that it is. He cites the Pischei Teshuvah: someone who raises his hand after being insulted must do teshuvah, but he is not called a rasha.

Sometimes avoiding anger takes real sacrifice. In [Rosh Hashana in a Cemetery](/daf/rosh-hashanah/16/rosh-hashana-in-a-cemetery) (Berachos 18b), a pious man leaves home on Rosh Hashanah night rather than keep quarreling. The Iyun Yaakov notes that getting angry would be the very opposite of a good omen for the new year. And he slept in the cemetery, not at a friend's house, so no one would think badly of his wife.

Patience can also be practiced on purpose. [One in a Million](/daf/bava-basra/145/one-in-a-million) starts from Bava Basra 145a and the verse "the good-hearted has a continual feast." It brings Rabbi Zelig Pliskin's advice to treat a long line as a chance to work on patience. On a lighter note, [It’s A Wash!](/daf/chullin/106/its-a-wash) opens with a man who threw pickles at a friend, and wonders whether pausing to wash his hands might have cooled him off.

lashon-hara.heading: Lashon Hara in the Gemara: Guarding Our Speech
lashon-hara.description: Lashon hara in the Gemara: speaking before three (Bava Basra 39b), too much praise (Bava Basra 164b), sparing shame (Rosh Hashanah 26b), Doeg and Nov.
lashon-hara.intro:
The Gemara treats hurtful speech with great seriousness. One line in Bava Basra 39b seems surprising: "anything said in front of three people is not lashon hara." [Lashon Hara: “Say It Ain’t So, Joe”](/daf/bava-basra/39/lashon-hara-say-it-aint-so-joe) shows how the Chofetz Chaim rejects the idea that a bigger audience makes it permitted. Tosfos in Arachin explains that the line is about a remark that could be taken either way. Said before three people, the speaker knows it will get back, so he says it kindly and the listeners hear it kindly.

Even praise can turn into lashon hara. Twice in Bava Basra 164b, Rebbe tells his son to stop speaking lashon hara for naming the scribe Rebbi Yehudah Chayata. [Bound To Get Criticized](/daf/bava-basra/164/bound-to-get-criticized) brings the Rashbam (too much praise invites a "but…") and other explanations of how praise can hide criticism. [The Butterfly Effect](/daf/bava-basra/73/the-butterfly-effect) retells how Doeg's slander about the kohanim of Nov led King Shaul to destroy the whole city.

The Gemara also guards against shaming others, even people who deserve it. In Rosh Hashanah 26b, a man who was robbed tells Levi about it in an obscure word. He did not want to shame the thief. [Tidy Words In A Tidy World](/daf/rosh-hashanah/26/tidy-words-in-a-tidy-world) adds Bilam's donkey, which died so that even Bilam would be spared embarrassment. It also tells of Rav Moshe Feinstein, who stayed silent when a car door closed on his fingers. [The Spinmeisters](/daf/yoma/66/the-spinmeisters) ends with the Chofetz Chaim's offer to a bachur. If he never again spoke or listened to lashon hara, he would have a place with him in Gan Eden.

shalom.heading: Shalom in the Gemara: Making Peace at Home and in the Community
shalom.description: Shalom in the Gemara: a chassid sleeps in a cemetery (Berachos 18b), Reuven's confession (Sotah 7b), Yosef's brothers fear him (Yevamos 65a).
shalom.intro:
The Gemara shows how far great people went for the sake of peace. Berachos 18b tells of a pious man who gave a dinar to a poor man in a year of famine. His wife was upset, so he slept on Rosh Hashanah night in a cemetery. Why not at a friend's house? The Iyun Yaakov explains that he did not want anyone to suspect his wife. [Rosh Hashana in a Cemetery](/daf/rosh-hashanah/16/rosh-hashana-in-a-cemetery) tells what he heard there.

Sotah 7b says Reuven publicly confessed to moving his father's bed. Normally one should not announce his sins. But Reuven wanted to spare his brothers from suspecting one another. In [Whodunit?](/daf/sotah/7/whodunit), Rav Yitzchak Zilberstein applies this to a tenant who burned a neighbor's stroller. Peace can also be lost through misunderstanding. On Yevamos 65a, Yosef's brothers invent a message from their father, afraid that Yosef still bore a grudge. [She’asah Nissim](/daf/yevamos/65/sheasah-nissim) shows how even tzaddikim can misjudge each other.

Shalom bayis has a special place. The Gemara says Shabbos candles exist to promote peace at home. So if a couple's candle minhagim cause strife, the Shevet HaLevi says the wife should keep hers. Rabbi Sebrow explains in [Light Up The Night](/daf/shabbos/23/light-up-the-night). The young Chofetz Chaim turned down rich dowries and married his poor step-sister. He did it for peace between his mother and step-father, as [Keeping It In the Family](/daf/yevamos/21/keeping-it-in-the-family) relates. In a South African shul, Rav Moshe Sternbuch saw no real problem with rounded Luchos. Still, he had them squared off for peace, as [Fair and Square](/daf/bava-basra/14/fair-and-square) relates.

derech-eretz.heading: Derech Eretz in the Gemara: Manners, Respect and Sensitivity
derech-eretz.description: Derech Eretz in the Gemara: what is degrading is forbidden (Nazir 45a), litigants' clothing (Shevuos 31a), how to speak of a convert (Yevamos 22a).
derech-eretz.intro:
The Gemara teaches that proper conduct is expected even where no verse spells it out. On Nazir 45a, the Torah is not read to mean a nazir shaves at the entrance of the Sanctuary, because that would be degrading. Rav Yosef Engel explains that a prohibition based on simple logic has the force of Torah law. In [The Fifth Shulchan Aruch](/daf/nazir/45/the-fifth-shulchan-aruch), Rabbi Sebrow answers the man who asked, "Where does it say in the Torah you have to be nice?"

Derech eretz begins with how we see people. Shevuos 31a tells a judge to have a richly dressed litigant change clothes or dress his poor opponent too. [Courtly Appearances](/daf/shevuos/31/courtly-appearances) brings Rav Yehuda Leib Chasman: even a righteous judge is swayed by what he sees. So are we, when we greet visitors in shul. On Yevamos 22a, a convert is like a newborn child. The Ritva learns from the Gemara's wording that one should not refer to a ger as "a gentile who converted." Rabbi Sebrow explains in [Department Of Redundancy Department](/daf/yevamos/22/department-of-redundancy-department).

Respect means sparing others shame. On Rosh Hashanah 26b, a man tells Levi that someone was "kava" him, a rare word for theft. He chose it so as not to embarrass the thief in front of others. [Tidy Words In A Tidy World](/daf/rosh-hashanah/26/tidy-words-in-a-tidy-world) adds that Bilam's donkey died so Bilam would not be shamed. Even turning down food takes tact. During a famine, Rebbe Yochanan HaChorani refused moist olives by saying "I don't eat olives." He would rather go hungry than imply that his host kept a lower standard, as [Olive What He’s Having](/daf/yevamos/15/olive-what-hes-having) explains.

kavod-hatorah.heading: Kavod HaTorah in the Gemara: Honoring Torah and Its Teachers
kavod-hatorah.description: Kavod HaTorah in the Gemara: a student equals his rebbe (Niddah 14b), Rav Huna sends Rabbah to Rav Chisda (Bava Metzia 33), Rebbe Chiya (Bava Metzia 85b).
kavod-hatorah.intro:
The Gemara teaches that every word of Torah deserves respect. The Gemara records that Rav Nachman calls one of Shmuel's teachings superb and another not good. Rava rebukes him: one who says some teachings are nice and others are not will lose the glory of Torah. In [It’s All Good](/daf/eruvin/64/its-all-good), Rabbi Sebrow brings the Maharsha, who says even praising one teaching is a problem. The Rashash disagrees.

Honor for one's rebbe is a major theme. The Gemara in Eruvin says Yehoshua was punished for deciding a halacha in front of Moshe Rabbeinu, even as he defended Moshe's honor. [Searching Ourselves](/daf/pesachim/10/searching-ourselves) asks how this happened, and warns us to check that our own zeal truly brings kavod Shamayim. What if a student surpasses his rebbe? On Niddah 14b, Rebbe Chiya addresses Rebbe as plain "you," and Tosfos explain that he had become his rebbe's equal. [When The Student Becomes The Rebbe](/daf/niddah/14/when-the-student-becomes-the-rebbe) adds that Rebbe himself grew beyond his own rebbe by teaching many students.

Kavod HaTorah also means valuing a sage's guidance for life. On Bava Metzia 33, Rav Huna sends his son Rabbah to Rav Chisda, though Rav Chisda taught mostly about healthy living. [Da’as Torah](/daf/bava-metzia/33/daas-torah) recalls Rav Henoch Leibowitz explaining that da'as Torah is the Torah's own view, drawn from its sources. And on Bava Metzia 85b, Rebbe Chiya plants flax, hunts deer and writes Chumashim to teach children. [Rebbe Chiya: The Ultimate Teacher](/daf/bava-metzia/85/rebbe-chiya-the-ultimate-teacher) shows why Rebbe said, "How great are the deeds of Rebbe Chiya!"

mussar.heading: Mussar in the Gemara: Lessons for Growth From Chazal
mussar.description: Mussar in the Gemara: Rav Chisda and the Malach HaMaves (Makkos 10), acting on inspiration at once (Sukkah 44a), Reish Lakish's saffron (Gittin 47a).
mussar.intro:
The Gemara teaches that a whole life can be service of Hashem. On Makkos 10, the Malach HaMaves cannot take Rav Chisda while he is learning. Why not come while he eats or sleeps? The Chofetz Chaim answers that for Rav Chisda, even eating and sleeping were mitzvos. In [Lifelong Goal](/daf/makkos/10/lifelong-goal), Rav Henoch Leibowitz adds that we may not reach this level, but we must at least make it our goal.

Inspiration must be acted on at once. On Sukkah 44a, a wealthy man learns that his workers may not take Shemittah olives as wages. He rushes off in the middle of the conversation to stop it. Rav Yisrael Salanter explains that this zeal is what impressed Rebbe Elazar bar Tzadok, in [Without Delay](/daf/sukkah/44/without-delay). [Seizing the Spark: Preserving Inspiration in Halacha and Life](/daf/chullin/95/seizing-the-spark-preserving-inspiration-in-halacha-and-life) adds Palti ben Layish. His sword was a reminder that kept his resolve for years.

Time is life itself. On Gittin 47a, the dying Reish Lakish laments the saffron he left his children, since he spent precious time earning what he never needed. In [Life is Precious](/daf/gittin/47/life-is-precious), the Chofetz Chaim says he is already pained over the seforim he owns.

The Gemara is honest about the yetzer hara. On Kiddushin 81a, Rav Amram Chasida climbs a ladder in desire, then stops halfway and shouts "Fire!" [Moral Of The Story](/daf/kiddushin/81/moral-of-the-story) explains that such stories show tzaddikim struggle too, so we should never mock those who fall. And despair is the yetzer hara's tool, as Rav Henoch's father taught him in [Don’t Despair](/daf/rosh-hashanah/30/dont-despair).

kiddush-hashem.heading: Kiddush Hashem in the Gemara: Sanctifying Hashem's Name
kiddush-hashem.description: Kiddush Hashem in the Gemara: Rabbi Chanina ben Teradyon (Avodah Zarah 18), Rebbe Meir's escape (Avodah Zarah 18b), Mordechai and Haman (Sanhedrin 61b).
kiddush-hashem.intro:
The Gemara tells of sages who gave their lives to sanctify Hashem's Name. When Rome forbade semichah on pain of death, Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava ordained the next generation's leaders between two cities. When soldiers came, he stayed behind so his students could escape. Sanhedrin 14a says they made him "like a sieve" with their spears. [No Ordinary Ordination](/daf/sanhedrin/92/no-ordinary-ordination) asks why he died this way. On Avodah Zarah 18, Rabbi Chanina ben Teradyon is condemned for teaching Torah, and his wife accepts her fate as just. [Accounting For All](/daf/avodah-zarah/18/accounting-for-all) draws the lesson that we answer for wrongs we could have prevented.

Even a Jew who seemed lost can rise to Kiddush Hashem. Yosef Meshisa looted the Menorah for the Romans, then refused to go back in and died al kiddush Hashem. [The Good In The Bad](/daf/yevamos/49/the-good-in-the-bad) shows the spark hidden in every Jew. [A Time for Torah](/daf/bava-kamma/77/a-time-for-torah) brings a tradition that the Baalei Tosfos wrote the long Tosfos on Bava Kamma 77a on their last night before martyrdom.

Where is the line? Avodah Zarah 18b tells that Rebbe Meir, hunted by the Romans, dipped one finger in non-kosher food and sucked another. The Shulchan Aruch learns that one may create a false impression to save his life, but never deny his faith outright. [Keeping the Faith](/daf/avodah-zarah/26/keeping-the-faith) applies this to ships flying Muslim symbols in the Red Sea. Sanhedrin 61b says bowing to a person out of respect is permitted. So why did Mordechai refuse to bow to Haman? [Should Mordechai Have Bowed to Haman?](/daf/sanhedrin/61/should-mordechai-have-bowed-to-haman) brings Tosafos: he chose to make a Kiddush Hashem.

leadership.heading: Leadership in the Gemara: What Chazal Demand of Leaders
leadership.description: Leadership in the Gemara: Rabbi Zecharia ben Avkolos (Gittin 55b), Dovid HaMelech's famine (Yevamos 78b), choosing a rosh yeshiva (Bava Kamma 67b).
leadership.intro:
The Gemara teaches that a leader is held to a higher standard. Sometimes a leader cannot afford to be humble. Gittin 55b blames the churban on the humility of Rabbi Zecharia ben Avkolos. In [Misplaced Modesty](/daf/gittin/55/misplaced-modesty), the Pardas Shaul explains: a decisive lenient ruling was needed, and he held back because he felt unworthy.

A leader also answers for results he never intended. On Yevamos 78b, a famine strikes in Dovid HaMelech's days. The Urim v'Tumim reveals that it came partly because of King Shaul. His destruction of Nov left the Givonim, who supplied it, without support, and seven of them died. [Still Waters Run Deep](/daf/yevamos/78/still-waters-run-deep) shows how deep Hashem's judgment goes. Leaders must also admit mistakes, as Moshe Rabbeinu did on Zevachim 101a, in [Excuses, Excuses](/daf/zevachim/101/excuses-excuses).

The Gemara shows how leaders were chosen and how they rose. On Bava Kamma 67b, Rav Yosef was the preferred choice for rosh yeshiva, yet he stepped aside for Rabbah for twenty-two years. [Do Not Despair](/daf/bava-kamma/67/do-not-despair) tells how he later answered Abaye's old question. On Chullin 6b, King Chizkiyahu destroys the copper snake that his righteous ancestors had left standing. [Serpentine Path to Prominence](/daf/chullin/6/serpentine-path-to-prominence) explains that they left him room to achieve prominence. Even a Kohen Gadol whose post was bought could grow into greatness, as [An Ignorant Kohen Gadol?](/daf/yoma/18/an-ignorant-kohen-gadol) explains.

jealousy.heading: Jealousy in the Gemara: Kinah and Being Happy With One's Lot
jealousy.description: Jealousy in the Gemara: six collection boxes for the kohanim (Menachos 107), Doeg's envy of Dovid (Zevachim 54b), the moon and Korach (Shevuos 9a).
jealousy.intro:
The Gemara teaches that no one can take what is meant for another. Yoma 38b says a person cannot touch even a hair's breadth of what is destined for his fellow. In [Calm and Collected](/daf/menachos/107/calm-and-collected), Rabbi Sebrow applies this to the Beis HaMikdash. The kohen families were jealous over the extra animal hides each day brought. Chizkiyah explains that six separate collection boxes helped each family see that the others' gain was not their loss.

Jealousy can destroy a person. On Zevachim 54b, Doeg was jealous that Dovid HaMelech found the site of the Beis HaMikdash, a secret Doeg had worked hard to discover. [Sleeping Duty](/daf/zevachim/54/sleeping-duty) traces the tragic results. Korach, too, did not value his position as a Levi. Shevuos 9a tells of the moon made smaller for wanting equal stature with the sun. [The Gist Of The Jugs](/daf/shevuos/9/the-gist-of-the-jugs) teaches that Hashem gives each person exactly what his mission needs. Yaakov Avinu even went back for small jugs.

Some jealousy is healthy. Bava Basra 21 says "kinas sofrim tarbeh chochmah": competition among teachers increases wisdom. [Schooled On The Competition](/daf/bava-basra/21/schooled-on-the-competition) explains why a new school may open near an old one, though it may not recruit the other's students. And to cure envy, [Cultivating Gratitude](/daf/nedarim/50/cultivating-gratitude) advises looking at those who have less than us.

ahavas-yisrael.heading: Ahavas Yisrael in the Gemara: Loving Every Jew
ahavas-yisrael.description: Ahavas Yisrael in the Gemara: love even for the condemned (Kesubos 37b), Kol Yisrael areivim (Avodah Zarah 18), davening for those in need (Nedarim 64b).
ahavas-yisrael.intro:
The Gemara stretches "love your neighbor as yourself" further than we might expect. Kesubos 37b applies it to a man condemned to death by beis din: he must be given the least painful death. Yet the Rambam says one should hate a sinner who was warned and did not repent. In [Love Thy Neighbor](/daf/kesubos/37/love-thy-neighbor), Rabbi Sebrow brings several answers. The Baal HaTanya says we hate the evil deeds but love the spark of G-dliness in every Jew. [Hitting Rock Bottom](/daf/sanhedrin/44/hitting-rock-bottom) adds that the women of Yerushalayim brought the condemned man a drink to dull his pain.

No Jew is ever beyond hope. In Menachos, Avraham Avinu pleads for his exiled children, and Hashem compares Klal Yisrael to an olive tree that will yet bear fruit. [Never Too Late For Teshuvah](/daf/menachos/53/never-too-late-for-teshuvah) recalls how Avraham honored even idol-worshipping travelers, because every person is made b'tzelem Elokim.

Love also means responsibility. On Avodah Zarah 18, the wife of Rabbi Chanina ben Teradyon is punished for failing to protest. [Accounting For All](/daf/avodah-zarah/18/accounting-for-all) explains that Kol Yisrael areivim zeh lazeh, and urges us to reach out to every Jew we can. Nedarim 64b lists four people considered like the dead: the poor, the metzora, the blind and the childless. Tosfos says the Gemara teaches this to make us daven harder for them, as [A Powerful Tefillah](/daf/nedarim/64/a-powerful-tefillah) explains.

simchah.heading: Simchah in the Gemara: Joy in Mitzvos, Torah and Life
simchah.description: Simchah in the Gemara: Tu B'Av and Yom Kippur (Taanis 26b), "the good-hearted has a continual feast" (Bava Basra 145a), candles of joy (Sanhedrin 32b).
simchah.intro:
The Gemara teaches that the most joyous days of the year were Yom Kippur and Tu B'Av. Yom Kippur brought forgiveness, but why Tu B'Av? Rabbah and Rav Yosef say it was the day they finished cutting wood for the mizbeach. In [The Simcha of a Siyum](/daf/taanis/26/the-simcha-of-a-siyum), the Rashbam explains that completing a mitzvah is cause for celebration. The Nimukei Yosef calls this the source for a seudah when finishing a masechta. [Who Knows Fifteen?](/daf/taanis/30/who-knows-fifteen) adds another reason: the dead of Beitar were found not to have decayed when burial was finally allowed.

Joy is also a way of living. Mishlei says "the good-hearted has a continual feast," and Bava Basra 145a applies it to one who studies Mishnah. The Baalei Mussar read it as the power to see any situation in a positive light. [One in a Million](/daf/bava-basra/145/one-in-a-million) tells of a man who rejoiced at a flat tire, because his doctor had just cleared him to lift heavy objects.

Sanhedrin 32b tells that under a cruel decree, Jews lit candles by day to signal a simcha. The Minchas Asher learns that candles are a sign of joy, even when the light is not needed. Rabbi Sebrow explains in [Illuminating The Shabbos Blessing](/daf/sanhedrin/32/illuminating-the-shabbos-blessing). And joy is contagious. In [The Key to Success in Chinuch](/daf/yevamos/114/the-key-to-success-in-chinuch), Rav Moshe Feinstein says children keep the mitzvos they hear their parents enjoy.

lifnim-meshuras-hadin.heading: Lifnim Meshuras HaDin in the Gemara: Going Beyond the Letter of the Law
lifnim-meshuras-hadin.description: Lifnim Meshuras HaDin in the Gemara: Rabbah bar bar Chana's workers (Bava Metzia 83a), Yerushalayim destroyed for strict justice (Bava Metzia 30b).
lifnim-meshuras-hadin.intro:
The Gemara teaches that keeping the law is not always enough. On Bava Metzia 83a, workers broke Rabbah bar bar Chana's barrels of wine through negligence, and he took their cloaks. Rav told him to return them, and since the workers were poor, to pay their wages too. In [A Cut Above](/daf/bava-metzia/83/a-cut-above), the Vilna Gaon explains the verse Rav quoted. Forgiving a debt is "the road of the good," while paying what is not owed is "the path of the righteous." [Who Knows Nine?](/daf/bava-metzia/99/who-knows-nine) brings the Aruch HaShulchan: this applies to us too, and a judge should tell the employer so.

Why does it matter so much? Bava Metzia 30b says Yerushalayim was destroyed because its people insisted on the strict law. The Chofetz Chaim explains that Hashem judges us the way we judge others. [The Fifth Shulchan Aruch](/daf/nazir/45/the-fifth-shulchan-aruch) adds that the Torah's command to do "what is just and good" covers conduct no book spells out. And [A Matter Of Great Interest](/daf/bava-metzia/70/a-matter-of-great-interest) brings Tosfos on Bava Metzia 70b. One who does only what is permitted may escape punishment, yet lose a great reward.

tochachah.heading: Tochachah in the Gemara: When and How to Rebuke
tochachah.description: Tochachah in the Gemara: the wife of Rabbi Chanina ben Teradyon (Avodah Zarah 18), Bar Kamtza's shame (Gittin 55b), Rebbe and his son (Bava Basra 164b).
tochachah.intro:
The Gemara teaches that one who could protest a wrong and does not is held responsible. On Avodah Zarah 18, the wife of Rabbi Chanina ben Teradyon is punished for failing to correct others. [Accounting For All](/daf/avodah-zarah/18/accounting-for-all) explains that this is why we confess sins we never did ourselves. The Midrash on Gittin 55b blames Rabbi Zecharia ben Avkolos, who was at the party and could have protested Bar Kamtza's shame. Rabbi Sebrow explains in [Misplaced Modesty](/daf/gittin/55/misplaced-modesty) that his humility held him back.

The Gemara also shows sages giving rebuke. On Bava Basra 164b, Rebbe's son Rebbe Shimon blames a sloppy document on the scribe. Rebbe answers, "Desist from this lashon hara." [Bound To Get Criticized](/daf/bava-basra/164/bound-to-get-criticized) explains why even naming the scribe of a beautiful Tehillim was wrong. And when Rav Nachman called one teaching good and another not, Rava rebuked him, as [It’s All Good](/daf/eruvin/64/its-all-good) relates.

yetzer-hara.heading: Yetzer Hara in the Gemara: Tzaddikim, Temptation and Heavenly Help
yetzer-hara.description: Yetzer Hara in the Gemara: tzaddikim who fled temptation (Kiddushin 39b), Rav Amram Chasida's cry of fire (Kiddushin 81a) and Rav Hutner on setbacks.
yetzer-hara.intro:
The Gemara does not pretend that great people are free of temptation. Kiddushin 39b tells of tzaddikim who escaped a noblewoman's advances. Rabbi Tzadok climbed into her lit oven. Rav Kahana threw himself off a roof, and Eliyahu HaNavi came to catch him. On Kiddushin 81a, Rav Amram Chasida stopped halfway up a ladder and shouted that his house was on fire, so the rabbis would come running.

The Gemara then tells of Rebbe Chiya bar Ashi, who believed he had sinned and fasted for the rest of his life. Why tell stories of near failure? In [Moral Of The Story](/daf/kiddushin/81/moral-of-the-story), Rabbi Sebrow brings the Divrei Shaul. These stories show that tzaddikim have the same yetzer hara we do, so their victories can truly inspire us. The Pele Yoetz adds that we should not ridicule those who give in, but thank Hashem for our own protection.

[The Spinmeisters](/daf/yoma/66/the-spinmeisters) quotes a letter from Rav Hutner to a discouraged student. People see the Chofetz Chaim's pure speech, he wrote, but not his battles, slumps and regressions. His advice: "Lose battles but win wars." [A Minor Point](/daf/sanhedrin/2/a-minor-point) cites the Mesillas Yesharim. No one beats the yetzer hara without Divine help, but Hashem helps only the person who first tries.

emunah-and-bitachon.heading: Emunah and Bitachon in the Gemara: Faith and Trust in Hashem
emunah-and-bitachon.description: Faith and trust in Hashem in the Gemara: the daily manna (Yoma 76a), Elisha's bears (Sotah 46b), Chizkiyahu (Berachos 10a), the rain and Adam (Chullin 60b).
emunah-and-bitachon.intro:
The Gemara teaches that trust in Hashem grows through needing Him every day. Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's students asked why the manna fell daily and not once a year. He answered with a parable: a king gave his son his allowance once a year, and the son visited only once a year. So the king gave it day by day, and the son came every day (Yoma 76a). In [Keep In Touch](/daf/chullin/60/keep-in-touch), Rabbi Sebrow pairs this with Chullin 60b: rain did not fall until Adam prayed for it. Hard times can be Hashem's invitation to come closer.

The same empty cupboard can be a curse or a blessing. In [Taster’s Choice](/daf/menachos/103/tasters-choice), Rebbe Chanin reads a verse of the tochachah as describing someone who buys his food day by day. Rav Chaim Shmulevitz explains that for someone with bitachon, this is the greatest blessing. In [A Miracle Within a Miracle](/daf/sotah/46/a-miracle-within-a-miracle), the youths who mocked Elisha HaNavi are called katanim, "little" in faith (Sotah 46b). The Steipler explains their mistake: they thought their livelihood came from their own efforts.

Bitachon also means trusting that what we have is what we need. The Gemara in Chullin says Yaakov Avinu went back across the river for a few small jugs. In [The Gist Of The Jugs](/daf/shevuos/9/the-gist-of-the-jugs), the Arizal explains that he knew every possession had a purpose. [Leave the Rest to Hashem](/daf/yevamos/49/leave-the-rest-to-hashem) tells how Yeshaya HaNavi told King Chizkiyahu to marry and leave the future to Hashem (Berachos 10a). Rav Henoch Leibowitz draws the lesson: follow the halacha now, and leave the rest to Hashem.

miracles.heading: Miracles in the Gemara: Nissim, Nature and Halachah
miracles.description: Miracles in the Gemara: who merits a miracle (Bava Metzia 106), the Ginai River (Chullin 7a), wheat from the sky (Menachos 69b) and the oven of Achnai.
miracles.intro:
Can an ordinary person expect a miracle? Bava Metzia 106 discusses a shepherd who leaves his flock while a wolf eats a sheep. Rav Sheishes asks why we ignore the chance of a miracle, like Dovid HaMelech's victory over a lion and a bear. The Gemara answers that a deserving owner could get a miracle anyway. Rebbe Chanina ben Dosa's goat once came home with a dead lion on its horns. In [Not Above The Law](/daf/bava-metzia/106/not-above-the-law), Rabbi Sebrow notes Tosfos: through tefillah, even ordinary people can merit miracles.

Nature is also a miracle. On Chullin 7a, Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair ordered the Ginai River to split. The river argued that it too was doing Hashem's will by flowing to the sea. [Mitzvah Mission](/daf/chullin/7/mitzvah-mission) uses this to answer the Beis Yosef's question about Chanukah. The extra day celebrates the fact that oil burns at all, since nature is simply Hashem's will.

Miracles also raise halachic questions. Menachos 69b tells of wheat that rained down on a merchant named Adi. Could it be used for the Shtei HaLechem, which must come from Eretz Yisrael? [It’s Raining Wheat](/daf/menachos/69/its-raining-wheat) shows how Tosafos's view bears on Rav Chaim Brisker's famous question about miraculous Chanukah oil. [She’asah Nissim](/daf/yevamos/65/sheasah-nissim) explains the berachah said at the place of a miracle, which Yosef recited at his pit.

Yet a miracle does not decide halachah. On Bava Metzia 59b, Rebbe Eliezer called on a carob tree, a canal and the walls of the beis midrash to prove his view. The Sages still refused. [A Halachic Argument](/daf/bava-metzia/59/a-halachic-argument) brings the Maharsha, who reads each wonder as a logical argument.

olam-haba.heading: Olam Haba in the Gemara: Reward, Martyrs and the World to Come
olam-haba.description: Olam Haba in the Gemara: the martyrs of Lod (Bava Basra 10b), Hillel and Shevna's deal (Sotah 21a) and King Menashe's share (Sanhedrin 102b).
olam-haba.intro:
The Gemara offers rare glimpses of the World to Come. On Bava Basra 10b, Yosef the son of Rebbe Yehoshua briefly died and saw "an inverted world." He heard that those executed by the government hold a place so exalted that no one can stand there. The Gemara concludes this means the martyrs of Lod, Luleyanus and Pappas. They falsely confessed to the murder of Trajan's daughter to save the Jewish community. [A Holy Place in the World to Come](/daf/bava-basra/10/a-holy-place-in-the-world-to-come) brings Rav Chaim Shmuelevitz. He applied this to soldiers who gave their lives protecting Jews.

Can a share in Olam Haba be bought? On Sotah 21a, Shevna offered his brother Hillel half his wealth for half of Hillel's reward for Torah. A Heavenly voice scorned the offer. [Is Olam Haba for Sale?](/daf/sotah/21/is-olam-haba-for-sale) explains, with the Tashbetz and the Rema, that one can share reward only by enabling learning in advance. [Is Olam Habah for Sale?](/daf/shekalim/14/is-olam-habah-for-sale) adds the Netziv's parable: mitzvos are like medicine, and only the one who takes them benefits.

The Mishnah in Sanhedrin lists three kings with no share in the World to Come, including Menashe. In [Breaking Bread](/daf/sanhedrin/102/breaking-bread), Menashe appears to Rav Ashi in a dream and teaches him where to cut the bread for ha'motzi. Rebbe Yehuda holds that Menashe does have a share, because he did teshuvah. Even the worst sinner can find his way back.

moshiach-and-geulah.heading: Moshiach and Geulah in the Gemara: Preparing for the Redemption
moshiach-and-geulah.description: Moshiach in the Gemara: Rome claims its reward (Avodah Zarah 2a), the birth pangs of Moshiach (Sanhedrin 98b) and the hopeful takanah of Rosh Hashanah 30a.
moshiach-and-geulah.intro:
The Gemara looks ahead to the days of Moshiach. Avodah Zarah 2a describes a scene that has not happened yet. Hashem will hold up a Torah and invite all who occupied themselves with it to collect their reward. Rome will claim its markets, bathhouses and gold were all built so the Jews could learn. In [Road to Redemption](/daf/avodah-zarah/2/road-to-redemption), Rabbi Sebrow brings the Chiddushei HaGriz: Rome is foolish, not lying, because Hashem directed its deeds toward Torah. He shows it with Derech HaOfel, a road paved for a pope in 1964 that now carries Torah learners.

How does one prepare? On Sanhedrin 98b, Rabbah feared the travails before Moshiach. Abaye reminded him that Torah and chesed protect a person, and Rabbah answered that his sins might still expose him. [Keep Calm And Chesed On](/daf/yevamos/105/keep-calm-and-chesed-on) uses this to weigh Torah study against acts of kindness.

Hope matters too. Rosh Hashanah 30a records two takanos of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai after the Churban. In [Takana Considerations](/daf/rosh-hashanah/30/takana-considerations), Rav Moshe Betzalel explains why they came together. The first, taking the lulav all seven days, saddened the people. The second, about new grain, showed that the Beis HaMikdash might be rebuilt that very year.

Some questions will wait for Eliyahu HaNavi. The Gemara's unresolved "Teiku" is read as a hint that Eliyahu will answer them. On Bava Metzia 114b, Eliyahu reveals he is from Shevet Binyamin, not a kohen. [Eliyahu HaNavi Zachur La’Tov](/daf/bava-metzia/114/eliyahu-hanavi-zachur-latov) explains his hint about Moshiach ben Yosef.

tzaddikim.heading: Tzaddikim in the Gemara: Protection, Merit and Humility
tzaddikim.description: Tzaddikim in the Gemara: the donkey of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair (Chullin 7a), Rava and Rav Ilish (Bava Basra 133b) and the rainbow (Kesubos 77b).
tzaddikim.intro:
The Gemara teaches that Hashem guards the righteous. On Chullin 7a, the donkey of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair refused to eat barley that had not been tithed. The Gemara draws a sweeping rule. If Hashem does not let the animals of tzaddikim stumble, surely He protects the tzaddikim themselves. [The Pious Donkey, the Muzzled Camels, and the Elephant in the Room](/daf/chullin/7/the-pious-donkey-the-muzzled-camels-and-the-elephant-in-the-room) asks why Avraham Avinu's camels needed muzzles. One answer, from Rabbi Eliyahu Mizrachi, is that we do not rely on miracles.

How far does that protection reach? On Bava Basra 133b, Rava corrected Rav Ilish, who was embarrassed. Rava comforted him: Hashem made sure Rava was there the one time Rav Ilish would have erred. In [Of Mules and Mussar](/daf/bava-basra/133/of-mules-and-mussar), Rabbi Sebrow tells how the Rashbam almost boarded a wagon pulled by a horse and a mule. His brother Rabbeinu Tam stopped him. Rabbeinu Tam held that this special protection applies only to forbidden foods.

Tzaddikim can protect the whole world. On Kesubos 77b, Rebbe Shimon bar Yochai asked Rebbe Yehoshua ben Levi if a rainbow was seen in his lifetime. He said yes, though none was, out of humility. [A G-d-Based Moral Bucket List](/daf/kesubos/77/a-g-d-based-moral-bucket-list) explains why he kept up his humility even in Gan Eden. And [A Tzaddik Before Birth?](/daf/yoma/82/a-tzaddik-before-birth) tells of a pregnant woman on Yom Kippur. She held back from eating and gave birth to Rebbe Yochanan (Yoma 82b).

dreams.heading: Dreams in the Gemara: Signs, Spirits and Halachah
dreams.description: Dreams in the Gemara: Rebbe Yannai's splintered reed (Yevamos 93a), the Maharam's dream on a sick worker (Kiddushin 17a) and spirits in a cemetery.
dreams.intro:
The Gemara takes dreams seriously, but carefully. On Yevamos 93a, Rebbe Yannai separated terumah and maaser for fruit that had not yet arrived, so he could enjoy it on Shabbos. Then he dreamed the words "a splintered reed" and feared he had erred. His rebbe, Rebbe Chiya, read the dream the other way: he had ruled according to the truth. [Oneg Shabbos](/daf/yevamos/93/oneg-shabbos) shows how oneg Shabbos allows special leniencies.

Can a dream decide halachah? Kiddushin 17a rules that if an eved Ivri falls ill, his master absorbs the loss. The Maharam MiRottenberg said a different explanation was revealed to him in a dream. In [The Price to Pay](/daf/kiddushin/17/the-price-to-pay), Rabbi Sebrow notes that the Shach was not impressed, since dreams carry little halachic weight.

[Rosh Hashana in a Cemetery](/daf/rosh-hashanah/16/rosh-hashana-in-a-cemetery) retells a story from Berachos 18b. A pious man slept in a cemetery on Rosh Hashanah night and overheard two spirits discussing hail. He planted late and his crops were saved. The Noda B'Yehuda explains that the whole episode was a dream, a reward for his tzedakah.

segulos.heading: Segulos in the Gemara: Signs, Customs and Their Limits
segulos.description: Segulos in the Gemara: forbidden divination and Eliezer's sign (Chullin 95a), spilled wine as a blessing (Eruvin 65a) and Rebbi Yehuda HaChassid's will.
segulos.intro:
Chazal take signs seriously, but they also set limits. Chullin 95a discusses nichush, forbidden divination. It names two classic examples: Eliezer's sign at the well and Yonasan's sign before attacking the Philistines. Tosfos asks how such tzaddikim could rely on signs. In [Seizing the Spark: Preserving Inspiration in Halacha and Life](/daf/chullin/95/seizing-the-spark-preserving-inspiration-in-halacha-and-life), Rabbi Sebrow brings their answers. He also shares the Gur Aryeh's insight: Eliezer gave Rivka the bracelets at once so as not to lose his moment of inspiration.

Some segulos grow out of a Gemara. Eruvin 65a says that a house where wine is not spilled like water is not among the blessed. [Don’t Cry Over Spilled Wine](/daf/eruvin/65/dont-cry-over-spilled-wine) traces the Rema's custom of spilling wine at Havdalah. The Taz reads the Gemara as praise for one who does not get angry over spills. Yet he still let his cup overflow.

Others come from tzaddikim. [Cautionary Customs](/daf/menachos/29/cautionary-customs) examines the will of Rebbi Yehuda HaChassid, which warns against marrying someone with a parent's name. The Noda BeYehuda held it was meant for his descendants. Yet Rav Moshe Shternbuch tells how the Steipler had a sick man's wife change her name, and he recovered. [Happy Birthday](/daf/avodah-zarah/5/happy-birthday) collects views on birthdays. Some treat the day as a segulah for blessing and a time for personal requests.

angels-and-sheidim.heading: Angels and Sheidim in the Gemara: The Hidden World at Work
angels-and-sheidim.description: Angels and Sheidim in the Gemara: Rav Chisda and the Angel of Death (Makkos 10), angels in the Purim story (Megillah 15b) and Sanhedrin 38b.
angels-and-sheidim.intro:
The Gemara describes malachim at work in our world. In Makkos 10, the Malach HaMaves could not take Rav Chisda, because he never stopped learning. Only when a pillar of the beis midrash snapped, startling him, did he die. In [Lifelong Goal](/daf/makkos/10/lifelong-goal), Rabbi Sebrow brings the Chofetz Chaim's question: why not take him while he ate or slept? Because even Rav Chisda's eating and sleeping were service of Hashem.

Angels also shaped the Purim story. Megillah 15b says an angel gave Esther irresistible charm. Angels disguised as men uprooted Achashverosh's trees, saying Haman had ordered it. Another pushed Haman onto Esther's couch. [Royal Motives](/daf/megillah/15/royal-motives) shows how many miracles it took, and why Esther still worked to make the people daven harder.

The angels can teach us, too. On Sanhedrin 38b, Hashem consulted the angels before creating man. [Words of Advice](/daf/sanhedrin/38/words-of-advice) explains, with Rashi, that this teaches humility: seek advice even from those of lesser stature. When the angels wished to sing as the Egyptians drowned, Hashem stopped them (Megillah 10b). [Our Better Halves](/daf/megillah/17/our-better-halves) ties this to the half Hallel of the last days of Pesach.

The Gemara also tells of spirits. In [Rosh Hashana in a Cemetery](/daf/rosh-hashanah/16/rosh-hashana-in-a-cemetery), a pious man overhears two spirits reveal the year's decree about crops.

nevuah.heading: Nevuah in the Gemara: The Lives of the Nevi'im
nevuah.description: Nevuah in the Gemara: Hashem spoke to Yonah only twice (Yevamos 98a), Menashe's charge against Yeshayahu (Yevamos 49b) and Elisha's bears (Sotah 46b).
nevuah.intro:
The Gemara looks closely at the lives of the Nevi'im. On Yevamos 98a, Rebbe Akiva says Hashem spoke to Yonah only twice, not three times. The Radak explains that this was a punishment for refusing to go to Ninveh. In [Yonah & His Prophesies](/daf/yevamos/98/yonah-his-prophesies), Rabbi Sebrow works through Tosfos and the Maharsha on the verses where Hashem does speak to Yonah again.

Yeshayahu HaNavi was killed by his own grandson. Yevamos 49b says King Menashe declared him a false prophet. [Leave the Rest to Hashem](/daf/yevamos/49/leave-the-rest-to-hashem) goes back to Berachos 10a. Yeshayahu told the sick Chizkiyahu that he was punished for not marrying, and that the future must be left to Hashem. [When To Say It In Aramaic](/daf/pesachim/87/when-to-say-it-in-aramaic) explains one of Menashe's charges. The Torah says Hashem is close whenever we call, yet Yeshayahu said to seek Him "when He can be found."

On Sotah 46b, youths mocked Elisha HaNavi after he healed Yericho's water and ruined their water business. Bears came out of a forest and attacked them. Was the forest a miracle too? [A Miracle Within a Miracle](/daf/sotah/46/a-miracle-within-a-miracle) brings the Steipler. The youths failed to see that their livelihood was already a miracle hidden in nature.

avodah-zarah.heading: Avodah Zarah in the Gemara: Images, Bowing and the Golden Calf
avodah-zarah.description: Avodah Zarah in the Gemara: Rabban Gamliel's moon pictures (Avodah Zarah 43), Mordechai and Haman (Sanhedrin 61b) and the copper snake (Chullin 6b).
avodah-zarah.intro:
The Torah's ban on idolatry reaches beyond bowing to statues. In Avodah Zarah 43, the Gemara asks how Rabban Gamliel could own pictures of the moon. He used them to question witnesses about the new moon, yet such images are forbidden. [Over the Moon](/daf/avodah-zarah/43/over-the-moon) explains the answers: a non-Jew drew them, and as Nasi he was above suspicion. Rabbi Sebrow adds Rav Dovid Feinstein's view on moon pictures in children's textbooks.

What about bowing? Sanhedrin 61b allows bowing to a person out of respect. Abaye and Rava argue about one who serves an idol out of fear. [Should Mordechai Have Bowed to Haman?](/daf/sanhedrin/61/should-mordechai-have-bowed-to-haman) uses this to ask why Mordechai refused. Perhaps Haman wore idols, as the Terumas HaDeshen holds. Or perhaps, as Tosafos suggests, Mordechai chose to make a kiddush Hashem.

The Gemara also looks at idolatry in our own history. On Sanhedrin 6a, Aharon saw Chur lying dead and let the people make the Golden Calf rather than kill him too. In [Choosing The Lesser Evil](/daf/sanhedrin/6/choosing-the-lesser-evil), the Meiri says this was wrong, since one may not call a sin permitted. Chullin 6b tells how people worshipped Moshe's copper snake 700 years later, until Chizkiyahu destroyed it. [Serpentine Path to Prominence](/daf/chullin/6/serpentine-path-to-prominence) asks why righteous kings before him left it standing.

medicine-and-health.heading: Medicine and Health in the Gemara: Healthy Living and Pikuach Nefesh
medicine-and-health.description: Medicine and Health in the Gemara: overeating (Gittin 70a), walking after a meal (Bava Metzia 113b), remote danger (Kesubos 39a) and bikur cholim.
medicine-and-health.intro:
The Gemara gives practical health advice. Gittin 70a warns that one who fills his belly with anything will become sick. Eliyahu HaNavi told Rebbe Nosson to stop eating when two-thirds full. In [Eat but Don’t Overeat](/daf/gittin/70/eat-but-dont-overeat), Rabbi Sebrow brings the Raavad: holding back for the sake of Heaven is greater than a fast. The Kaf HaChaim says this applies even to Shabbos meals.

On Bava Metzia 113b, a creditor must leave a debtor two beds, one for eating and one for sleeping. Shmuel warns that sleeping right after a meal, without a few steps, is harmful. [Walks of Life](/daf/bava-metzia/113/walks-of-life) explains that Chazal knew people need a push to keep healthy habits.

Saving a life overrides almost everything, yet there are limits. On Kesubos 39a, the Sages tell a person to rely on "Hashem protects the simpletons" rather than use a forbidden safeguard. [To Save a Life](/daf/kesubos/39/to-save-a-life) weighs the Binyan Tziyon and the Achiezer on remote dangers. It also brings Rav Shlomo Zalman's view on getting a vaccine on Shabbos. [Required Eating on Yom Kippur?](/daf/shevuos/28/required-eating-on-yom-kippur) tells how Rav Yisrael Salanter had his kehillah eat on Yom Kippur during the 1848 cholera epidemic.

Caring for the sick is a mitzvah too. Bava Metzia 30b derives bikur cholim from a verse. [Visiting the Sick](/daf/bava-metzia/30/visiting-the-sick) cites the Rema: a visitor who did not daven for the patient has not fulfilled the mitzvah. Rav Moshe Feinstein held that a phone call fulfills it in part.

aveilus.heading: Aveilus in the Gemara: Mourning, Bad News and Comfort
aveilus.description: Aveilus in the Gemara: how Rav broke sad news to Rabbi Chiya (Moed Katan 20a), letting the mourner speak first (Moed Katan 28b) and a kohen's tumah.
aveilus.intro:
On Moed Katan 20a, Rav arrived from Bavel and his uncle Rabbi Chiya asked, "Is father alive?" Rav answered with questions of his own. From that, Rabbi Chiya understood that his brother and sister had died. He had his shoes removed, but still planned to go to the bathhouse that day. In [Spreading The News](/daf/moed-katan/20/spreading-the-news), Rabbi Sebrow draws the halachos. One who hears late mourns only briefly. There is no duty to share bad news, it should be told indirectly, and one may not lie. He adds how the Alter of Slabodka hid a father's death from the young Rav Ruderman so he could finish Shas.

How do we comfort a mourner? Rebbe Yochanan teaches that visitors should not speak until the mourner speaks first (Moed Katan 28b). [A Halacha That’s Clear-Cut](/daf/moed-katan/28/a-halacha-thats-clear-cut) brings Rav Moshe Feinstein. "HaMakom yenachem" is a blessing, not the comfort itself, so it may be said first. Real comfort comes from talking with the mourner.

Mourning can also clash with other mitzvos. Zevachim 100a tells of Yosef HaKohen, whose wife died on Erev Pesach. His friends forced him under the tent so he would not bring the Korban Pesach as an onen. [A Forced Tumah](/daf/zevachim/100/a-forced-tumah) shows how he then cared for his orphans. And [The Great Leap Forward](/daf/shekalim/2/the-great-leap-forward) asks when to observe a yahrzeit in a leap year. The Rema says Adar Rishon, and the Mishnah Berurah advises fasting in both months.

gedolim.heading: Gedolim in the Gemara: Learning From Great Rabbanim
gedolim.description: Gedolim in the Gemara: Rav Huna sends Rabbah to Rav Chisda (Bava Metzia 33), the Chasam Sofer's misquoted quip (Kiddushin 8a) and tributes to gedolim.
gedolim.intro:
The Gemara shows that we learn from great people far beyond the page. On Bava Metzia 33, Rav Huna rebuked his son Rabbah for avoiding Rav Chisda's lessons. Rabbah said Rav Chisda only taught him about healthy living. That, said Rav Huna, is exactly why you should go. In [Da’as Torah](/daf/bava-metzia/33/daas-torah), Rabbi Sebrow recalls his rosh yeshiva, Rav Henoch Leibowitz. A gadol applies the Torah's principles to life questions, just as Rav Moshe Feinstein applied sources to new halachic questions.

Watching gedolim takes care. In [A Kohen By Any Other Name](/daf/kiddushin/8/a-kohen-by-any-other-name), Rav Moshe put down a milk carton at a bris. People decided he rejected its hechsher, but the carton was simply empty. The Chasam Sofer once made a clever remark at a pidyon haben, based on Tosfos on Kiddushin 8a. He was horrified to hear it quoted as halachah.

Rabbi Sebrow also writes tributes. [Glimpse of a Gadol: Rav Dovid Feinstein, zt’l](/beyond-the-daf/glimpse-of-a-gadol-rav-dovid-feinstein-ztl) shows a gadol who kept his own chumros without burdening others. He bought challos after Pesach from a Jewish bakery that had been closed for nine days. [Sar HaTorah: Rav Chaim Kanievsky, zt”l](/beyond-the-daf/sar-hatorah-rav-chaim-kanievsky-zt-l) tells how Rav Chaim stayed learning at the back of his son's cheder so the boy would not cry. [Our Rosh Yeshiva](/beyond-the-daf/our-rosh-yeshiva) recalls Rav Henoch Leibowitz handing a bachur his own yarmulke instead of rebuking him.

technology-and-halacha.heading: Technology and Halacha in the Gemara: Old Principles, New Machines
technology-and-halacha.description: Technology and Halacha: Moshe's "autopen" and voice devices (Menachos 30a), lightbulbs for Havdalah (Pesachim 8a) and the crockpot (Bava Basra 19a).
technology-and-halacha.intro:
The Gemara never saw a freezer or a crockpot, yet its principles reach them. Menachos 30a asks who wrote the last eight pesukim of the Torah. If Moshe died on Shabbos, how could he have written them that day? In [The Modern Autopen](/daf/menachos/30/the-modern-autopen-menachos -30), Rabbi Sebrow brings the Shelah HaKadosh. Moshe used hashbuas kulmus, a supernatural way of making the pen write. That leads to voice-activated devices and self-driving cars on Shabbos, where the Steipler and Rav Chaim Kanievsky reason differently.

Pesachim 8a prefers a torch for Havdalah but a single candle for bedikas chametz. [Sparking Debate](/daf/pesachim/8/sparking-debate) tells how Rav Chaim Ozer Grodzinski allowed a lightbulb for Havdalah. He wanted to publicize that turning one on is lighting a fire. Most poskim permit a flashlight for bedikas chametz, and Rav Moshe Feinstein preferred it.

Everyday appliances raise questions too. In [Machmir Or Make Cool?](/daf/kesubos/6/machmir-or-make-cool), Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach permits opening a freezer on Shabbos, since the compressor starts only indirectly. [Crockpot Controversies](/daf/bava-basra/19/crockpot-controversies) builds on Tosfos on Bava Basra 19a about flintstones. Rav Moshe explained that Chazal's decree of hatmana covers only what they listed. Rav Pinchas Scheinberg applied the same logic to the crockpot.

jewish-history.heading: Jewish History in the Gemara: Martyrs, Fasts and Turning Points
jewish-history.description: Jewish History in the Gemara: the dead of Beitar and the end of the spies' decree (Taanis 30b), Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava (Sanhedrin 14a), Bava Kamma 77a.
jewish-history.intro:
The Gemara remembers moments that shaped our people and our calendar. Taanis 30b asks why Tu B'Av was so joyous. Rav Masneh says it was the day the Romans finally allowed burial of the slain of Beitar. Miraculously, the bodies had not decayed. Another reason: that day the generation of the spies stopped dying in the desert. In [Who Knows Fifteen?](/daf/taanis/30/who-knows-fifteen), Rabbi Sebrow works through the numbers in the Midrash.

Our fast days hold history as well. [Ta’anis In Teves](/daf/megillah/9/taanis-in-teves) explains the old custom to fast on the eighth and ninth of Teves. On the eighth, King Ptolemy had 72 elders translate the Torah into Greek, a sad day despite its miracle (Megillah 9). The ninth may mark the passing of Ezra, and also the massacre of the Jews of Granada.

The Gemara also honors those who gave their lives for Torah. After Hadrian banned semichah, Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava ordained the next generation's leading sages between Usha and Shafram. He stayed behind to block the Romans, who killed him with 300 spears (Sanhedrin 14a). [No Ordinary Ordination](/daf/sanhedrin/92/no-ordinary-ordination) links his death to a teaching on Sanhedrin 92a. [A Time for Torah](/daf/bava-kamma/77/a-time-for-torah) brings a tradition from the Bnei Yissaschar. The two long Tosfos on Bava Kamma 77a were written by the Baalei Tosfos on their last night before martyrdom.

eretz-yisrael.heading: Eretz Yisrael in the Gemara: Its Holiness and Living There
eretz-yisrael.description: Eretz Yisrael in the Gemara: Kalev's prayer in Chevron (Sotah 34b), dividing the land by lot (Zevachim 119b) and Rebbe Zeira's move (Chullin 18b).
eretz-yisrael.intro:
Love of Eretz Yisrael runs through the Gemara. On Sotah 34b, Kalev went alone to Chevron to pray that he would be saved from the spies' plot. He was rewarded with Chevron as his inheritance. In [The Power to Withstand the Pressure](/daf/sotah/34/the-power-to-withstand-the-pressure), Rabbi Sebrow brings Rav Avrohom Trop. Kalev spoke as the spies did, yet his love for the land stayed whole. He also tells how Rav Kanarek's father defied his neighbors and sent his sons to yeshiva, which later saved them.

The land itself was divided with care. Zevachim 119b explains that Shiloh is called "nachalah" because Yehoshua divided the land there by lottery for seven tribes. [Lots Of Land: Daf 119b in Zevachim](/daf/zevachim/119/lots-of-land-daf-119b-in-zevachim) applies this to drawing lots for honors in shul.

Living in the land changes a person's halachah. On Chullin 18b, Rebbe Zeira fasted a hundred fasts and moved to Eretz Yisrael. There he ate meat that Bavel forbade, because one follows the customs of a new home. [A Tale of Two Riddles: The Vacuuming Wife and the Havdala Surprise](/daf/chullin/18/a-tale-of-two-riddles-the-vacuuming-wife-and-the-havdala-surprise) applies this to Yom Tov Sheni. The Chazon Ish rules that one who decides to settle there in the middle of Yom Tov Sheni makes Havdalah at once.

The holiness remains even after the Churban. [Still Sacred](/daf/zevachim/107/still-sacred) explains the dispute about whether the Beis HaMikdash site keeps its sanctity. The Rambam and the Mishnah Berurah rule that it does. The Steipler and Rav Shach ruled that no one should go up on Har HaBayis.

non-jews.heading: Non-Jews in the Gemara: Converts, Neighbors and the Nations
non-jews.description: Non-Jews in the Gemara: Haman's descendants learning Torah (Gittin 57b), Shmuel and Avleit (Avodah Zarah 30a) and the non-Jew at the Korban Pesach.
non-jews.intro:
Gittin 57b makes a surprising list. Naaman became a ger toshav, and Nevuzaradan became a full convert. Haman's descendants learned Torah in Bnei Brak, and Sancheriv's descendants taught Torah in public. In [Converting Bad Into Good](/daf/gittin/57/converting-bad-into-good), Rabbi Sebrow asks how a descendant of Haman could convert, if converts from Amalek are not accepted. The Kli Chemda answers that Haman sold himself as Mordechai's slave, which erased his lineage. Rav Yaakov Kamenetsky adds that these enemies unintentionally caused a kiddush Hashem, and Hashem does not withhold any reward.

The Gemara also shows respect between Jews and gentiles. On Avodah Zarah 30a, Avleit, a gentile scholar, was careful not to touch Shmuel's wine. Shmuel told him not to worry, since the wine was cooked. [Mevushal or Lo Mevushal: That Is The Question](/daf/avodah-zarah/30/mevushal-or-lo-mevushal-that-is-the-question) explains why pasteurized wine counts as cooked for Rav Moshe Feinstein but not for Rav Elyashiv.

Sometimes non-Jews tested the Torah. In [A Case of Pikuach Nefesh](/daf/bava-kamma/60/a-case-of-pikuach-nefesh), two Roman officers study in a yeshiva and find one law they dislike. The Yam Shel Shlomo learns that the rabbis could not change the halachah even to avoid danger. [Who is Obligated?](/daf/chagigah/2/who-is-obligated) tells of a non-Jew who ate the Korban Pesach in disguise each year. Rabbi Yehudah ben Besaira told him to ask for the fat tail, which is burned on the Mizbeiach, and he was exposed.

animals.heading: Animals in the Gemara: Compassion, Kashrus and Halachah
animals.description: Animals in the Gemara: feeding wild dogs on Shabbos (Shabbos 155), an elephant as a sukkah wall (Sukkah 23), pets and muktzeh, and giraffe (Chullin 45a).
animals.intro:
The Gemara shows real concern for animals. Shabbos 155 teaches that one may not bother on Shabbos to feed animals that are not his. Yet one may give a little food to wild dogs, since their food is scarce. In [Dog Foodies](/daf/shabbos/155/dog-foodies), Rabbi Sebrow notes that the Magen Avraham calls this a mitzvah. He also explains how the Aruch HaShulchan defends feeding birds on Shabbos Shirah.

Animals turn up in surprising halachos. Sukkah 23 discusses using a live elephant as a sukkah wall, tied up so it cannot walk away. [A Sukkah Made Out of Elephants](/daf/sukkah/23/a-sukkah-made-out-of-elephants) asks whether mitzvah items should come only from kosher animals. Tosfos on Bava Metzia 46b says a cow counts as a utensil for a kinyan. In [Are Pets Muktzeh?](/daf/bava-metzia/46/are-pets-muktzeh), Rav Yaakov Hagiz uses this to rule that a singing bird is not muktzeh. Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach says the same of a seeing-eye dog.

Which animals may we eat? Chullin 45a says the whole length of the neck is fit for shechitah, so a giraffe's long neck is no obstacle. [From Savanna to Supper?](/daf/chullin/45/from-savanna-to-supper) shows that the real question is mesorah. The Pri Megadim and the Chazon Ish disagree, which decides the status of zebu and bison. And [The Test Of A Nest](/daf/chullin/138/the-test-of-a-nest) follows Rabbi Sebrow's own attempt at shiluach haken, with Rav Chaim Kanievsky's advice on eggs laid on one's property.

travel.heading: Travel in the Gemara: Davening on the Road and Tefillas HaDerech
travel.description: Travel in the Gemara: davening while riding (Berachos 30a), standing for avodah (Zevachim 23b), Tefillas HaDerech (Pesachim 104b) and a sinking ship.
travel.intro:
Halachah travels with us. On Berachos 30a, Rebbe rules that a rider need not get off his donkey to daven. The Mishnah Berurah explains that he would rush to continue his trip and lose his focus. In [Fasten Your Seatbelts](/daf/berachos/30/fasten-your-seatbelts), Rabbi Sebrow brings Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach. One should daven sitting on a plane rather than block the aisle or the bathrooms. But one should not daven while driving, since a car needs the driver's full attention.

Why do we stand for Shemoneh Esrei in the first place? Zevachim 23b rules that avodah done sitting is invalid, and tefillah takes the place of a korban. [Davening on a Plane](/daf/zevachim/23/davening-on-a-plane) adds the Rema's ruling. A rider who cannot step back after Shemoneh Esrei has his animal take three steps back. Rav Shlomo Zalman applies this to a wheelchair.

Why does Tefillas HaDerech not open with "Baruch atah"? [On the Way](/daf/pesachim/104/on-the-way) brings the Maharam MiRotenburg, who says it was meant to follow another berachah. So the Mishnah Berurah advises saying it after Asher Yatzar or an after-blessing. Tosfos on Pesachim 104b calls it a prayer phrased as a blessing. That is why Rav Shlomo Zalman allowed adding personal requests.

Travel can bring danger too. [Gold Overboard](/daf/bava-kamma/116/gold-overboard) works through Bava Kamma 116b. When cargo must be thrown off a sinking ship, Rashi says each traveler throws off the same weight.

daf-quiz.heading: Daf Quiz
daf-quiz.description: Daf Quiz: test yourself on covering the challah (Pesachim 100a), with three reasons from the Rishonim and fifteen questions, from Seudah Shlishis to cake.
daf-quiz.intro:
Why do we cover the challah on Shabbos? Pesachim 100a-b touches on the practice, and the Rishonim give three reasons. Rav Achai Gaon says it shows the meal is in honor of Shabbos. Another reason recalls the dew that covered the manna above and below. A third protects the challah from "shame," since on Shabbos we say the berachah on wine first.

In [A Challah Covering Quiz](/daf/pesachim/100/a-challah-covering-quiz-pesachim-100), Rabbi Sebrow turns these reasons into fifteen questions. Must you cover the challah at Seudah Shlishis? Is a clear plastic cover enough? What about a guest's own roll at a big Friday night meal, or cake at a Shabbos kiddush? Each answer depends on which reason applies. Along the way he brings Rav Moshe Feinstein, Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach and Rav Nissim Karelitz.

rodeif.heading: Rodeif in the Gemara: Stopping a Pursuer
rodeif.description: Rodeif in the Gemara: the pursuer, the mother in dangerous childbirth, and Sheva ben Bichri (Sanhedrin 72b), with Rav Elyashiv's ruling on a pilot.
rodeif.intro:
The Gemara in Sanhedrin teaches that one may stop a rodeif, a person pursuing another to kill him. The Rambam rules that anyone who sees the pursuer should stop him. Yet the Gemara also rules that once a baby is partly born, we may not harm it to save the mother. Rashi on Sanhedrin 72b compares the case of Sheva ben Bichri, whom a besieged city handed over to save itself.

Rabbi Sebrow explores these sources through two dramatic stories. In [Strings Attached](/daf/sanhedrin/72/strings-attached), a rescue pilot may fire on disguised commandos. In [When Do You Kill a Rodeif?](/daf/sanhedrin/72/when-do-you-kill-a-rodeif), a pilot is unknowingly carrying a deadly drug to sick campers. Is an unwitting pilot a rodeif? The Rambam and the Tiferes Yisrael point in different directions. Rav Elyashiv ruled that such a pilot is the opposite of a rodeif, since he is risking his life to save others.
